A search for similar-sign W boson pairs, consisting of either two charged leptons or a charged lepton and missing transverse momentum, has been carried out using 137 fb$^{-1}$ of LHC data collected at 13 TeV. Observed occurrences exceeding 4.3 standard deviations above background predictions include three instances of same-sign W$^+$W$^+$ production and one instance of same-sign W$^-$W$^-$ production. Also, this search is the first to yield data-driven limits on standard model W boson pair production, providing the most restrictive lower bound to date on the phase factor $\mathcal{K}$ governing the ratio of $\mathrm{W}\mathrm{W}$ to $\mathrm{W}\mathrm{Z}$ production probabilities at high $\mathrm{W}\mathrm{Z}$ mass. Furthermore, this search offers the most sensitive constraint on the coupling between the $\mathrm{W}$ boson and fermions, with a 5.5 (22) standard deviation suppression of the $\mathrm{W}\mathrm{W}$ production probability governing the $\mathrm{W}\mathrm{W}\mathrm{H}$ ($\mathrm{W}\mathrm{W}\mathrm{Z}$) process at high $\mathrm{W}\mathrm{Z}$ mass as theory suggests but is instead 3.7 (0.7) standard deviations above background predictions for $\mathrm{W}\mathrm{W}\mathrm{H}$ and

Recently, video colorization techniques are gaining more attention, with current approaches either relying on rigid pose estimation or applying unsupervised methods with limited results due to their inability to incorporate prior knowledge. Our proposed technique, FlexColor, offers a flexible and effective solution for colorizing videos with arbitrary poses by incorporating 3D human mesh predictions. Similar to other unsupervised methods, FlexColor uses a neural network to find a shape that minimizes the difference between predicted and target images, but to enhance its accuracy, we added a constraint that uses a prior mesh model. This technique allows for flexible applications on new poses without requiring additional training, while also providing improved performance compared to existing unsupervised methods and reducing errors compared to rigid pose-based techniques.

We introduce a new $P(q)$ model which includes non-flat space, defined by $R_{\text{GC}}(s) = 1 + 0.0011\left(\frac{s+1}{s-1}\right)$ and $q(s) = 1 + 0.00054\left(\frac{s+1}{s-1}\right)^2$, parameterized such that $A_L = 1$. This model is then analyzed using Planck data 2015, with findings showing discrepancies in cosmological parameter constraints between it and the original $P(q)$ model. Furthermore, while the original $P(q)$ model yielded parameters consistent with $\Lambda$CDM, our new model reveals a $0.05\%$ deviation from its value for $A_L(1-H^2)/c^2 and a $0.7\sigma$ deviation for $N_{\text{eff}}$, with the remainder of parameters showing normal linear behavior. We observe that although Planck data exclusively favors our new model, they are computationally equivalent within a $0.9\%$ difference.

In collaborative coding projects, multiple researchers contribute and maintain shared files through their repository management systems, such as Git. These systems store all historical versions of shared files, but the developers of these systems do not utilize this information effectively. Our study reveals that how contributors update and keep shared files varies significantly across different projects. Furthermore, our analysis shows that identifying and removing outdated code from shared files during development can be beneficial. To achieve this, developers need to understand the purpose of the code and the context in which it is used. Our research demonstrates that the effectiveness of this process also relies on the maintenance practices of the project's repository, including the practices of maintaining shared files and the project's documentation. Our findings suggest that a customized, project-dependent approach is necessary to efficiently remove outdated code.

Our detailed analysis of the multi-color photometric data collected from the study of BD And reveals that this star is part of a binary system consisting of at least two stars with significantly different sizes. These observations also hint at the presence of an even larger third star. Using various techniques to extract the binary signal, we identified a most likely period of 84.634 days and determined that the smaller star, with a size of approximately 12.65 R and 2.01 M, orbits the larger star, which has properties similar to the Sun, with a size of approximately 1.03 R and 1.04 M. Further examination of the data suggests the possibility of a third star, detected as a SEED, with a size of approximately 2.96 R and 3.05 M, based on varying results. This potential third star, with a 3:1 resonance and epicyclic motion, causes slight discrepancies in the fitted patterns. These findings will be further confirmed by next observations and can lead to a more precise understanding of the system.

This research shows that given any $N$-dimensional manifold and an arbitrary smooth metric, there will always exist a solution to the Yamabe flow that is invariant under a group of isometries of maximal type. It will also be a conformal vector that varies linearly with time. This result has been proven for manifolds with a group of isometries that preserves the metric. As a consequence, it has been proven that there exists a solution to the inverse Yamabe problem in a manifold with a group of isometries that preserves the metric.

To capture user preferences from diverse item aspects, we develop a self-attention based pre-trainning method for recommendation systems. Specifically, we introduce the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, which combines multiple items to extract general user preferences and integrates learned information with existing interaction matrices to update preference mappings. By leveraging GAPE, our proposed Self-Aptation Preference Learning (SAPL) method surpasses existing methods in various benchmark datasets. Moreover, SAPL's effectiveness is further validated by demonstrating its superiority on two downstream tasks - item ranking and cross-stitch personalization.

We develop an obstruction theory for symplectic sheaves of type $(\spadesuit, \spadesuit)$ on smooth projective varieties. Specifically, we establish that the space of representations of the Lusztig's braid group acting on the hypercohomology spaces is a finite-dimensional manifold. Furthermore, we determine that the obstructions to the existence of symplectic embeddings reside in the even-dimensional components of these manifolds.

We employ generating functions to identify symmetries and divisibility properties of integer partitions that have specific multiples of certain numbers within them. These findings have practical implications for understanding the partition function of a number and its connections to number theory more broadly.

We investigate weighted least squares methods for finite difference approximations of higher-order partial differential equations, focusing on when the weights can ensure stability and optimality with exact sample data. Our work is related to the use of regularization methods and optimal scaling in statistical modeling and least squares regression. We establish an expression for the stability of weighted least squares schemes and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality. We then apply these findings to second and fourth-order partial differential equations, identifying specific weight functions that provide stable and optimal approximations. We confirm the efficiency of these weights through numerical experiments and highlight their potential applications in mathematical statistics and least squares regression.

Our research explores X(3872) particle formation in the extremely hot and dense environments that existed in the early universe, specifically following the Big Bang. To advance our understanding, we simulated the hadronic phase and tracked the formation of X(3872) using relativistic hydrodynamics. We considered various internal structures of the X(3872), such as a compactly bound state and a more spread-out state with a short-range interaction, to study their respective impacts on reaction rates and initial conditions. We discovered that the internal structure significantly affects both the reaction rates and the pre-existing conditions in the hadronic phase. Consequently, this influences theoretical estimates of the X(3872) mass and formation temperature. Our study also found that the X(3872) is formed more rapidly in the more spread-out configuration. We have provided a detailed mathematical representation of the X(3872) formation process and specified the relevant physical parameters that govern this process. Our research demonstrates that the X(3872) formation process is distinct from typical hadronic reactions and highlights the significance of understanding the microphysical processes behind its discovery.

A detailed examination of the interacting components in disordered semiconductors like Si:P reveals that Kondo-like behavior arises from magnetically responsive carriers rather than electrons. The moment associated with the carrier is stabilized by the strong magnetic influence of the host site and its surrounding lattice and is influenced by exchange with carrier spin. The complexity of this problem is resolved by comparing experimental results with calculations of the Si:P system, which demonstrates that Kondo behavior can be solely attributed to interactions involving carriers by accounting for electron spin coupling with both the host and carrier moments.

We derive the exchange relations for the generalized standard model of the finite classical Coxeter group Bn in terms of a parameterized set of reflections. By applying this definition, we determine the exchange laws for each generalized standard element in Bn. It's demonstrated that the exchange laws depend on the Coxeter length and descent set of Bn. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the generalized standard elements of Bn and those of An+, displaying symmetry in their exchange relations.

We analyze the impact of explicit symmetry breaking in scalar field theories using a novel approach. The approach relies on a transformation that exposes U(1) symmetry breaking, allowing for a clear derivation of its consequences. Our study reveals that even with explicit symmetry breaking, U(1) symmetry is conserved in certain situations. Furthermore, this approach enables the creation of anomalous Ward identities, which provides a new method for calculating loop corrections to symmetry-breaking terms. The method is versatile and can be applied to a range of symmetry situations.

When robots learn from experience, they typically assume that past events are drawn from a probability distribution that can be identified through a statistical model. However, in real-world settings, this model assumption often doesn't hold, leading to flawed learning outcomes due to unaccounted confounding elements. These elements, often present in practical scenarios, lead to misguided conclusions and reduce the reliability of learned models. To resolve this issue, we've developed a hierarchical Bayesian framework that recognizes the generation of observations as a complex process affected by these confounding elements and incorporates their uncertainty in the learning process. This new model also offers an efficient way to handle large datasets by applying the loopy belief propagation algorithm. Through theoretical analysis and practical testing, we've demonstrated that our framework has the capacity to quantify the uncertainty associated with its own accuracy, thereby providing guarantees about performance in new, unseen scenarios. We've put our model to the test in simulation environments and used it successfully to predict the movement of humans and animals from previous experiences.

Let $X$ be a topological space and $H$ be a family of continuous functions from $X$ to $\mathbb{R}$, where $X$ may be real or not. The space $\tilde{X}_H$ represents a compactification of $X$ with respect to $H$. In $\tilde{X}_H$, we define two topologies, the whisker topology $W\tilde{X}_H$ and the lasso topology $L\tilde{X}_H$, which are different but share a key characteristic when the space $X$ is metrizable or countable. However, there is an example that shows these topologies are not always equivalent when the space $X$ is not metrizable or countable. Nonetheless, there are certain conditions under which these topologies do compare as follows: if $X$ is metrizable or countable then $W\tilde{X}_H$ and $L\tilde{X}_H$ are equal, but if $X$ is not metrizable or countable then $W\tilde{X}_H$ and $L\tilde{X}_H$ are equal and $L\tilde{X}_H$ is first countable.

Recent research has integrated deep reinforcement learning into motion planning, creating policies that generate optimal trajectories on the go with little data. Although DRL methods leverage large datasets in training, the sampled trajectory distribution may not accurately represent real-world driving conditions due to policy sampling noise. Furthermore, motion planning DRL approaches often overlook the benefits of pre-trained driving skills, overlooking potential transfer learning and shape concert. To address these limitations, our research introduces DROPT, a dual-stage motion planning framework grounded in DRL. DROPT's motion planning stage adapts a pre-trained driving skill into a meaningful prior distribution through Bayesian learning. In contrast to typical DRL methods, which rely on policy sampling for test time, DROPT utilizes a prior-guided policy to maintain consistency between training and test times. In the optimization stage, a non-myopic sequential optimization process, inspired by prior knowledge, refines the prior-truncated search space. Through systematic policy sampling and optimization, DROPT identifies the optimal trajectory by exploring a diverse set of high-quality states. Empirical evaluations demonstrate DROPT's superiority over current state-of-the-art motion planning DRL approaches, showcasing the benefits of prior learning, Bayesian learning, and non-myopic optimization.

Our research resolves the long-standing issue of why black holes are so massive by introducing an Eddington-type gas disk accretion process. Model simulations indicate that this process accounts for the majority, approximately 90%, of the total mass of central black holes over typical star-formation durations. The Eddington-type accretion process significantly surpasses previously considered mechanisms, such as major mergers and gravitational wave emission, in terms of its impact on black hole mass growth. The findings of our research are consistent with observed black hole mass distributions and provide a theoretical explanation for their formation and growth.

Deep neural networks excel at various tasks such as image classification, yet they often fail to accurately identify uncertainties in their own conclusions. Incorporating uncertainty quantification into prediction results enhances reliability and strengthens trust in the model's capabilities. This paper presents an efficient approach to training classification networks that incorporates uncertainty by limiting the output probability distribution to a reliable, yet flexible bound. Unlike existing methods, our approach doesn't require pre-computing a confidence margin. Furthermore, the method facilitates seamless integration with a wide range of existing training pipelines. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets, showing improved accuracy and prediction reliability.

The influence of preprints on scientific communication has been a significant topic of discussion in the scientific community for many years. Certain fields, such as infectious disease research, have relied on preprints as critical tools for rapid dissemination, while others have been more hesitant due to concerns over the lack of peer review. Despite this, little is known about the overall effect of preprints on these fields. To address this knowledge gap, our research examines how preprints influence article speed and citation rates, using a dataset of over 1 million papers listed in the Web of Science, spanning 16 fields and years 2013 through 2018. Our analysis reveals that authors using preprints publish more quickly and receive more citations sooner, with fields related to COVID-19 showing the highest adoption rates of preprints. Notably, our study discovers varying levels of preprint impact across different fields, as in computer science, where it appears to have little effect, to neuroscience and psychiatry, where it increases citation rates by more than 60%. Our findings suggest the importance of distinguishing between different fields and research types when evaluating the influence of preprints. Additionally, they highlight potential applications in research evaluation and provide foundational insights for future studies on the effects of preprints.

One of the primary benefits of using AI and ML in laboratory testing is the reduction of human error. By automating data processing and analysis, clinicians can free up time to focus on high-value tasks, and state-of-the-art instruments can produce results with enhanced precision. However, contemporary laboratory information systems (LIS) are ill-equipped to manage the vast amounts of unstructured data generated during testing, leading to increased risks of medical mistakes. This research proposes an LIS enhancement using AI and ML capabilities to improve data analysis and comprehension, ultimately reducing human mistakes. An experimental system incorporating the proposed architecture was successfully deployed in a real-world laboratory setting, leading to an approximate 30% decrease in LIS-related errors. The project's code and data are publicly accessible on GitHub.

The vast number of equilibrium phases found in nature and their countless variations make it challenging to identify all possible material combinations through experimental means. Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of this complexity by predicting the composition of invariable phases based on machine learning models. Recent advances in using machine learning to forecast the properties of materials have been particularly successful. However, there is a distinct lack of comprehensive research regarding the use of machine learning to predict the formation of invariable phases and the mechanical properties of materials. To bridge this knowledge gap, we have compiled an exhaustive database of primary experimental data for binary and ternary invariable phases and their corresponding shear moduli. Subsequently, we employed least-squares support vector machines to develop predictive models for invariable phase compositions and mechanical properties. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our models, as they exhibit remarkable agreement with experimental data for both invariable phase compositions and shear moduli. Additionally, our models enable the prediction of new, potentially stable invariable phase zones that are in agreement with existing knowledge. The implications of these predictions will be the subject of a future study.

This study reconstructs the $T_{cc}^{++}$ in $B$-decays through $D\bar{D}$ or $D\bar{D}^*$ intermediate states. The $D\bar{D}^*$ contribution significantly surpasses the $D\bar{D}$ contribution in the resonance's total width, accounting for approximately $45\%$ of its decay width. The analysis considers resonances up to fifth order and models their interactions using the $K$-matrix approach.

The application of graph neural networks to subspace learning has gained significant interest in recent times. Graph neural networks are particularly well-suited for this task as they possess inherent capabilities to capture geometric structures within large datasets. However, incorporating graph neural networks into subspace learning poses a challenge due to the inherent absence of a predefined graph structure. To address this limitation, researchers have developed various methods to establish a meaningful graph structure for the task. In this study, a novel approach utilizing affinity graph neural networks is presented, where the graph structure is derived from the neural network's embedding of the data points. The proposed model combines state-of-the-art methods with additional enhancements, incorporating orthogonal projection and a weighted loss function. The efficacy of the model is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on multiple partial partial less than subspace learning datasets.

In this study, we comprehensiveely solve the Sidon set issue for the finite affine plane, drawing inspiration from a corresponding solution proposed by Billingsley and Street for the projective plane. We approach this problem by the method of reduction, proposing a revised problem which exhibits equivalent Sidon set properties. Building on this idea, we extend Billingsley and Street's concept of hyperbolas to ellipses, establishing the ellipse equation based on a specific back-coupling constant. Moreover, we introduce the concept of focus-translation congruences, essentially equivalent to hyperbolas, and identify unique properties within the affine plane. Additionally, in addressing intersections of sidon sets, we introduce the concept of complementary hyperbolas and establish a complement of a sidon set when intersected with a complementary hyperbola. Furthermore, in exploring sidon set extensions, we identify translation congruences and focus-translation congruences as potential candidates for extensions, confirming this possibility for hyperbolas and ellipses.

Researchers examining binary matrices constructed from random sampling often focus on the column space when investigating its fundamental properties. To address questions related to the column space, researchers often resort to extremely computationally demanding methods such as the Lattice Basis Reduction algorithm. As a result, studies are usually carried out with small-scale data. To address this limitation, this study proposes an efficient and straightforward approach to generating 'typical' binary matrices. By employing this approach, this study demonstrates the existence of a binary matrix containing at least m linearly independent columns. Additionally, this study explores various extensions to the original problem, offering both strengthened and independent numerical evidence. Furthermore, this study examines binary matrices constructed using non-uniform sampling and reveals significant differences in their structural properties when compared to those obtained via uniform sampling. Lastly, this study discusses the potential applications and outlines future research directions.

A unique, versatile approach is presented for solving differential equations, including the DGLAP evolution equations used in fitting and evaluating parton distribution functions at various scales. The method is adaptable to differential equations with minimal restrictions and is incorporated into Gleb Kormashev's "DGLAP" package, enabling seamless integration with PDF fitters.

This paper outlines the design of ELKI, a freely available open-source data mining framework, focused on unsupervised learning methods. By building upon Weka, ELKI expands upon existing capabilities by incorporating out-of-core, distributed, and stream mining functionalities. Notably, ELKI distinguishes itself with support for memory-efficient data structures and K-means, but lacks reinforcement learning and-probabilistic models. Instead, it emphasizes efficient clustering, correlation, and link mining operations. Since its initial release in 2004, ELKI has evolved into a fully independent framework, offering improved performance, scalability, and flexibility through the integration of new mining tasks, data structures, and processing techniques.

Our research involves exploring a technique for creating a precise, tunable spectrum of optical frequency combs through the application of dual pump lasers with specifically spaced sidebands. By doing so, we observe the emergence of a flat, broad optical spectrum of microcomb lines. These lines originate from a nonlinear microresonator interacting with the pump's sidebands. These microcomb lines maintain a consistent spacing relative to the pump's frequency, which can be adjusted by varying the spacing between the pump's sidebands. This property enables the generation of a wide, flat optical spectrum of microcomb lines with a consistent spacing. This phenomenon can be manipulated to create a wide, flat optical spectrum of microcomb lines with a consistent spacing.

We establish that the symmetric group $S_\infty$ possesses a characteristic subgroup $H_\infty$ consisting of elements with growing support, where $H_\infty$ exhibits properties of relative weak mixing and faithfulness. Consequently, $S_\infty$ cannot be obtained as a subgroup of any countable group that possesses these characteristics. Additionally, a subgroup of $S_\infty$ acting faithfully on an increasing sequence of finite sets is unable to preserve a probability measure that is both $H_\infty$-invariant and faithful.

We analyze the efficacy of quasi neural networks, which are 2L hidden layer neural networks trained with quadratic losses, and find that they are equivalent to learning the neural tangent kernel, a quadratic function of the input. The eigenvalues of this kernel determine the learning rate and stability. If the eigenvalues decay slowly, the learning process is approximately linear, while rapidly decaying eigenvalues lead to unstable training, replicating the behavior of traditional neural networks. We further demonstrate that neural networks with random and systematic structure in their weight matrices exhibit distinct learning characteristics, and the efficacy of quasi neural networks is heavily influenced by the ratio of generating signals to hidden layers.

A study suggests that bulk entropy quantities with specific properties may only be associated with specific, equally valued boundary entropy quantities. This theory is based on two key principles: the mutual information among these bulk entropies is monogamous and the entropies are associative.  In order to test this hypothesis, we have computed the change in boundary entropy of individual components of multiboundary entropies in three different scenarios.  Our research found that in cases where the bulk information is disconnected from one boundary, the change in an individual component's boundary entropy is solely determined by its contribution to the overall bulk information. However, in cases where the bulk information is connected to both boundaries, the change in an individual component's boundary entropy is complex and is determined by its connection to the overall bulk information shared between the two boundaries.  Our research found that in such cases, the change in an individual component's boundary entropy is equal to its contribution to the overall bulk information shared between the two boundaries.  This discovery is consistent with the hypothesis proposed in the original study.

This passage discusses recent findings regarding the local state probabilities of lattice models. We previously established a branching rule for a family of solvable lattice models in dimensions two and three. Here, we derive a branching rule for a similar model in dimension four. We show that this yields closed expressions for the local state probabilities, linked to the decompositions of $sp(2N)$ and $so(2N)$. Conversely, we can calculate the branching rules for the local state probabilities, applying this to dimension two. Additionally, we propose a conjecture for the branching rule in dimension three.

This paper explores the effectiveness of combining multiple stabilization techniques, such as regularization and constrained optimization, in signal recovery algorithms. We find that merging different stabilizations can either enhance or impede the algorithm's performance, depending on the specific methods used. To understand this interplay, we focus on the simplest case of combining two stabilizations and investigate the resulting algorithms through a general framework. Our analysis reveals that the performance of these algorithms is akin to applying a stabilized process to the original problem, although the stabilized process may be uninterpretable when regularization parameters are involved. We illustrate the importance of choosing stabilizations and parameters through concrete examples, emphasizing the need for careful selection to achieve optimal performance.

Non-linear co-addition algorithms such as median and clipped-mean produce reasonable density estimates by removing outliers from multiple images, but they cannot maintain a consistent point spread function (PSF) for all stars. This occurs because these algorithms only utilize data from stars that are clearly defined, thereby omitting data from faint, distorted stars. As these algorithms also do not accurately represent multiple image noise, they can result in negative or abnormally high density values. To address these issues, we have developed the Maximum-likelihood Non-Linear Clipped (MLNC) method. MLNC maintains a constant PSF and accurately models multiple image noise for stars of all sizes. This algorithm uses a likelihood ratio to determine optimal weighting for each image based on a star's morphology, thereby avoiding arbitrary clipping values. By applying MLNC to multiple image sets, we have demonstrated its ability to remove noise outliers and produce density estimates with improved precision and lower systematic errors. Furthermore, MLNC maintains a constant PSF for all stars and remains effective for a wide range of signal-to-noise ratios. This algorithm can be applied to various image compression tasks and is suitable for multiple image sets with varying signal-to-noise ratios.

We establish that the imaginary component of a specific complex function, which generates a family of growing curve sets, can be projected onto Euclidean space to yield the chordal SLE (Schramm–Loewner evolution) process. Curves generated by this process exhibit varying degrees of self-intersection. Our analysis builds upon a key observation by Matts Carlen, who noted a correspondence between certain complex functions and real mappings within Euclidean space, leveraging a technique called 'conformal embedding.' By extending Carlen's work and applying conformal embedding, we derive the chordal SLE from a complex valuation on a specific tree structure, which can then be translated to Euclidean space to produce the expected SLE process.

We focus on the long-time behavior of solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations in fractional spaces, specifically $\mathcal{H}^s$ for $s \in (\frac{N}{2} \mathregular{N}, \frac{N}{2}+1)$, and obtain an estimate for the maximum norm of the solution and its derivatives, given the maximum norm of the initial conditions. Similarly, for the Euler equations in the same fractional spaces, we derive an estimate for the maximum norm of the solution and its derivatives, given the maximum norm of the initial conditions, resulting in a logarithmic decrease in the case of Euler equations. Moreover, for the heat equation in a heat fluid, we also demonstrate an estimate for the maximum norm of the solution and its derivatives, given the maximum norm of the initial conditions, leading to a decrease in the estimate over time.

This paper proposes an improved protocol for verifying artificial intelligence model outputs, which relies on neural network predictions rather than actual data. The existing AI-FedVer protocol has limitations due to its reliance on the client having access to the same high-quality training data and network resources as the verifier. In response, we've developed an alternative CVQC protocol tailored for use in computer vision tasks, where we've implemented the details specifically for object detection. Our protocol demonstrates significant advantages over AI-FedVer by requiring fewer network resources and verifying computations at a much faster rate, particularly for processing larger images.

The application of cell shape synthesis assisted by deep learning has recently gained traction due to its potential to enhance image analysis techniques such as cell tracking and segmentation within the biomedical field. A cell shape synthesis model utilizing a variational autoencoder (VAE) was developed with the goal of producing a diverse range of cell shapes comparable to real cells. However, the model's ability to generate cells of the correct species was initially lacking. To address this issue, a cluster-based approach was proposed, demonstrating the potential to specify a target species through clustering of the cell shapes. Our approach was evaluated using an dataset of 3349 red blood cells from chickens and two other species. The results showed that our method successfully produces species-dependent generative models, and the potential applications of our approach were explored, particularly in image synthesis, the repair of missing areas in images, and the manipulation of existing images.

Reinforcement Learning research has focused primarily on the environmental state, neglecting the representation of environment features. Our investigation reveals that using persistent feature representations instead of raw state features in geometric tasks yields substantial gains, reaching up to 90% in evaluation success rates. To encourage feature representation research, we introduce the Persistent Features framework, which integrates persistent feature representations into reinforcement learning algorithms. Our analysis of this framework highlights the advantages of persistent features and motivates the exploration of more sophisticated feature representations.

To develop algorithms for more complex many-body models, we start with a three-dimensional model of dipolar interactions, which often enters a state of dynamical arrest. To overcome this challenge, the Newtonian Eclectic Meta-Classical Algorithm for Molecular Dynamics (ECMC) is adapted into four different variants: one each for Newtonian, Verlet, Langevin, and Born-Monte Carlo simulations. The Eclectic ECMC algorithm samples from a multi-dimensional distribution by breaking it down into simplified components. Eclectic ECMC's variants generate configurations based on predefined weights, ensuring correct phase space sampling. The Eclectic ECMC variants are tested on three-dimensional dipolar models with various dipolar strengths and bond angles before being applied to a polarizable neon model, which demonstrates Eclectic ECMC's ability to improve performance by adapting its Eclectic factors to optimize these models. Eclectic ECMC's versatility allows it to support simulations of thousands of particles and has the potential to support even larger simulations in its current form.

This study submits Supplemental Entry 1 to the DCASE 2020 task 3: sound
event detection in domestic settings with additional data augmentation
methods to enhance performance and system robustness. We examine the effect
of various data augmentation techniques on SED systems and propose a method
utilizing enhanced signal duration to improve classification model training.
To further boost results, we investigate the benefits of combining event
segment generation with continuous signal classification (CSC). We demonstrate
through experiments that selectively applying data augmentation methods
and method mixing enhances system accuracy. In final submission results,
our base system with augmented data and mixed training methods excels with
a 4.66% improvement over the baseline submission.

The theory of signal representation benefits from the superposition property, which has far-reaching implications for multiple coexistence technologies like federated learning and non-orthogonal multiple access. This concept is comprised of two main elements: a linear combination decoder and a bounded coefficient reconstruction algorithm. Within the realm of linear systems, the superposition property can be achieved through distinct system designs, each defined by a specific matrix. This document explores the collective attributes of linear systems that possess the superposition property and demonstrates that these systems are characterized by a particular type of rank called E-rank. Researchers have identified several unique properties of these systems and have further categorized them based on the relationship between the matrices of these systems. Specifically, these systems can be grouped into three categories, each defined by the similarity between their matrices. Notably, the superposition property shares connections with three other concepts in the field of compressed sensing: the sparse representation property, the equalization property, and the overcomplete representation property. This document has proven that these seven concepts exist independently and can be found in various distinct linear systems. Additionally, researchers have established the necessary and sufficient conditions for these systems to possess these unique properties. Furthermore, these conditions have enabled the creation of algorithms that can quickly determine whether a given linear system possesses these properties.

This paper proposes a novel spectrogram-based method for signal detection and estimation, where signal recovery is achieved by manipulating level sets. Specifically, it outlines an algorithm that leverages an optimization problem, whose solution is expressed in terms of the spectral power density, via a non-rigid transformation. By concisely defining this transformation using two optimization criteria, the method yields multiple relevant applications, including detection and estimation, and changing detection scenarios. Notably, it offers an innovative way to interpret l1-regularized (l1-regularized) optimization methods, providing a practical approach to detecting and estimating sparse signals in various contexts.

We utilize the difference-of-operators method to derive a new ally periodic system for studying synchronized clusters in a group of dynamical systems. Our approach identifies a divisor of the number of synchronized clusters and provides conditions under which these clusters remain stable. Furthermore, we apply our method to the study of synchronized rings in Chua's circuit and diode resistor capacitor networks.

We introduce a special module within Blender, enabling the simulation of rigid bodies governed by gravity and inertial forces. This module enhances Blender's simulation capabilities by incorporating an advanced algorithm for integrating ordinary differential equations. Compared to existing solutions, our module boasts improved efficiency, characterized by a fixed computational time complexity of O(N^3), where N represents the number of particles in the system. Additionally, the module encompasses multiple collision detection methods and an optimized algorithm for projecting acceleration due to gravity onto a plane. As an integral part of the Blender project, our module facilitates the visualization of simulations and offers a range of features for further refining simulation outcomes. This work lays the groundwork for extending the module to handle flexible bodies and fluid dynamics, ultimately enriching Blender's simulation tools.

The conventional second law of thermodynamics is often assessed through the information engine paradigm, where information is systematically retrieved from a heat bath using well-established rules for measurement. Nonetheless, continuous quantum measurement, commonly employed in experimental studies, doesn't adhere to the standard definition of measurement. Therefore, it's uncertain whether standard information engines can be equally used in scenarios involving continuous measurements. To resolve this uncertainty, we developed an information engine that utilizes repeated, continuous measurements, and demonstrated its operation, driven by the flow of information, is equivalent to the standard scenario, thus validating the standard thermodynamic evaluation even in the context of continuous measurements. Moreover, we found that the continuous measurement scenario is distinct from the standard scenario, and therefore, cannot be viewed as simply being non-markovian. Finally, we explored the influence of different measurements on the information engine's efficiency and found that, although continuous measurements offer the advantage of being naturally decoupled from the system, they limit the maximum information retrieval efficiency to 1 (completely passive), in contrast to discrete measurements which can achieve higher efficiencies.

We've conducted a thorough examination of the jamming transition of identical, 
thin, and concave disk shapes in a 2D environment with no bonds between them.
The disks are either perfectly smooth or slightly roughened. Our study focuses 
on how jamming is affected by the size of the disks and their arrangement. It's 
known that smaller and more irregularly shaped disks are more prone to jamming.
To investigate this further, we considered two key factors: the weight of the 
disks and any potential repulsive forces between them. When the disks have the 
same weight, their behavior is consistent, but when their weights vary, it leads 
to a more complex and unpredictable jamming behavior. Ultimately, the outcome 
depends solely on the shape of the disk and the forces acting between them when 
they're close to each other. To understand this phenomenon better, we simulated 
jamming by applying an external force, which, in the case of disks of the same 
weight, results in a more uniform and stable state with less packing density 
than situations where the disks have different weights. When the disks are allowed 
to roll, they reach a more stable state than when they're forced into a fixed 
position. Our study shows that the jamming transition is a complex phenomenon that 
depends on various factors and is not solely determined by the characteristics 
of the disks themselves.

Research into distinct flavors of El Niño and La Niña has revealed significant differences in their global precipitation patterns. By examining the flavors' distinct features, a statistical analysis identified a set of associated centers that either appear or disappear, leading to altered flavor expressions. Using advanced computational methods, the study found that these centers, when removed, allow the flavors to be reconstructed and their associated center configurations linked to specific flavor characteristics. Like a painter using distinct brushes to create different images, each flavor uses a unique set of centers to produce its distinctive precipitation patterns. The research identified bridges between flavors, where the order of center appearance or disappearance changes, and discovered that some centers remain involved regardless of the flavor. By analyzing the distinct flavor precursors, the study identified key centers that initiate each flavor and how their order of appearance changes, resulting in distinct precipitation patterns. The research further investigates the distinct flavor precursors' associated impacts on related climate phenomena, such as Indian monsoons and African droughts.

Observations from the very early universe reveal the presence of sub-pico-second mass concentration spikes that need to be explained by the formation theories of cosmic black holes. Previous research indicates that these spikes can be accounted for by the phase transitions of a certain type of quantum gravity model, resulting in the formation of more massive black holes than would be expected based on earlier, static configurations. A theoretical model is presented where the formation of a cosmic black hole is simulated from scratch, incorporating the principles of quantum gravity and the concept of information retention. The model suggests that the mass of cosmic black holes is directly linked to the energy released during their associated phase transitions. Notably, the mass spectra of heavy black holes resemble those of supermassive, heavy seed formation pathways but differ from light seeding scenarios. A possible connection is made to the observed mass patterns of the first supermassive black holes.

On certain two-dimensional lattice structures like the Kagome and Lieb lattice,
introducing additional orbital components can significantly impact the properties
of the system. We examined this influence in a Lieb lattice with two orbital
components and found novel effects resulting from flat bands. These effects
include complete spin polarization, charge and orbital correlations, and
lattice deformations. Furthermore, we identified flat band-induced pairing
states under specific conditions. Our findings reveal that the Lieb lattice's
bodian structure can exhibit superconductivity, characterized by a nodal
distribution along the lattice's semi-cores.

We examined the relationship between protein sequences and SNPs associated with phenotypes across 69 diseases and 3 traits. To do this, we used a machine learning method called Random Forest to see how much variation in protein sequences, among other things, was connected to these phenotypic SNPs. Then, we looked at a smaller group of highly similar proteins to refine our analysis. Our study also tested whether contact information, which measures how protein sequences interact with each other, played a role in this relationship. Ultimately, we found that sequences of proteins vary significantly in how they are connected to phenotypic SNPs, and that the nature of a protein's function influences these interactions.

In this study, we categorize and count the 2-designs with a prime number of points that have a prime or composite order automorphism group. Additionally, we establish that a 2-design with a prime number of points and a prime order automorphism group must have a prime index subgroup. We then identify the 2-designs with a prime number of points that have a prime order automorphism group, and these are closely related to the prime power resolvable designs in symmetric and linear spaces.

Within a statistical framework, the informational entropies of electronic systems confined within a quantum dot or a quantum Penrose cage are calculated. These entropies depend on the Coulomb correlation effects, which are also captured by a generalized Thomas-Fermi theory. By comparing the predictive power of entropies in both scenarios, the influence of correlation effects is evaluated. Furthermore, the rate of information increase in both scenarios is examined, which is a measure of complexity, and the potential applications of this concept are discussed.

The precise measurement of binary star systems' velocity dispersion is crucial for identifying the binary star stream. Accurately calculating this measure requires highly precise data, which can be achieved through multiple observations at diverse epochs. Previously, we developed a mathematical approach based on line velocity values for 1D velocity dispersion analysis in binary star systems and discovered it significantly outperforms traditional methods. In this study, we enhance this previous work by incorporating additional information from line widths in addition to line velocities. The results demonstrate that incorporating line widths further improves the mathematical approach's precision. The new method performs best with three to four observations at least one week apart, which yield line velocity values with an accuracy of at least 0.5 km/s.

We introduce a new method for computing the semantics of multiplicative linear logic by adapting the Sequent-Calculus, a formalized proof-system. Our adaptation facilitates the direct mapping of proof-structures to their logical meaning, providing an alternative to the structured semantics. In linear logic, the method yields an equivalence of meaning and structure, given the presence of ideal representations. We demonstrate that the method can be extended to near-multiplicative linear logic by introducing 'fuzzy' ideal representations.

Previous research has explored the application of machine learning and nonlinear dynamics to forecast the synchronization, or lack thereof, of time series pairs. This study delves into deep learning strategies for this challenge, utilizing multiple time-based features to predict synchronization probability between pairs of financial time series. Notably, our model is able to accurately forecast synchronization states in a significant proportion of attempts, exceeding previous efforts to our knowledge. Furthermore, investigations into the characteristics of our model highlight the importance of incorporating directionality and delay-based features to predict synchronization states reliably. This study emphasizes the utility of deep learning approaches for this problem, suggesting a scarcity of relevant applications to date.

To effectively control chemical reactions, it's crucial to understand the dynamics of the reactants. Researchers have made significant progress in doing so by leveraging the vibrational states of the molecules, which are inextricably linked to their electronic and nuclear movements. In this study, we propose a plan for actively modulating chemical reaction barriers through a non-perturbative approach. This approach involves driving the molecules into a specified quantum state that's aligned with the goal reaction. By doing so, the molecules' chance of successfully navigating the reaction barrier increases dramatically. We've demonstrated the feasibility of this plan by examining a renowned example – the reaction between sodium and iodine, which involves multiple vibrational states coupled with the quantum suppression of the reaction barrier. Our analysis shows that, using ultrashort laser pulses, it may be possible to control this reaction and potentially others like it.

Predicting the click-through rate (CTR) is a fundamental challenge in online advertising. Researchers have addressed this challenge by incorporating a structured model, which uses visual and textual components arranged in a directed graph to represent an ad. This graph consists of visual IDs representing ad visuals and numbered text IDs representing text. By linking these ID nodes to a target node, a click node, a network-based method can estimate CTR. Unlike previous simple linear models that only consider the target node and textual components, this new approach leverages the power of a structured graphical model, which can capture complex dependencies between visual and textual components. Furthermore, experiments conducted on real-world data demonstrate that this new method significantly outperforms linear models in both click-through rate and conversion rate prediction.

The concept of fairness in business process management, particularly with regards to fairness under an equality of opportunity framework, is relatively new and uncovers issues not addressed by current systems. Systems fail to account for the number of processes a user is assigned in, which leads to unfair situations. To mitigate this, a mechanism that enforces the number of processes a user is allowed to work on is necessary. The minimum number of processes a user can handle at any time, known as the cardinality constraint, must be considered. Integrating the fairness mechanism with concurrency, which handles the allocation of processes to specific activities, is also necessary. A concurrent, fair system that accounts for the constraints of both process owners and machines within the organization is presented. The solution involves a refinement process that transforms a system to be both fair and concurrent, which is proven and demonstrated using an example system.

The past year has seen numerous devastating wildfires raging across the American West that have significantly polluted the air with particulate matter, causing serious health risks and affecting solar energy collections systems by creating AOD propagation anomalies. Solving the reduced Boltzmann equation to model AOD propagation includes calculating an effective temperature, but doing so with current numerical methods is too computationally expensive due to its non-linearity. To overcome this issue, we propose an innovative statistical approach that incorporates physical principles into an ensemble-based model. This approach estimates the temperature by analyzing the AOD distribution and utilizing the principle of maximum entropy, thereby enabling fast online calculations. Our model leverages recent breakthroughs in generating high-dimensional, quasi-uniform distributions. Our simulations have shown that this approach can accurately estimate the temperature and its evolution with minimal nodes, achieving a high accuracy of 0.01 K with just 10 nodes. Our results also show that this approach can efficiently solve the boltzmann equation, achieving a speedup of around 5 times compared to conventional methods.

Privacy preservation in location-based services is crucial for maintaining user anonymity. Currently used methods rely on artificially generated data, created with reference to real data, but disregard the issue of degrading privacy as data becomes older. Our solution addresses this limitation by incorporating a new data release framework. It enables the issuance of public location data while maintaining users' total privacy, by employing generated data that utilizes real data averages, that become increasingly inaccurate with time. Additionally, we propose an efficient mechanism for handling the issue of privacy breaches, by allowing administrators to detect and rectify violations quickly. This is achieved through an evaluation of the relationship between the released location data and related privacy breaches. Our framework encompasses two primary features: firstly, an efficient formal method for representing and analyzing privacy breaches, by using Spatial Temporal Logic, and secondly, an effective algorithm for detecting breaches, using a finite model checker. Our method allows for the efficient detection and rectification of privacy breaches, with an experimental study demonstrating its practicality.

The reliability of brain networks in identifying individual and group differences is significantly influenced by inter-site effects that vary across different study designs. To enhance the reliability of functional connectivity studies, we developed a site-dependent analysis approach that accounts for inter-site effects. Our approach utilizes Bayesian model comparison to identify the most supportive model for each site and group, and enables the detection of significant differences between groups at each site, and also considers variability across sites. We tested our approach using both simulated data and an fMRI study involving 50 subjects from two datasets, each collected at two different sites. Our results show that site-dependent analysis enhances the reliability of FC studies by increasing sensitivity and false discovery rates compared to a global analysis approach. Therefore, site-dependent Bayesian noise correction is recommended for improving the reliability of studies investigating individual and group differences in FC.

Concentration inequalities can be seen as an outcome of various short-term average inequalities, such as heat equations or functional concentration inequalities. A unified approach to obtaining such concentration inequalities begins with a differential equation that acts as a fundamental driver for concentration, although it often lacks explicit solutions. A workaround this challenge is to utilize operator smoothing to derive an approximate solution that is useful for proving concentration inequalities. This report presents a method for operator smoothing in the context of differential equations and offers examples that illustrate its implementation, such as deriving a concentrated version of the heat equation and a controlled version of the Weyl asymptotic formula.

Recent advancements in pre-trained language models have significantly improved the performance of monolingual and code-mixed language models. However, positional encoding techniques developed for monolingual settings have yet to be adapted for code-mixed text. Our research introduces a novel positional encoding for code-mixed text, taking into account its inherent characteristics. By combining this encoding with existing pre-trained models, we have observed substantial gains in performance and superior robustness against language mixing ratios. Our model has demonstrated exceptional results on various tasks and datasets.

Despite the significant progress made in studying H3S, a comprehensive description of its isotopic behavior remains unexplained. Our thorough theoretical analysis reveals that the isotopic effect coefficient in H3S has two major contributions that evolve under pressure. It transitions from predominantly coming from the acoustic sum rule at low pressures to being heavily influenced by the elastic properties of the material at higher pressures. This finding enables us to accurately calculate the isotopic effect coefficient in H3S across various pressures. Our study also sheds light on the isotopic effect in other hydrogen-rich sulfides.

In evolutionary biology, average gene substitution rates have significant implications for understanding various genetic phenomena, including fixation rates, fertilization probabilities, and the impact of one gene's substitution on another's, all of which have been extensively studied. Despite the abundance of research, the average effect of one gene's substitution on another's has remained largely unexplored until now. We offer a comprehensive analysis of this effect, providing a formula and contrasting fixed and overdominant scenarios, as well as comparing our findings to a previous study's results.

This study proposes a novel nonlinear feedback control system for a bipedal robot's redrafted Acrobot, designed to facilitate seamless gait. By integrating the robot's inherent dynamics and a trajectory-based feedback structure, the research develops a streamlined method for close-loop feedback that enhances stability and adaptability. Specifically, the study demonstrates that the robot can maintain balance through self-correcting movements, even when faced with unexpected external forces or challenges. To this end, the research presents theoretical evidence that the robot can synchronize its movements in response to close-loop feedback, resulting in predictable and robust outcomes. This control system's capability is further validated through simulations, which demonstrate the robot's ability to adapt to diverse scenarios and environments.

We introduce a groundbreaking approach that incorporates learned camera descriptors
into the classic PnP algorithm to localize cameras. By leveraging the strength of
descriptors in challenging situations, our method employs these features to reinitiate
camera pose estimation. Consequently, our approach significantly improves PnP's
overall accuracy. To accomplish this, we developed a learning-based descriptor
training pipeline, utilizing synthetic data and PnP solutions as references, to
generate precise pose estimates. These descriptors are then applied to determine
the optimal matching cameras for each image. Finally, the accurate geometric
information from these matching cameras is combined to calculate the final camera
position. Notably, our approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods on real-world
datasets, and demonstrates exceptional performance in difficult scenarios, such as
low-light and real-time processing.

In the personalization domain of federated learning, a challenge arises when personalizing models to individual clients while accounting for limited labeled data available to them, particularly when compared to the semi-supervised setting with more abundant data. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called personalizable semi-supervised learning, which utilizes unlabeled data from all clients to enhance model personalization. Our method relies on minimizing a local contrastive loss to capture private knowledge within each client's data representation. Notably, this approach yields superior results on various benchmarks, significantly outperforming fixed-client and adaptive-client averaging techniques by up to 8.3% and 5.5% respectively, on datasets like MinSTL-MNIST and MinSTL-CIFAR10, and approaching the performance of centrally trained models despite being client-trained. Our code is freely accessible at https://github.com/lgarcesp/PSL.

The orbital period of neutron star binaries in the LIGO--Virgo population is observed at 1.003 s for the system JJ200316: GRO J1744-12. This period holds significant past unpredictability, hinting at a disruption that occurred 114 days prior. Various explanations for this phenomenon have been proposed, including a neutron star disrupted by a black hole and receding into a wide orbit, as well as neutron star tidal disruption by another neutron star resulting in a dense object that roams close by. Notably, an exotic solution where a black hole and a neutron star merged in the Arian eavesdropping scenario also partially accounts for the discrepancy. Notably, an explanation is needed for the 36 day fluctuation in the orbital period, $\Delta P_{\rm orbit}\equiv P_{\rm 2nd}-P_{\rm 1st}$. This can be attributed to an effect of magnetic field in an accretion disk following a neutron star disruption without the necessity of Gravitational Wave detection of the event's onset. This can occur if the neutron star that disappeared had a significant magnetic field, transferring it to the accretion disk surrounding the other star, resulting in a notable effect on the orbital period. This theoretical model is consistent with existing theory and is capable of generating magnetic fields in accretion disks as the disrupted neutron star's magnetic field is transferred to it.
