We've proven that for a typical compact Riemann surface, the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class can be broken down into three distinct components, which are in direct proportion to the degree of a line bundle, the square of the degree of a line bundle minus one, and the space of holomorphic quadratic differentials, all within a specific mathematical framework. This breakdown has significant implications for the topology of Riemann surfaces and their associated moduli spaces.

This study examines various methods for proving the existence and uniqueness of a quasi-stationary distribution for Markov processes. We explore under what conditions a quasi-stationary distribution is unique and demonstrate that uniqueness is equivalent to exponential convergence in certain cases. Our work also identifies criteria for weak convergence towards a unique quasi-stationary limit distribution, particularly in scenarios where a finite number of eigenvalues lie within the spectral gap. To facilitate applications, we provide concrete criteria for unique quasi-stationary distributions in the contexts of random graphs, epidemic models, and individual-based modeling.

This study examines the interaction between graphene and dielectric nanospheres in the vicinity of an electrode. Graphene is modeled as a two-dimensional conductor with a chemically variable surface, for which the chemical potential can be adjusted. In a simulation environment, the chem graphene is surrounded by a three-dimensional space of water, in which a dielectric nanosphere was placed. The nanosphere was subjected to an external force field originating from the electrode and the chem graphene. The positions of the nanosphere in equilibrium were determined as a function of chemical potential, distance from the chem graphene, and applied force. The chem graphene was found to attract the nanosphere more strongly at lower chemical values. Additionally, the nanosphere was observed to move closer to the chem graphene as the applied force increased. Furthermore, the nanosphere exhibited a greater response to the chem graphene for smaller values of dielectric constant in the nanosphere.

To determine the Emergency Department's ideal length of stay, researchers analyzed a million-pound patient treatment dataset from 2021. They employed difference-in-differences analysis to isolate the pure staffing impact by comparing two scenarios: increased treatment time due to extra staff and standard treatment time. A change of 30 minutes in treatment time was found to result in a 0.4% increase in visits to the Emergency Department within 30 days, primarily due to minor conditions. This 30-minute increase also led to a 1.3% rise in Emergency Department visits and a 1.4% increase in hospital admissions within 30 days, with visitors to the Emergency Department experiencing more severe conditions. Additionally, a 30-minute increase in treatment time caused a 1.6% rise in hospital admissions and a 2.2% increase in 30-day all-cause hospital readmissions. Based on the data, maintaining treatment times under 4 hours appears desirable.

This study investigates how multiple agents, each having a difficulty level for a task, interact and decide on a task to complete. Building upon an existing finding that a specific strategy known as the Randomized Maximum Margin (RMM) strategy leads to an optimal outcome, we provide a new characterization of RMM and extend its application to scenarios with additional constraints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RMM's performance can be affected by the distribution of task difficulties and, in some cases, may not yield an optimal outcome when this distribution deviates from a specific pattern. To address this issue, we develop a new method, Maximum Margin (MM), and show through analysis and numerical results that it outperforms RMM in a wider range of distribution scenarios. Additionally, we explore how to combine these two algorithms to achieve better performance.

Our investigation reveals that events with extreme local charge conservation, occurring at the LHC with PbPb collisions, are heavily influenced by petrological characteristics as anticipated by event-shape engineering. Studies of charge distribution within these events, in relation to their orientation, reveal a significant geometric anisotropy. Analysis of charge dependence in two-particle correlations, considering anisotropic flow coefficients, demonstrates that extreme events exhibit a splitting along with a decrease in geometric anisotropy. Computational phenomena, observed within the 200 GeV - 1800 GeV energy spectrum, do not correlate with energy increases. Research indicates that event Shap Engineering represents a valuable analytical tool, facilitating insights into collective behavior, encompassing the entire energy range from the RHIC to the LHC.

This study introduces a comprehensive framework for crowd evaluation that encompasses
three core components: crowd behavior, project attributes, and campaign launch strategies.
Building on text analysis and network physics, we have developed a predictive model that
assesses the likelihood of a project's success based on crowd behavior, along with a pair of
surprising discoveries. To facilitate comparison with traditional human-based evaluation,
we have conducted an in-depth examination of our model's performance, taking into consideration
the intricacies of crowd classification, project representation, and training optimization.

In federated learning, multiple organizations collaborate on training a machine learning model while maintaining their local data's privacy. This collaboration is particularly beneficial for network intrusion detection, as organizations can share information about detected incidents. However, a question arises - what if an organization discovers a malicious intrusion during shared training? Can it trust the other organizations not to exploit this information for malicious purposes? Inspired by nature, we've introduced an Intrusion Detection agent, modeled after a Swan's warning cry in Ra's Valley, that alerts other organizations to potential threats without revealing incident details. This abstract presents a novel, evolutionary approach to designing an Intrusion Detection agent capable of protecting federated learning participants from potential threats and malicious data injection attacks.

The increasing complexity of complex robotic systems has resulted in higher costs and extended development times, thus indicating the need for more efficient and powerful software tools. These sophisticated systems demand high-level task automation capabilities to lower costs and times. Although model-based programming (MBP) offers a suitable solution for automating tasks due to its efficiency and task independence, its potential is hindered by the time consumed during task execution. This study aims to enhance MBP's efficiency by reducing the processing time. Initially, we examined MBP's core execution processes and pinpointed two primary bottlenecks. Subsequently, we developed and tested an optimized algorithm addressing these bottlenecks. This optimized algorithm is now integrated with MBLE, and our research demonstrates an average speedup of approximately 63 times with an average task execution time reduction of about 98 percent. This speedup enables designers to program MBLEs with more sophisticated algorithms previously considered too complex for MBLEs, as well as task executions comparable to those of programmable logics. This research paves the way for MBLEs to tackle a variety of practical applications, such as real-time control, navigation, and learning at the edge.

The study of electron transport within gated double layers, a fundamental component in semiconductor research, can be expanded to include the use of gate materials other than gold. This study investigates the non-adsorbed surface states and electron mobility at the interface with various gate materials, employing a technique to modulate electron transport independently of the gate. The study utilizes a thin Fermion system created by backing a semiconductor channel with a highly conductive material. The findings demonstrate that the type of gate material used significantly impacts the effectiveness of electron transport. The study also verifies that the electron transport is not influenced by the gate material's properties and identifies a key factor in achieving high electron transport mobility.

Our research focuses on the stability of robust phase-synchronized patterns in complex networks of oscillators, with a particular emphasis on their response to minor fluctuations in system parameters. Using advanced analysis and a reduction method, we derived a precise criterion for temporary phase synchronization near a robust group synchronization state. This criterion indicates that minor system variations cause phase synchronization to be stable if and only if the oscillation frequency difference is within a certain range. This outcome is further validated through numerical experiments on specific network architectures, which demonstrate that even small differences in system parameters can facilitate robust group synchronization in complex networks.

Our study examines the perceived bias of Western search engines towards YouTube. It's evident from YouTube's prominent inclusion in search results that these engines are biased towards the platform. To better understand this phenomenon, we conducted research to determine the extent of this bias and whether it varies between different search engines. Our study involved gathering a substantial number of search results from Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo following various inquiries about YouTube. By comparing the presence of YouTube in search results to the presence of other popular online platforms, we identified a clear pattern of bias in all three search engines. Interestingly, YouTube's presence in search results consistently surpasses that of Twitch and Facebook. It's worth noting that YouTube's inclusion in search results may be an effort by the search engines to promote their partnership with YouTube or an attempt to provide users with alternative entertainment content. However, this bias likely holds implications for the search engines' overall neutrality and fairness in their search output.

We introduce and investigate the behavior of an extended $\beta$-function for representations of a Lie algebra that incorporate multiple general monodromy defects. The function relates the central charge of a Lie superalgebra to the charges of a Lie algebra in the presence of these defects. The study employs a holographic example to illustrate its behavior and find its coefficients. The analysis also covers the case of one defect and discusses its connection to entanglement entropy.

In this study, we establish the optimal level to which the Birch and Swinnerton-Darcy conjecture can be refined for elliptic curves over certain types of number fields, based on recent findings from the Darmon-Eisenstein and Fontaine-Mazur theory. Specifically, for Galois extensions of S3, D4, or A4, we prove that the conjecture can be precisely formulated even when the elliptic curve has a rationally defined point of order 13. For larger Galois groups D5, D6, and S4, we require the presence of a point with a 13th root, defined rationically, to make sense of the refined conjecture. These results extend earlier work of Berger and Boeckle who handled the case for S3 and D4 extensions.

The temporal characteristics of network delay have been categorized into pure, mixed, and infinite delay domains. However, the majority of existing work focuses on the pure and mixed domains, despite the potential for delay to reach infinity in networked systems. In this study, we explore the potential benefits and obstacles of implementing infinite delay domains within network protocols. To achieve this, we apply the concept of operator algebras to the development of protocol design. Specifically, the study incorporates non-commutative elements, which are common in network communication, into its analysis. The research further illustrates the challenges of implementing infinite delay domains through examples based on standard protocols, highlighting that even basic principles are crucial to fulfill the protocol's objectives.

Semi-supervised node classification in graph neural networks often utilizes node pseudo-labeling to incorporate abundant unlabeled data, yet conventional methods assign labels without considering the interdependence between node features and neighbouring nodes. As a result, these methods can degrade GNN performance by introducing inconsistent labels. To address this issue, we introduce a self-supervised pseudo-labeling method called InfoSPL, which utilizes mutual information maximization to enforce dependency alignment between node labels and adjacent node features. InfoSPL has been combined with GNN-based models to form an integrated learning framework. Our experimental results demonstrate that InfoSPL outperforms conventional pseudo-labeling techniques and related self-supervised graph learning methods on multiple benchmark datasets.

Our research introduces PatchNet, a lightweight neural network model designed to efficiently handle large and long-lasting visual data such as videos. By incorporating patch-based attention and long-term memory, PatchNet outperforms other models like MobileNetV2 and MobileNetV2+UNI on various object detection tasks while being more efficient. The code for PatchNet can be freely accessed at this link: https://github.com/dark2/patchnet.

A review of recent findings regarding multi-point distributions in discrete time TASEP models is presented. These models exhibit unique properties in terms of multi-point distributions, especially under the maintenance of certain symmetry conditions. The discussion includes a comparison with similar studies on continuous time TASEP. The focus is on exploring the influence of initial configurations and boundary conditions, as well as on analyzing the long-term behavior of these models.

This study investigates the optimization of data transfer rates in wireless communication networks that utilize simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT). We introduce an innovative technique called generalized antenna-switching method (GASM) that enhances energy efficiency by allocating part of the transmitter's power to receive information and the rest to transmit information. GASM relies on two modes: separate transmission (where the transmitter uses a specific channel to send information) and joint transmission (where the transmitter uses multiple channels to send information). To implement GASMI that incorporates imperfect transmission mode selection, we developed an optimization method based on a hybrid approach of evolutionary algorithms and particle swarm optimization. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of a combination of evolutionary algorithms and particle swarm optimization in achieving optimal performance. Additionally, we investigated the performance of GASMI and evaluated its limitations due to the influence of noise in selected channels. To mitigate this issue, we proposed a method called channel-assignment and mode-switching (CASMI) that incorporates Casmi and examined its benefits and limitations. Our results indicate that CASMI outperforms GASM and gasMI in most scenarios. However, CASMI's potential for improving energy efficiency is hindered by the presence of noise in selected channels.

This study introduces a novel perturbation theory for SU(N) fermions, applying a perturbative approach to the SU(N) symmetry while keeping the chiral symmetry exact. To achieve this, we adapt the perturbation calculations to involve only the SU(N) generators in the Fock space, thereby exactly preserving the chiral symmetry. Furthermore, our approach enables the reconstruction of loop-level amplitudes directly from tree-level processes, thereby simplifying the perturbative analysis. Although the method bears some resemblance to second-order perturbation theory, it demonstrates significant differences in analytical outcomes. This work specifically examines the perturbative spectrum of the SU(3) fermion model with a I=1, S=0 meson, whereas the perturbative decay width and sum of amplitudes for the SU(3) fermion decays are investigated across various SU(3) colors.

In optomechanics, the combined behavior of electromagnetic fields and mechanical objects can often be accurately reduced to simplified electric circuit models, where the standard quantum approach applies when considering high occupation numbers. The accuracy of a proposed standard approach to deriving these circuit models, based on the Hamiltonian of the optomechanical system, is examined in this study. The approach is validated through calculations involving single, dual, and quadrupole optomechanical configurations in free-space scenarios. The analysis specifically focuses on the preservation of quantum fluctuations in occupied modes, determining if the circuit models genuinely conserve energy, and whether the derived equations are solvable. The study reveals that the proposed method efficiently generates circuit models for any given optomechanical configuration, thereby facilitating the accurate description of nonclassical phenomena within occupied modes.

On the nonnonzero real line, a new family of generalized polynomial weights is introduced, leading to the development of a related system of orthogonal polynomials. This is contrasted with a different representation of generalized Airy polynomials, and it's demonstrated that a generalized sextic Freud weight actually belongs to this new family rather than the generalized Airy polynomial system. Furthermore, another representation is formulated for generalized Freud weights, and it's shown that a generalized octic Freud weight belongs to a different family. Additionally, a new polynomial system is introduced and a generalized heptagon Freud weight is positioned at its boundary.

This research examines how a robot that follows walls navigates based on sensors that measure the angle of inclination and the presence of corners. We investigate various scenarios by changing the robot's field of view, the sensor's field of view, the robot's speed, and the layout of the environment. We discovered that the robot's trajectory significantly changes in different scenarios. To facilitate straightforward analysis, we defined two metrics to assess the robot's performance: one is how closely it stays by the wall, and the other is how direct its path is. We used these metrics to identify the most reliable settings for the robot, such as when it has a wide field of view, moves slowly, and can detect peripherally. Additionally, we identified a critical distance beyond which the robot no longer benefits from looking beyond its immediate path.

This paper focuses on perturbative algebraic quantum field theory from a categorical perspective. It explores the concept of subtheories within perturbative algebraic quantum field theory, defined through restrictions to spatial regions. This approach is equivalent to selecting specific Lagrangians within a family of classical actions, which are parametrized by choices of Cauchy surfaces. Consequently, such subtheories are assigned categories. The paper investigates linear structures within these categories, demonstrating that they are not commutative in general. However, it does prove that the first homology group of the algebraic structure underlying these quantum fields plays a key role in simplifying the linear structures. Specifically, it shows that linear structures from different Cauchy surfaces are equivalent up to a torsion element when compared on a Borel rescaled sphere.

The accuracy of accurate smoke detection in surgical settings has been hampered by the limited scope and tiny size of training datasets. Researchers have attempted to resolve this issue by utilizing domain adaptation and learning from a single image, yet these approaches remain prone to errors. To address this challenge, we introduce an advanced method called the Accurate Smoke Dataset (ASD), which produces high-quality, large training datasets through the application of Generative Adversarial Networks. Unlike previous approaches, our dataset is created without needing numerous images or labels by leveraging existing large datasets. Instead, our system identifies smoke images through a trained model and selects non-smoke images randomly to build a comprehensive dataset. Studies have shown that this approach leads to significantly improved smoke detection accuracy, with an overall accuracy gain of 14% for our best model. The ASDF dataset and our code are available for public use at \url{https://smokedetection.com/}.

We introduce a set of robust molecular gate methods inspired by superadiabatic logic, which enable the creation of entangled states within ion chains despite frequency fluctuations. Unlike traditional Molmer-Sorensen gates, our frequency-resistant design employs a specific pulse shape tailored to counter the effects of spectroscopic differences. Notably, while traditional gates limit entanglement among a limited number of ions, our frequency-resistant design enables broader distribution of entanglement among more ions before becoming less effective due to reduced robustness. This improved performance, coupled with the potential for further optimization, makes our design a valuable resource for precise state manipulation and quantum computation on ion chains.

The equilibrium structure of the perovskite LaBO$_3$ with various A-cations (Ba, Ca, Sr) was investigated through ab-initio calculations. The findings reveal that the volatility of the A-cation and the chemical composition significantly impact the distribution of B-cations in the lattice. While Ba results in an off-centered atomic structure, Ca leads to partial off-centering. The main challenge is reducing the positive charge of the A-cation to $+1$, which is achievable with Sr but not with larger ions. The study also discovered that this can be done through reduction of the oxygen bond length, which contracts the lattice and facilitates partial off-centering of the B-cation even when paired with Ba. This provides a new understanding of the partial off-centering of the B-cation, which is usually attributed to next-nearest-neighbor interactions.

Multivariate Gaussian process regressions that maintain conditional independence between different processes can be represented through conditional independency graphs. This concept is utilized to introduce a new method for constrained multivariate regression, where multiple constraints are represented on an graph, restricting the correlation between corresponding processes. The method starts by converting the graph into a corresponding Gaussian Wishart process model, which incurs minimal loss compared to a multivariate Gaussian process model under the graph. The model is then optimized over the graph's structure to minimize the predicted loss. Notably, this framework offers flexible combinations of constrained multivariate regression problems.

Our proposed model, the Recurrent Quantum Circuit, serves as a quantum neural network approach, applying a pre-trained neural network architecture trained on random data to generate diverse circuit patterns, which are then utilized in various quantum physics applications. By employing a recurrent architecture, we circumvent the challenge of quantum errors affecting long-time simulations, while also capturing persistent circuit dynamics. For instance, we demonstrated that our model's trained patterns can be employed directly in Monte Carlo simulations to calculate the ground state energy and other essential ground state properties of complex molecular systems. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between our model's weights and physical antiferromagnetic correlations in the lattice, highlighting its potential to simulate intricate quantum phenomena.

We investigate the computational complexity of convex optimization problems, focusing on data-independent and data-dependent methods like Chebyshev's and gradient descent. Our findings reveal that the generalized Chebyshev method, a data-independent technique, has an average-case complexity comparable to or better than that of gradient descent on smooth and strongly-convex problems, along with average-case complexity advantages over other data-independent methods. Furthermore, GC's complexity advantages hold in scenarios where the optimal solution lies on a boundary. In addition, GC offers improved performance compared to classical optimization methods like subgradient descent and level-set methods. In contrast, non-smooth, strongly-convex optimization problems are more effectively solved by other data-independent methods. Interestingly, the average-case complexity of data-dependent methods, such as follow-the-regularized-prior (FTRP), is superior to that of the data-independent generalized Chebyshev method on smooth, strongly-convex problems.

Moiré superlattices in transition metal dichalcogenides enable unique physics within interlayer space. Our model shows that interlayer excitons are the primary entities giving rise to specific features in optical spectra and 1.5 T magnetic field-induced states. The interlayer exciton binding energy is highly sensitive to the moiré geometry and likely strong coupling. This interlayer phenomenon may be directly observed through specific features in optical spectra or the application of electrical current that corresponds to interlayer charge transfer.

This study proposes an adaptive algorithm that uses probabilistic data association algorithms to determine a mobile entity's location in complex and dynamic environments. The method is tested using simulated data and real-recorded trajectories obtained through sensors equipped to a mobile entity collecting adaptive sampling data. The experimental results demonstrate the algorithm's ability to accurately determine location in scenarios that pose significant challenges for location estimation, such as low signal power, high motion velocities, and crowded radio space due to interfering signals.

ATLAS and CMS collaborations have conducted an analysis to determine whether the polarization properties of $W^{\pm}$ bosons deviate from Standard Model predictions. This was achieved by examining collisions between a 7 TeV $p$-beam and a 8 TeV $p$-beam, corresponding to 2.03 fb$^{-1}$ and 25.11 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosities, respectively. This study focused on helicity fractions of polarization for $W^{\pm}$ and $Z$ bosons produced in electroweak decays of these particles. The results for $W^{\pm}$ boson helicity fractions were found to be within 1 standard deviation of Standard Model predictions. However, the joint helicity fraction for the $Z$ boson, accounting for experimental uncertainties, revealed a deviation of approximately 3.4 sigma from Standard Model expectations. This study implemented various controls to validate the accuracy of measurements, including control samples of $J/\psi$, $\Upsilon$, and $Z$ boson decays.

A novel approach to couple General Relativity with a BF theory in a specific way enables us to link a gravity's vacuum to a specific state in the BF theory. This BF theory's ground state, which is determined by the Cotton tensor, disappearing everywhere in the 3D space as a indicator, suggests a crucial ground state that is related to the General Relativity framework. Furthermore, we propose a reformulated action for a reformulated General Relativity and show that the original General Relativity emerges as a limit when a specific field in the reformulated theory is set to zero.
We have established a direct equivalence between the categories of orthomodular lattices and orthomodular spaces, both having the structure of biclosed bicartesian closed categories.

Recent advances in deep learning-based methods have led to significant progress in legal proof reasoning, enabling the representation of arguments in a abstract and readable format. Our research builds upon this progress by introducing a novel approach called Argo, which provides human-like support for legal proof review through artificial intelligence. By using a proof representation generated by a previous model, Argo enhances the understanding of a proof by identifying missing components, pinpointing inconsistencies, and detecting aspects of the proof that do not conform to applicable pre-defined legal standards. Argo's proof analysis is grounded in formal concepts rooted in logic and controlled vocabulary, thereby enabling it to identify issues related to evidence admissibility, factual accuracy, and compliance with pre-defined legal criteria such as the Federal Rules of Evidence.

We explore a challenge initially proposed by Watson, linking the $l$-function's moments to the square of the central value of the $l$-function itself. While this connection is tied to the modularity theorem, our investigation specifically focuses on the behavior of odd cubic characters. However, rather than tackling the problem as a whole, we instead delve into its implications at its theoretical pinnacle, where the character in question reduces to 1. It is within this context that our analysis ties together Watson's formula with Soundararajan and Harper's work, all while considering how moments of $l$-functions are connected to the square of the central value of $\pi$ itself.

This study focuses on enhancing the efficiency of interior point methods used for linear and quadratic optimization problems. An early inner iteration termination approach is proposed, which allows for stopping interior point methods iterations before completing inner loops when progress slows down. A quasi-interior point method is developed based on this concept and proven to be equivalent to standard interior point methods when no termination occurs. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this approach results in a potentially faster convergence time. Computational experiments are performed to examine the impact of termination thresholds on the quasi-interior point method. Consequently, these experiments reveal the effectiveness of adjusting the threshold to facilitate premature termination of inner iterations for both linear and quadratic optimization problems.

The transition function $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$, which describes how a quark transition evolves as the quark mass $m_q$ varies, has different forms at low and high $m_q$. At low $m_q$, it has a logarithmic dependence, while at high $m_q$, it has a linear dependence. However, for the exact intermediate range, the transition function exhibits an irregular mass dependence. To resolve this issue, the transition function can be expressed through the difference in two color singlet transition functions: one for a quark and two quarks, and another for a quark and a gluon. The latter, $C_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$, is known and doesn't exhibit an irregular mass dependence. On the other hand, the former, $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$, is still not fully understood and is the focus of this study. By assuming the transition function has a simple logarithmic structure, a universal logarithmic term can be removed, revealing a remaining polynomial $m_q$ term. This polynomial term can be removed by introducing matching conditions at two extreme $m_q$ values. One is when $m_q$ approaches zero, and the other is when $m_q$ approaches its Wolff limit $m_W$. Machine learning system training remains an ongoing, complex process with considerable challenges. To overcome these challenges, we believe that sharing knowledge about incidents that occur during training is essential. To help address this need, we have created an incident reporting database that gathers experiences of researchers and practitioners. This database not only serves as a resource for submitting and viewing incident reports but also provides various tools and statistics to aid in understanding incidents and their connections. Furthermore, we have conducted an initial analysis of the database to offer insights and facilitate the development of intelligent systems. We propose incident reporting to be an integral part of the ML research process, and the database will be regularly updated with fresh content and improved functionality.

The Dubrovin Fock-Goncharov model's connection, originally described in terms of the Lax-Friedman equation, gains new perspectives through two alternative formulations: the ERG differential equation, effectively a flow equation for the gauge-invariant mean field approximation; and the Lax-Hitchin equation, formulated in terms of a connection for a specific bundle. Building on these findings, we propose an extension of the gauge theory that can be described through a system of ERG equations, providing a more comprehensive framework for understanding the model's thermodynamic properties.

To address a monitored process's deviation from several execution protocols, a monitoring system must notify the administrator and potentially resume the process. However, the common approach doesn't reconcile conflicts between multiple process specifications and one-sided recovery isn't sufficient. Therefore, we introduce a new model for runtime monitoring, which accounts for several execution protocols and provides recovery mechanisms that can resolve conflicts between them. The proposed model is based on a monitoring system that tracks and interprets runtime states and understands the process specifications and their relationships. The structure of this model allows it to resolve conflicts between recovery mechanisms for individual processes and those applied during runtime monitoring. The introduced model is evaluated through a monitoring system's implementation and its analysis in scenarios that highlight its capabilities.

Proto-Quipper-M provides an interactive way to design quantum circuits in a high-level web-based environment, focusing particularly on circuit units that can avoid copying quantum states. It incorporates tools for both linear and non-linear transformations of quantum states, allowing for compound circuit units that adhere to the non-cloning theorem. Proto-Quipper-M also implements an optimized performance evaluator that efficiently compares different quantum circuit designs based on metrics such as circuit size, depth, and width. Future updates to Proto-Quipper-M will incorporate a search function and integration with the search tool from Quipper, further enhancing its interactive features.

The distribution of the largest eigenvalue in a three-dimensional Gaussian matrix ensemble has been analyzed numerically using the Kirkwood-Swendsen algorithm to gather data for systems of varying sizes. These findings have been compared with the theoretical predictions derived from the one-loop expansion of an effective field theory. Good agreement has been observed between the numerical data and these predictions, indicating that the underlying random matrix theory is self-consistent. Additionally, the numerical results provide further evidence that the behavior of eigenvalue distributions in such models follows universal patterns, independent of the underlying matrix elements.

Our study explores the principles of quantum engineering for enhanced precision in optical sensing. By creating two-mode squeezing devices using nonlinear optical systems, we can implement quantum-enhanced sensing of an optical phase. We present a concise framework for analyzing the quantum filtering problem related to this process. Initially, we examine the characteristics of two-mode squeezing in phase sensing. Next, we formulate the quantum filtering problem for this scenario. Subsequently, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed strategy in maintaining the quantum features of the two-mode squeezing state despite noise. Specifically, we show that our method preserves two-mode squeezing in the presence of noise. We support our findings with numerical simulations. Ultimately, we discuss the potential applications and limitations of our approach.

One of the key computational challenges in assembling eukaryotic genomes involves multiway number partitioning, a problem that has seen limited study outside the realm of genome assembly. This issue involves taking multiple integer sums as inputs and finding a single integer partition that can satisfy all those sums simultaneously. In the context of genome assembly, these sums represent the overlapping degree distributions of assembled sequences, and finding an optimal partition can significantly improve sequence quality by allocating coverage fairly across the genome. Unfortunately, this problem falls under the NP-hard category, making it previously inaccessible to practical computation. A newly proposed method, multiway number partitioning with constraints, includes a polynomial-time algorithm that meets practical needs. We demonstrate the efficiency of this approach in genome assembly for model organisms, resulting in significantly improved results. Additionally, the algorithm's potential applications extend beyond genome assembly to any domain where constraint-based integer partitioning is required.

In resource-limited environments, the simplest mathematical models of cell growth often necessitate the introduction of constraints, such as a finite resource supply, to prevent uncontrolled cell proliferation. Cell population models typically utilize the logistic equation, but it falls short in this regard. Nevertheless, incorporating spatial constraints still poses significant computational challenges. As an alternative, we propose a new delayed logistic equation, which ensures the solution converges to a positive equilibrium, even in the absence of spatial constraints. This study focuses on developing a hybrid numerical approach, combining adaptive stepsize selection and switching between two discrete forms of the equation, to demonstrate its hybrid convergence to the theoretical equilibrium. Moreover, we examine the behavior of the hybrid system at equilibrium through bifurcation analysis and switchpoint investigations.

The Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) method provides a way to compare event times in spatial point processes by projecting them onto a unified space. However, the computational intensity and memory requirements associated with ILR pose challenges for practical applications, particularly for large-scale datasets and long-term simulations. To overcome these limitations, we've developed an extended version of the ILR method, known as eILR, for efficient computation on massive datasets. The approach involves breaking down the data into smaller sections, applying ILR transformation separately to each, and then combining the results. A novel technique is used to merge the transformed sections while maintaining consistency across the entire dataset. The developed method is theoretically sound and demonstrates convergence to the ILR transformation as the number of sections increases. We've tested the eILR method on two extensive spatial datasets, one containing simulations of seismic swarms in California and the other featuring earthquake data from the National Earthquake Information Center. The results show that eILR offers a viable alternative to more resource-intensive methods, enabling the analysis of large-scale data sets with reasonable computational requirements.

In hybrid quantum conductors combining a host material and a doped
superconductor, the cooperation between entangled Cooper pairs and host
electrons enables the flow of charge carrier. The impact of entangled Cooper
pairs on this hybrid material transport remains poorly understood. The present
study reveals the presence of these pairs significantly influences the hybrid
material conductivity, causing it to exhibit a thermally activated behavior over
a broad temperature range. This conductive behavior is observed in materials
like La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ and Bi$_{2}$CaCu$_3$O$_{7}$, as shown in
previous experiments. The study suggests an alternative explanation for the
observed conductive processes in these materials.

The production of a 82Ge beam via the ARIS facility's separation using the MR-ToF system was investigated. Research focused on 82Ge's nuclear structure, specifically its nuclear levels near the neutron number 40, where 82Ge exhibits a four-quasparticle configuration. To study this, 82Ge was bombarded with a beam of 58Co and allowed to interact at energies of 4.5 and 4.8 MeV per nucleon. The resulting fusion produced an ensemble of emission spectra. The observed ensemble displayed a significant decrease in the nuclear over neutron ratio as neutron number increased beyond 40. The same phenomenon was observed in 78Ge and 74Ge but the effect was less prominent. The two measured nuclear energy levels in 82Ge exhibited a notable increase in level spacing as neutron number increased beyond 40. The observed nuclear structure around the neutron number 40 in 82Ge resembles that of 60Ni, indicating a transition from the four-proton structure characteristic of lighter germanium nuclei to the four-neutron structure characteristic of heavier nickel nuclei. The observed nuclear structure can be explained by the presence of a long-deformed nitron 0+ state.

To analyze the properties of rapidly decaying, neutron-deficient isotopes, the authors employed the $B\\ho$-IMS method in conjunction with a high-resolution detector at the JIEPAC TRIGA Mark III nuclear reactor. A study focused on six 64Ni isotopes with varying spin orientations discovered five new, extremely short-lived isotopes and established the half-lives of three previously known isotopes. The findings were further examined using theoretical shell-model calculations, which helped clarify the underlying nuclear structure. The researchers also utilized the detected data to determine production rates of these isotopes relative to 64Ni. This work marks the first occasion for the use of the $B\\ho$-IMS method in conjunction with a reactor for investigating a wide range of nuclear decays.

In this study, we develop U(1) gauge theory components within the context of normalizing flows, incorporating gauge symmetries through gauge-invariant representations of its functional. Our analysis draws from the formalism of path-integral discretizations of U(1) gauge theory, with discrete 1-form gauge symmetry. Furthermore, gauge transformations are implemented as a group action on the latent variables of the flow, enabling the generation of gauge-invariant configurations. Our findings align with the predicted outcomes of gauge-gravitational flow simulations. This development offers a novel method for simulating U(1) gauge theory, with possible applications in quantum chromodynamics.

This paper details advancements to the ZLORE model, which is a leading approach for recognizing mostly planar image markup. ZLORE significantly improves the poor accuracy rate of existing models on largely planar images, though it's mainly effective for novice users with minimal training. To enhance its performance for highly trained users with extensive training, we introduce two key enhancements. Firstly, we develop a pre-training stage that uses an unsupervised biasing technique to fine-tune ZLORE for specific text styles. This significantly boosts its accuracy in recognizing texts with the desired style. Secondly, we present a supervised stage with a sequence-aware loss function, optimizing ZLORE's overall accuracy. Combining these stages greatly improves the model's overall recognition accuracy for highly trained users, surpassing the current state-of-the-art model by a substantial margin.

The top quark production cross-section has been measured in proton-lead collisions at the LHC, using data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 8.16 TeV. The analysis involves 170 pb$^{-1}$ of collision data, and the results are in line with theoretical predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics. The measurement is based on the fast top quark decay products, and the results are accurate across a range of rapidity and momentum transverse to the beam.

Developing database-driven physical reasoning gadgets from language has gained significant attention because of its practical applications. Current approaches focus on transforming language into math or physics notations but don't consider the actual problem of solving physical tasks. Our research introduces a new framework that can express physical tasks in a suitable notation and accurately interpret them without needing actual database contents. The proposed framework outperforms existing methods by significantly enhancing execution accuracy in tasks lacking database contents.

We've used data from 13 hours of observations at 350 MHz with the LOFAR technique to study the angular clustering of galaxies from the GAMA survey that correspond to 1.1 < z < 2.1 and have absolute magnitudes between -21.85 and -19.00. This pressentation includes the results of our research on the topic. Section two describes the data we used, specifically the LoTSS and GAMA datasets, and explains the calibration and selection criteria for the analysis. Section three discusses methodological aspects such as the analysis of angular clustering statistics and how they relate to various cosmological and galaxy evolution scenarios. Section four presents our main findings, including measurements of angular clustering statistics at 350 MHz and a comparison with predictions based on the ΛCDM cosmology and observations at higher frequencies. Section five summarizes our research and suggests future directions, such as leveraging the full LoTSS dataset and incorporating more sophisticated galaxy evolution models.

We introduce an efficient algorithm that tackles the high-dimensional rank-limited problem, where we aim to recover a low-rank matrix by exploiting its restricted minimal singular-value tolerance. Traditionally, direct applications of the lasso method are hindered by the curse of dimensionality and poor scalability. To overcome these limitations, our adaptive-sieving-based approach partitions the problem into a hierarchy of embedded sub-problems, leveraging projected-singular-value decomposition and lasso solutions in each tier. This recursive strategy greatly enhances computational efficiency and scalability. Moreover, we describe a general framework for constructing suitable sieves and provide specific real-data examples for biomedical applications, where our algorithm consistently outperforms alternative methods.

While there's only one optimal method for achieving a goal, there can be many ways to measure progress toward it. For maximizing entropy production in a basic system, the formula varies significantly depending on the specific definition of efficiency used. Since there's no universal definition of efficiency, it may seem like the concept is too ambiguous to be meaningful. However, the number of possible definitions is limited and they can all be linked back to a fundamental one, and therefore the idea of efficiency is not entirely arbitrary. The same principle applies to the definition of optimal performance, and in the case of a simple system, the optimal method is unique and can be identified through a straightforward process. However, this process becomes more complex as the system becomes more intricate and it may not always be possible to determine the optimal method. The same principles apply to the definition of maximum output and the optimal way to achieve it, and in the case of a simple system, the maximum output can be easily determined, but for more complex systems it may not be unique and the optimal way to achieve it may not exist.

As artificial intelligence continues to evolve, its presence in various sectors is increasing, from decision-making processes to consumer interactions like translation and recommendation services. The environmental impact of deep learning typically focuses on the energy used to train and operate these models, but a significant aspect is overlooked: the environmental impact of data collection, particularly through satellite data monitoring. Our research introduces a novel approach to assess the environmental impact of machine learning-based data collection, and we conduct a case study on the one-dimensional detection algorithm used to find objects in satellite images. We compare the current practice of integrating machine learning with conventional image processing and analyze the findings in terms of green house gas emissions. Interestingly, our case study reveals that integrating machine learning does not significantly alter the carbon footprint in this specific scenario. Nonetheless, we emphasize that this is a rare occurrence and highlight the importance of considering the environmental implications of data collection during model development. Moreover, we propose the application of life cycle assessment to deep learning technologies to understand their entire life cycle impact.

Current process mining techniques primarily focus on descriptive analysis, with only a handful of predictive methods being tested in practical scenarios. To improve the effectiveness of process mining, we need to broaden the range of methods and accurately evaluate them in real-world conditions. This study compares the performance of six predictive methods for estimating case completion times on six different business processes. Unlike previous evaluations, which often relied on artificial data or limited testing samples, this research works directly with substantial datasets from actual processes. The study reveals that the conventional measures used to assess predictive methods are insufficient, as these measures cannot capture the complexities of the processes. Therefore, this paper proposes two new criteria - predictive model flexibility and ease of deployment - to aid in the selection of suitable methods for specific processes. The findings indicate that the flexibility of predictive models is crucial to achieve good performance, given the variety of cycle times and process histories.

A dual-weighted residual method coupled with a quasi-reversible scheme has been implemented for coupled problems in fluid dynamics. This method uses a quasi-reversible approach to solve pressure and velocity discretization errors independently. A post-processed dual solution is also utilized to evaluate the errors. A locally projected residual method was used as an alternative approach to enhance error estimation. A threshold value was applied to the projected residual to identify areas where the solution needs refinement. The methods were evaluated on a range of flow configurations and were found to effectively identify flow features and detect boundaries, aligning closely with the actual solutions.

Graph packing is a graph theory challenge where multiple graphs are embedded into a single graph. Researchers have made progress on packing cycles, but obtaining precise bounds for vertex-disjoint paths problem remains difficult. A novel approach is presented for obtaining lower bound tightness in vertex-disjoint paths problem by converting an embedding of a graph into a network flow, then applying a flow lower bound, and finally converting this flow back into the vertex-disjoint paths problem. This technique yields a lower bound, but it remains limited compared to the established upper bounds. Nonetheless, it offers a practical tool for obtaining tight lower bounds in specific graph packing instances.

We examine a large-scale network of one-dimensional opinions that transition over time, similar to the Mukherjee-Schakleton model. Our research reveals that this system produces separate groups of individuals with distinct opinions. These groups develop when opinions diverge due to disagreement among network nodes. We derive a mathematical expression for the group's size that dominates the long-term system evolution, and it matches the results from Monte Carlo simulations. These groups form when the network's spanning tree is randomly structured, mimicking a typical small-world network characteristic. The groups persist over time, with opinions among nodes within the same group converging and remaining consistent. This is observed through analysis of the group size's distribution and transition dynamics. Additionally, we identify a critical parameter that separates system regimes, leading to the emergence of homogenous groups in one regime and the absence of groups in another.

We've investigated a four-dimensional dilaton black hole equipped with scalar properties using the entanglement entropy concept in its thermodynamic properties. This concept has shown promise in explaining the ductile electronic phase transitions in material physics. Our research focuses on a specific scalar-Gravity model with an $U(1)$ symmetrical element, in which a potential element is present but chooses to ignore it for simplicity's sake. By assuming that the scalar field's charge is linked to the duality gauge field, we successfully derived the black hole's scalar hair equations. These equations have analogs with those found in holographic superconductors, sharing similarities with the famous Bogoliubov-De Gennes equations in their respective fields. After solving the field equations, we found that our model exhibits similar symmetry-breaking phases and a charge-stable state, both of which display an ordinary spontaneous phase shift. Furthermore, our research enabled us to derive a set of first-order phase transitions, along with an initial phase transition threshold. This work may serve as a foundation for further research into the entanglement thermodynamics properties of similar black holes.

The process of mRNA creation involves transcription and processing, which spans across gene length and varies significantly with different genes. It's crucial to understand these processes in order to learn more about gene expression, but there's a lack of information due to the fact that transcription and processing often can't be separated in living cells. In our research, we examine the underlying causes of this challenge by studying a synthetic network capable of translating transcribed RNA into protein. Our results demonstrate that there's a minimum delay between transcription completion and mature mRNA production, which is proportional to the length of the gene. In more complex genes, this delay is masked by variable processing times. Our findings are consistent with existing data from yeast and mammalian cells, suggesting that there may be an evolutionary advantage to the length of genes.

The 64Ni nucleus, with its nearly closed 40N shell and primary single-particle configurations, provides an ideal environment to study the effects of the monopole interaction and the N = 40 subshell gap on excitation energy. Theoretical calculations using the 40N shell model, with the monopole interaction included, predict that the excitation energy will increase as the N = 40 subshell gap grows. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers plan to measure the 2_2^+ excitation energy of 64Ni using the TUNL n-p scattering length, which will be used to establish an energy scale based on accurate calculations. The study of other nuclei with similar properties will also be explored to gain a deeper understanding of the monopole interaction and its effect on excitation energy.

We extend existing knowledge about Weyl fermion anomalies in SU(N) gauge theories by introducing multiple Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation. Our findings reinforce the significance of both 'large-N' limits and local dilatination as approaches to understanding the underlying structure of these theories. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the anomalies exhibit a parallel increase with 'N', and we identify key constraints that must be satisfied for the SU(N) theory with multiple adjoint Weyl fermions to be anomaly-free. In particular, our results confirm that adding additional Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation to SU(N) theory will always introduce a dilaton anomaly unless the 'N' is a multiple of 2. We have successfully generalized existing formulas for the dilaton coupling and fermion mass terms to theories with multiple Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation of SU(N), and we have verified our derived formulas against known data for SU(N) with a single Weyl fermion in the adjoint representation. Our research has also demonstrated that the results for SU(N) with multiple Wyl fermions in the adjoint representation can be achieved by combining SU(N) theories with single Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation with higher-dimensional gauge theories based on the product of two SU(N) groups.

We establish the equivalence of group codes C and D, and D's dual code D^⊥, where codes C and D are defined using the Kronecker product of matrices from group algebra ℓ1(Γ;R/Z), where R/Z denotes the circle group. This equivalence is achieved by identifying a finite index subgroup of Γ, resulting in an equivalent code defined by the product code of two codes over ℓ1(Λ;R/Z), where Λ denotes the finite index subgroup.

Bucket Elimination is a general algorithm for graphical model inference and optimization. It's often inefficient due to its global nature, but we've found ways to improve its performance by incorporating local elimination processes. Depending on the available information, we can switch between two variants: Bucket Elimination and its dual version. We've also applied these ideas to clustering problems, and our methods have successful real-world applications in medicine and computer vision, outperforming other techniques.

The ability to drop objects is a fundamental action that involves coordinating multiple senses such as vision and kinesthesia. Research in this domain has primarily focused on the analysis of visual data. Unlike existing studies, our work integrates high-resolution visual information with kinesthetic data to accurately identify dropped objects. By merging both vision and kinesthesia, our system leverages the strengths of each modality to achieve a better outcome. To accomplish this, our proposed Spatio-Temporal Invariant Object detection (STIO) approach utilizes a Multi-Sensor Fusion Deep Neural Network to merge kinesthetic and visual data. The STIO's ability to generate dropped object representations is further enhanced through the use of an Invariant Object Embedding (IOE) component that draws from both vision and kinesthesia. Our research shows that the STIO outperforms other methods in identifying dropped objects, even when the identity of the object in question is unknown. To validate our method, our team conducted a series of human-like drop experiments using 21 everyday objects. The results of these experiments confirm that the STIO outperforms other existing methods, demonstrating a significant improvement of 44% and 10% over the second best method in identifying objects when the drop occurs either with the arm in neutral or to the side.

This study merges the theories of jamming and shear rheology to develop a comprehensive approach,  combining the principles of frictionless isotropic jamming, developed by a team led by Martin Weigand, and frictional shear jamming,  as described by J. N. Wilber, J. F. Bouchard, and J. F. Brady.  We derive a key set of equations that relate the yield stress, isotropic susceptibility, and shear modulus to key jamming parameters,  including the volume fraction at jamming, $ \phi_j $, and the exponents $ \alpha $ and $ \beta $ characterizing isotropic and shear jamming,  respectively.  Jamming occurs when the modulus or stress exceeds thresholds defined by $ \phi_j (1 - \phi_j) / \phi_j^\alpha $ and $ (1 - \phi_j)/\phi_j^\beta $,  where $ \phi_j $ is the volume fraction at jamming, and where $ \alpha $ and $ \beta $ equal 1.15, 1.5, and 1.75 for isotropic,  shear, and shear-isotropy jamming,  respectively.  This work challenges the widely held belief that jamming and shear jamming are separate phenomena,  and demonstrates that they are interconnected,  sharing common exponents and thresholds,  and where the absence of shear jamming is reflected in the absence of isot

A novel time series model known as MS(2)-AR(4) has been designed to capture short-term and medium-term dynamics in time series data. The model's reliability and effectiveness will be evaluated by comparing it to an autoregressive model, which is a commonly used method for forecasting, on a dataset consisting of historical electricity demand data from Germany. The comparison between MS(2)-AR(4) and AR(4) will be based on both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Additionally, the ability of the models to capture patterns and trends in data will be determined by examining the parameter estimates and the residual plots, as well as by computing the mean absolute error and the coefficients of determination for each model. The results of the analysis indicate that MS(2)-AR(4) is a reliable method for the given data, and it outperforms AR(4) in terms of capturing trends and forecasting accuracy.

In the United States, state and local professionals rely heavily on Google's search engine for essential tasks. These individuals need to be aware that Google's search outcomes are infrequently neutral, and algorithmic biases affect various groups. This research examines how Google's search results vary for male and female government workers in Seattle. By analyzing search data, we identified noticeable disparities in search outcomes. These results suggest that Google's algorithm favors men when searching for jobs related to law enforcement but favors women when searching for jobs in social services. This study highlights the importance for public professionals to be informed about the limitations of algorithmic search outcomes.

Our research framework generates programs by connecting pre-existing code snippets, 
and assesses the speed and accuracy of this approach using a large dataset of 
educational programs. It evaluates program synthesis via a multi-stage process where 
programs are repeatedly requested and assessed, with newly synthesized code reviewed 
for accuracy. The framework demonstrates program synthesis's reliability and swiftness, 
as it accurately reproduces 75% of program specifications within 1-3 seconds, with nearly 
all specifications accurately replicated within 1 minute. Analysis further indicates that 
most errors stem from a single or two code modifications. Additionally, the framework 
identifies and addresses four prevalent program synthesis challenges.

To tackle complex global problems like climate change, we need a clear understanding of the Earth's climate system. However, reducing the complexity of these systems through mathematical modeling is a significant challenge. Novel research employs model reduction techniques to analyze the main processes of the Earth's climate system, incorporating artificial intelligence and machine learning concepts. These advanced reduction methods enable the preservation of key climate mechanisms while eliminating unnecessary details. resulting in simplified models of the Earth's climate system.

The James Webb Space Telescope is poised to offer a precise observation of kilonova emissions in the infrared spectrum, which will be critical in determining the expansion velocity of the ejecta. However, kilonovae also emit radiation in a narrow wavelength range, known as fine structure lines. For instance, emission from iron can extend the boundary of observable kilonova emissions by indicating a higher expansion velocity than other signals. Although JWST's sub-millimeter instruments can detect some fine structure lines, other JWST instruments like NIRSpec can observe lines in the infrared spectrum. Yet, research has demonstrated that kilonova emissions in the sub-millimeter spectrum from iron can be detectable with a telescope that has a diameter of at least 8 meters, but not with JWST or other telescopes with similar diameters in the optical range. Our research contrasts these findings with observations of kilonovae from the gravitational wave event GW190814, which could be the result of a 2.26 solar mass neutron star merger or a 85 solar mass black hole merger. If the latter occurred, researchers estimate that a 2.26 solar mass neutron star was present, with a kilonova velocity of at least 0.2 that of a 85 solar mass black hole merger. As a result, a 8 to 10 meter telescope in the optical range would be necessary to observe kilonova emissions from a 85 solar mass black hole merger in JWST. However,

In recent years, the use of an increasing number of electronic devices near cancer treatment machines has led to (i) increased delivery times due to interruptions, (ii) a higher risk of patients being in the wrong position during treatment due to prolonged sessions, and (iii) a greater likelihood of radiation beams hitting unwanted areas. To mitigate these issues, a system called Monitored Respiration-Gated Radiotherapy has been developed to improve treatment efficiency and accuracy. However, this system can cause significant treatment delays, leading to a need for a new framework. Our proposed framework, called the PGRT framework, aims to minimize treatment time while minimizing the risk of patients being in the wrong position, even in the presence of interruptions. This framework uses (i) an algorithm that determines the optimal treatment time, taking into account potential interruptions, and (ii) an analysis of radiation doses to identify the maximum dose to any area of the body. This framework works by dividing the treatment process into smaller segments, and then calculating the optimal time for each segment based on whether the patient is in the correct position and potential interference from external devices. These calculations take into account several factors, including how quickly the patient needs to be in the correct position, compensation for any dose discrepancies, and a safety margin to account for any uncertainties. Our proposed framework has shown promising results in several tests, including cases involving patients with lung and brain cancer, even when not knowing the exact position of the patient in advance. Compositional data analysis is characterized by applying the log-ratio transformation to data vectors. This approach relies heavily on the assumption that the relative proportions of components in objects are sufficient to fully describe them. When that assumption is violated, the results of compositional data analysis are compromised by unwanted biases. We have developed methods to identify objects that induce inseparable projections in compositional data and proposed a strategy to eliminate partial leverage points through object pooling. The process of identifying partial collapse points is associated with the computation of principal components. For each projected object, we evaluate the degree of collapse and pool it with other objects within the same group if necessary. The performance of our approach was confirmed by simulation experiments and real-world applications of principal components and canonical variates.

The core accretion and stellar disk migration theories claim to explain planet formation, but a key issue with core accretation lies in it predicting the existence of giant planets orbiting close to their host stars. If these planets are detected in large numbers, it would support this theory. However, a massive dataset of 2,331 transiting giant planets does not provide the expected results, as these planets are not as close to their hosts as they should be. Instead, another mechanism such as photoevaporation that reduces the size of these planets over time by exposing their hotter, inner parts is more compatible with observed distributions. Recent studies using artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms have shown that they can effectively use observational data to solve problems in planet formation. Specifically, an analysis of a massive exoplanet dataset that incorporates migration and photoevaporation mechanisms shows that trained models can identify key factors such as planet mass and radius that are influenced by these processes. These models provide insights that would be difficult to obtain through traditional statistical analysis and can serve as a tool to better understand the effects of migration and photoevaporation on planetary mass and radius distributions.

In this analysis, we evaluate the AFMN model, a variant of the Gated Neural Network, through which an agent learns to forecast both visible and invisible states by retaining past unobserved data and modifying its memory structure in response to new information. To understand the AFMN model's performance, we examine its capability to track unobserved states and observe how its dynamic memory architecture enhances its predictive abilities with limited data. Our study indicates that the AFMN model achieves superior results compared to standard GNNs in certain challenging conditions. Additionally, we identify a crucial role for dynamic memory in handling difficult situations, and we explore the potential implications of dynamic memory for an agent's ability to solve problem-solving tasks.

A feeble interaction is developed between a standard model scalar and a dark matter candidate, where a new gauge symmetry is established, resulting in the new gauge boson decaying into a dark matter candidate and a standard model fermion. This interaction is further investigated as a means to generate the dark matter abundance. If the mass of the scalar mediator is less than the mass of the dark matter candidate, the resulting dark matter properties resemble an ideal WIMP; however, if the scalar mediator's mass surpasses the dark matter candidate's mass, its properties deviate from a standard WIMP, requiring an unconventional interpretation of the dark matter's present abundance. A dark matter mass, ranging from 1 to 10 TeV, is scrutinized for the cross section of the dark matter candidate for its scattering off of standard model quarks, where a series of numerical simulations, known as numerical simulations using MadGraph5~AMC@NLO and MadGraph5~AMC@NLO matched to CTES, determine the ratio of the branching fractions for the new gauge boson's decays. This is undertaken while adhering to the requirement that the dark matter candidate for its mass less than 1 TeV has not been detected at the Large Hadron Collider.

We introduce Mod-Cog, a comprehensive cognitive task battery, designed to
evaluate cognitive functioning in diverse populations. Building on existing
cognitive task assessments, Mod-Cog expands the landscape by incorporating
a broader range of tasks, increasing variety and cognitive difficulty. To
establish norms, Mod-Cog was applied to 1,017 healthy adults from 18 to
85 years old. Each participant completed an extensive 50-task battery, which
was analyzed along with cognitive performance data. Results establish baseline
performance standards for each task and correlate task performance with known
cognitive functions, demonstrating high reliability across tasks. Mod-Cog
offers a more extensive and nuanced assessment of cognitive function, allowing
for the detection of both mild and pronounced cognitive deficits and the
d distinction between different cognitive impairments.

The geometric approach of D. Benois to classifying nilpotent algebras is expanded to include a classification method for solvable algebras based on their Lie properties.  The variety of nilpotent algebras of a specific step can be reduced to a finite union of geometric varieties.  Each geometric variety is associated with a set of Markovian Lie properties and a corresponding irreducible algebra.  The dimension of the variety is determined by a numerical value.  The research provides a mathematical framework for solving problems related to nilpotent and solvable algebras and provides examples of its applications.  Additionally, the research demonstrates that geometric varieties resulting from different combinations of Lie properties are often non-densely intersecting, leading to previously unestablished results.  The research also provides an answer to a problem posed by A. Ovsyannikov and proves a statement made by M. Zaicev.

Large-scale structures, known as large-scale jets, play a significant role in understanding cosmic evolution through their widespread presence. These jets, composed of radiation, originate from inverse Compton interaction between high-speed electrons and microwaves, posing a significant challenge for researchers to uncover the cosmos' early secrets, as their intensity is significantly reduced by energy loss over vast distances. A new technique utilizes the distinct orientations of linear structures within jets to determine the velocity of high-speed electrons by analyzing polarization changes in radiation. This method was applied to a well-known jet called M84, allowing researchers to determine its velocity at 0.3 to 0.6 times the speed of light, consistent with theoretical models.

Tadmor and Arpenius introduced an 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization, 
expressing the Lorentz group in a straightforward manner, which can 
facilitate analytical expansions in general relativity. In this paper, 
an alternative, computationally efficient method is proposed for 
evaluating relativistic expansions. Additionally, a specific example is 
examined, comparing two methods for calculating relativistic expansions: 
one based on the 'pre-non-relativistic' method and the other employing 
the regular hyperbolic series. Our analysis demonstrates that both 
methods yield equivalent expansions, although the 'pre-non-relativistic' 
expansion appears more amenable to analytical analysis.

A novel, partially flexible image registration method is introduced, designed to overcome limitations in medical images where intensity contrast varies or is obscured by noise and abnormalities. Building on the SIFT-CPD (Conditional Probability Distribution) framework, this new approach develops flexible similarity measures tailored to each image pair, enhancing registration performance. The method's performance is evaluated against 2015 MICCAI IBSR 2009 dataset and compared with state-of-the-art SIFT-based variants, demonstrating improved results in terms of mean absolute three-dimensional average landmark distance (AAD) and computational speed. The novel method showcases reduced AAD distance of 0.118, 0.137, and 0.157 mm for SIFT-CPD, SIFT-CC and SIFT-CR, and its open-source implementation is accessible at https://github.com/pannevsift/sift-cpd-registration.

We have identified and analyzed a unique binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, which is known for exhibiting frequent and predictable eclipses. During our research, we obtained in-depth spectral data using the High Resolution Spectrometer on the Keck Haleakala Telescope, which revealed that this star system comprises two white dwarfs with sizes that are nearly identical, but with a slight disparity. These findings have enabled us to make a detailed prediction about the future stability of the star system. According to our calculations, the star system will experience a dramatic and cataclysmic transformation in approximately 70 years, resulting in the massive merger of the two white dwarfs, which will likely be preceded by significant changes in their orbital patterns. It is predicted that the star system will initially exhibit an irregular and pulse-driven instability during the final stages of its evolution, which will later give way to a stable and drum-regular oscillation pattern.

In deep learning, particularly in neural networks, incorporating domain-specific information often enhances performance but also adds complexity. The incorporation of additional constraints can facilitate this integration while optimizing outcomes. A specialized form of layer, the UOT-Pooling layer, allows for the implicit incorporation of domain-specific information within a network, thereby simplifying the optimization process. The UOT-Pooling layer builds upon Otto's optimal mapping theorem, enabling the direct translation of data features into optimized metrics, thereby serving as a layer for optimizing domain transfer. The integration of this layer within an neural network enables improved performance, specifically on datasets with varying feature dimensions, through the optimization of domain transfer. The implementation of this layer has been found to surpass previous methods in specific tasks, demonstrating a high potential for other tasks as well.

We analyzed the orientation of 29 Seyfert nuclei within galaxies using data from the Hubble Space Telescope. Their host galaxies' spiral arms were clearly visible, and we studied the distribution of these nuclei in relation to those arms. We discovered that, generally, the orientation of the nuclei is aligned with the direction of the arms. However, there's a significant difference between Type 1 and Type 2 nuclei: those of Type 2 are more likely to be aligned at less than 45 degrees with the arms' direction, whereas Type 1 nuclei are equally likely to be aligned at 45 to 90 degrees as they are at less than 45 degrees. We also found that the most active among the Type 1 nuclei tend to have their host galaxies' central regions less disordered. We discuss the possible explanations for these findings, including the impact of gas and radiation, and propose that the dimming of active nuclei is often caused by the obscuration of the host galaxy's central regions.

A new approach has been introduced to classify and identify flat general rotation surfaces based on their pointwise 1-type Gauss map. This method has been successfully applied to specific types of surfaces: Minkowski spaces, Bertrand curves, and planar curves. Furthermore, an equation has been developed to represent the pointwise 1-type Gauss map of a flat general rotation surface. This discovery provides a key concept for understanding the properties of these surfaces. Additionally, a condition has been established to define developing maps of flat general rotation surfaces. This has led to the discovery of a new class of surfaces known as 1-type rotation surfaces, which include Minkowski spaces, Bertrand curves, and planar curves. The paper also discusses the relationship between the pointwise 1-type Gauss map and the curvature of a flat general rotation surface.

Reconstructing 3D scenes from multiple images is a more complex task
requiring higher levels of collaboration between computer vision and
machine learning components than simple image estimation. Nevertheless, it
enables more efficient pre-training of models for downstream tasks. To do
this, however, we need a generic, vast dataset of accurate 3D reconstructions
to leverage as a training resource. The standard approach to creating such a
dataset involves collecting stereo correspondence labels for a multitude of
real-world images, an expensive and time-consuming process. In this research,
we suggest an alternative method, using scene geometry estimation instead of
classification, and a novel self-supervised learning approach based on
predicting the colors of pixels from adjacent viewpoints to generate these
reconstructions quickly and accurately. This method has performed successfully
