block binary vector, which significantly improves the compression ratio
of DNNs by 30%. The developed method enables the implementation of
high-accuracy DNNs on embedded devices while utilizing minimal memory.

Protein structure refinement using expert-based rules has been demonstrated to be effective in improving protein model accuracy through analysis of stereochemical properties. ProCS, a version of the program that uses expert rules on the Rosetta structure refinement framework, has been shown to significantly reduce overall energy scores in refined models. Building on previous work, an enhanced method, ProCS2, has been developed to incorporate additional expert rules and improve the accuracy of stereochemical properties used in the refinement process. In a series of experiments, it was found that ProCS2 outperformed the original method, and when used in ab-initio and template-based protein structure prediction, it significantly improved main chain accuracy across various scenarios.

Training deep networks relies on picking an appropriate choice of loss function, yet little has been done to explore how various loss functions affect their generalizability. Most research has centered around finding loss functions with good theoretical properties, but under-represented areas, such as KL Divergence, remain overlooked despite being commonly used in supervised and semi-supervised learning. Our findings show that leveraging KL Divergence in deep networks improves performance, and through thorough analysis under multiple scenarios, we uncover evidence suggesting it fostance generalizability by mitigating overfitting caused by correlated features. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of cross-validation in determining the best loss function for a specific problem. To facilitate the discovery of under-represented loss functions, we propose an efficient loss function search method, searching's an extensive library of loss functions, and discovers that KL Divergence outperforms traditional loss functions like cross-entropy in semi-supervised settings. Our research is the first to explore the effects of loss functions on deep neural networks' generalizability, and our findings are reproducible at the repository link.

We examine the fractional quartets model through the lens of the hamiltonian-derived model and parquet approximations. A key observation is that the former adheres to crossing symmetry and conservation laws, in stark contrast to the standard parquet amplitude. Notably, the hamiltonian-derived model's amplitude agrees with the parquet amplitude at the level of leading-order renormalization but differs at higher orders. Additionally, the larger class of hamiltonian-derived correlation functions offers more comprehensive insights compared to the parquet approximation. As such, the fractional quartets model serves as a critical test case to evaluate the limitations of these approximation methods.

In monolayer TiSe2, there's a transition from a CDW state with an incommensurate deviation to a structural transition at a specific critical point.  We've studied this transition through time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, examining the evolution of the CDW state as it progresses towards a fully saturated phase.  We discovered that an exciton condensation occurs in the final stages of the phase transition, combining with the CDW to form an exciton-CDW mixed state.  We've identified that an exciton condensation arises from strong many-body interactions within the Fermi surface, giving rise to an attractive effective mass.  We've also observed the activation of new excitonic states across the Brillouin zone during the final phase of the phase transition, indicating a strong exciton-phonon coupling that drives the initial CDW state in TiSe2.

Many modern emergency services are adopting text-based risk reporting systems to collect information from users more efficiently. However, the structure of these systems varies, causing difficulties in processing reports that don't conform to expected formats. To overcome this challenge, a trained neural model is proposed to learn the format of specific risk types from annotated data and subsequently classify reports into those categories. The model then uses those categories to learn the format of individual risks. Another approach is to only learn the dispatch information, ignoring the risk categories, and use a rule-based system to determine the format. A comparison of these methods shows that both perform well on test data, with the choice depending on the available resources and risk systems. The model is designed to be easily adapted to other risk systems by simply updating the training data. The implementation is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/academic-degree/FormatFormer.

The topological characteristics of a Fermi surface can significantly influence a material's magnetic properties in the superconducting state. According to the theory developed by Volovik, the magnetic susceptibility in the superconducting state is directly related to the Chern number of the Fermi surface. This concept has been successfully applied to unconventional superconductors based on heavy fermions and features-rich topological surfaces. Additionally, the importance of Fermi surface topology can be seen in the context of topological superconductors, where it directly influences readable quantities in quantum computation. This article discusses recent experimental findings indicating that Fermi surface topology plays a crucial role in the phenomenon of striped superconductivity observed in cuprates. Striped superconductivity is characterized by modulated superconducting order parameters that can be understood by considering the topology of extended Fermi surfaces across the Brillouin zone. This article examines the experimental evidence for striped superconductivity in cuprates and its relation to the topological characteristics of the Fermi surface.

Active learning algorithms enable the efficient selection of training data to minimize supervision costs. This paper presents an innovative, semi-supervised active learning algorithm driven by a minimax entropy function, designed to overcome the limitations of standard uncertainty and diversity criteria in sample choice. The proposed method guarantees a more balanced selection of high uncertainty and diverse samples compared to current approaches. Additionally, it is capable of function value-based sampling, a feature lacking in previous semi-supervised methods. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through comprehensive experimentation on a range of regression and classification tasks, showcasing its superior performance relative to established active learning techniques.

Through a collaborative filtering approach that leverages decoded audio features from neural models, we investigated the similarity of timbre in songs from different genres and different periods. Our method demonstrated considerable accuracy when applied to both categorization and similarity calculation tasks. Additionally, we analyzed the global trends in musical similarity over the decades by employing a similarity network that grouped songs based on their decade. The findings indicated a noticeable pattern of similarity in songs from the same decade and also revealed more subtle, persistent connections within certain musical styles across different eras. To enhance the robustness of our method, we incorporated a diversity principle.

This paper examines a stochastic process an agent observes over time, where each observation comes with reinforcement information about its statistical structure.  We study two variants of this process, where reinforcement is given both locally, i.e., relative to a specific observation, and globally, i.e., relative to the sample space.  Our analysis focuses on how the agent's knowledge about the underlying process evolves over time, particularly in terms of its entropy.  Under both scenarios, our results demonstrate that the number of blocks in the process the agent can distinguish between grows without bound as time progresses, where a block is defined as a collection of events with similar occurrence probabilities.

In proof-theoretic semantics, the relationship between principles is studied through containment and the converse relationship, drawing on cut-elimination and diametric reduction. This report explores these concepts within a general framework, applicable to a range of proof systems. It also examines the relationship between weaker and stronger forms of the weakening and contraction principles. The report is rooted in an informal proof-theoretic framework but also provides a formalized version, along with an example of its application to atomic logic.

Reward learning systems, which use agent feedback to update policies without a pre-defined reward function, can be inefficient as the reward function remains unknown. Utilizing human feedback, both online and offline, via comparative tasks has shown potential. However, current systems treat human feedback as binary, ignoring its comparative nature, and batch process this feedback poorly, leading to decreased efficiency. To improve this, we've developed an algorithm to batch process human comparisons, thereby reducing computational costs, and demonstrated its efficiency through theoretical bounds and practical tests on multiple domains. Moreover, our findings suggest comparing feedback from multiple sources could be an effective strategy. As a result, we're one step closer to leveraging human comparisons on a large scale for reward learning.

The Smyth powerspace is defined by a construction that involves taking the discrete powerspace of a framed pretopology. This construction was initially applied to compact frames but has been extended to general framed pretopologies. It has been discovered that the Smyth powerspace of any core-compact framed pretopology does not necessarily exhibit core-compact properties. However, it does preserve the properties of semi-core-compactness and weakly core-compactness. An example illustrates that these properties do not necessarily transfer from the original pretopology to the Smyth powerspace. The Smyth powerspace is defined as the valued space of continuous functions from a core-compact framed pretopology, and it has been found that the latter can be expressed as the valued space of lower semicontinuous affine functions from a certain specific type of Valued space.

For vortices in a two-dimensional body of fluid, the phase space of their trajectories is the space of oriented loops in the plane, starting and ending at the same point, with a fixed point as reference. This paper calculates the components of the gradient flow of the area these loops encircle, in the space of reparameterized loops. The calculations reveal that the gradient flow is constant in a particular configuration space, depending on the vorticity distribution. This result generalizes a previous finding, showing the area these loops encircle decreases over time, regardless of the distribution's shape, and now demonstrates the effect for any distribution with a certain symmetry property.

This research investigates how various conditions influence the AIPW estimator for nonlinear models. Our analysis reveals that AIPW is a biased estimator when no regularization is applied, yet becomes an almost sure winner at certain prediction points when AIPW is smoothed using random projections. However, both the original and smoothed AIPW estimators yield inconsistent results as the number of observations grows thinner. To address these findings, we propose an alternative method - the AIPW with Projections on Span of X (AIPW-POX) - which chooses the smoothed AIPW estimator from a set of finite values. Our study shows that AIPW-POX is a consistent and convergent estimator. To illustrate the performance of AIPW-POX, our research conducts a series of experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets.

The mass of the tau particle, at 1.775 GeV, falls within a favourable range for lattice studies. This allows researchers to utilise data from high-energy colliders such as LHCb, making the tau lepton a valuable focus of theoretical and experimental inquiry. The tau lepton's properties, particularly its form factors and decay widths, are being thoroughly explored by theoretical physicists. One notable aspect is the mixed action approach utilised in the Lattice QCD calculations. This technique involves matching ensembles with varying lattice spacings and quark masses. The challenges and successes of the mixed action approach are evident in the calculations for the tau lepton's form factors. Despite these complexities, notable progress has been made in the calculations. The LHCb detector's capabilities, including its detection efficiency and background rate, are also crucial in the experimental context. The incorporation of tau decay modes with lower branching ratios, such as tau to kaon and eta, could offer opportunities for further discovery. The opportunities and obstacles of the tau lepton's properties are being presented, highlighting the advancements in lattice QCD calculations and the prospects for future experimentation.

In a rapidly rotating annulus with a vertical wall and heated from within, highly organized baroclinic waves form near the surface, characterized by strong vorticity and temperature contrasts. These surface features, driven by the Baroclinic Vortex Formation Dynamics, arise from the interaction between the wall and the interior convection, forming distinct patterns through a nonlinear process. To investigate the development of these patterns, both laboratory and numerical investigations were conducted, focusing on the baroclinic wave dynamics and their variations in response to the width of the annulus. The resulting baroclinic waves, identified by their Nakanishi and Yoshida classification, exhibited either a sharp or gradual transition to the wall, determined by the intensity of the convective motion within the interior. These patterns, representing a unique balance between the convective and rotational influences, may offer a framework for the understanding of similar geological patterns, as well as those observed in atmospheric and oceanic systems, providing valuable insights into the intricate baroclinic wave dynamics.

This study proposes a Bayesian approach for estimating extreme value models, starting with the Generalized Pareto Distribution, and demonstrates the method's applicability to other models, such as the Log-Pareto Distribution, based on prior knowledge or data. A key aspect of this approach involves specifying a tuning parameter'm', which can significantly influence the estimation process. To mitigate uncertainty surrounding'm', we suggest two techniques: the use of multiple'm' values, and incorporating a predictive uncertainty measure into the estimation process. We examine the performance of these methods in simulations and real-world applications, while also exploring alternative tuning parameter options.

We ask whether reinforcement learning with a certain level of corruption is possible. Corruption, conceptualized as adversarial reinforcement learning problems, can be thought of as a limitation on the agency's ability to learn. To study this, we consider a robust reinforcement learning model where the learner aims to find the most beneficial policy in the presence of corruption. We give an algorithm that learns the optimal policy and remains stable when faced with corruption up to a certain point, even in the most challenging scenario. However, this algorithm changes significantly depending on the amount of corruption, so we examine what happens in the medium corruption case and discover that under specific conditions, a simpler algorithm can be stable up to a certain level of corruption, but not necessarily when corruption exceeds a certain point, so we set a limit on its usefulness. The problem becomes increasingly difficult as the amount of corruption grows.

This study examines the controllability of the impulsive heat equation in both finite and infinite dimensional spaces. The research demonstrates that impulse approximation can be used to achieve controllability in these spaces, and a parallel can be drawn with the smooth heat equation in terms of the role of impulse control. Specifically, it has been found that a finite number of impulsive controls can be sufficient for controllability in finite dimensional spaces, while a larger number of impulses may be required in infinite dimensional spaces.

Detecting data anomalies that lie outside of a model's training distribution is a crucial issue in artificial intelligence. Various methods have been developed for this purpose, but their performance is often tested on easily detectable out-of-distribution data. As real-world anomalies can be subtle and hard to identify, this study examined the effectiveness of these methods on more challenging anomaly detection tasks. Different from previous studies that use specific methods to create in-distribution and out-of-distribution data, this research relied on existing pre-trained language models to generate both data types. Our results show that deep learning methods using density-based detectors struggle with small and difficult cases, while shallower approaches, such as generative-based detectors, perform better in such scenarios. Moreover, this study revealed that incorporating data augmentation can significantly boost a model's anomaly detection accuracy. Our proposal, a density-independent detector that uses multiple preprocessing techniques, achieved the highest overall accuracy in detecting anomalies. Our work is based on anomaly detection in natural language, but the methods we developed are versatile and can be applied to detecting anomalies in various other data types.

In the center of every cell, the molecular structure of tubules like microtubers regulates the movement of molecules, allowing them to switch between growing and shrinking. This process is controlled by molecules like dynein, which changes the configuration of a headpiece in response to electrical stimuli, generating forces that can switch between pushing and pulling. Mathematical models based on experimental data describe this movement and how it's influenced by changes in the molecular structure, highlighting the importance of adapting movement patterns to maintain cell growth.

The main goal of this research is to explore how to convert a specific type of transducer, known as a non-deterministic two-way word transducer, into another form, specifically an origin-equivalent one-way transducer, utilizing a resynchronizer with bounded and regular origins. A series of examples will be provided to demonstrate that, in many instances, a resynchronizer cannot be defined without referencing all possible origins. These counterexamples will be analyzed to better understand their implications and characteristics.
Our analysis reveals that computing a specific entry in the f-Convolution can be done in $O(mn)$ time, a more efficient approach than calculating the entire convolution, which takes $O(mnc)$ time.

GJ 229B, a T-dwarf planet discovered in 1995 on GJ 229A, ranks as the first known object of its kind. GJ 229B was found to have atmospheric conditions different from initially measured chemical composition, discovered via direct spectroscopy at a wavelength of 7 microns. Cross-analyses of atmospheric spectra, obtained through multiple observations at various wavelengths, have uncovered significant alterations in chemical composition, prompting a review of primary formation theories for objects of intermediate nature, falling between planets and stars.

Quark model assumptions are scrutinized through a continuum renormalization approach that analyzes the spectral density in the correlator of two color singlets. This method allows for a thorough investigation of the corrolator's spectral density along with its interaction regions. Our results indicate that only certain quark model parameters, specifically those governing the linear potentials and color forces, have a tangible effect on the spectral density's structure, thereby implying the existence of tetraquark states. Conversely, potentials and forces influence the binding energies of the constituent quarks. This analysis sheds light on the nature of tetraquark states and potentially identifies the corrolator's spectral structure as a more sensitive indicator of bound states than lattice renormalon effects.

We've calculated the CP-violating phase, $\phi_s$, in the $B^0_s$-$\bar{B}^0_s$ oscillations
precisely within the Standard Model using QCD sum rules. The $\phi_s$ value is crucial
for verifying or dismiss new physical entities in searches for CP violation in $B^0_s \to J/
{\psi} \phi$. Additionally, our analysis allowed us to determine the $C P$-conserving phase,
$\beta_s$, which can be used to make more accurate measurements of the $B^0_s$ decay rate
width and search for new physical elements.

To evaluate the effectiveness of various models in predicting aerosol spread, researchers compared an simplified model to more intricate representations. The simplified model, well-mixed in nature, assumed aerosol particles are evenly distributed in a room and instantly reach equilibrium. In contrast, the intricate models simulated specific ventilation systems, accounting for room configurations and air circulation patterns. The study discovered that, under specific conditions, the well-mixed model yielded predictions comparable to those of the intricate models, with the caveat that it cannot simulate specific scenarios. The study examined aerosol dispersal from two sources: an infected person standing alone, or two infected people moving around a room together. In both cases, the well-mixed model's predictions were reasonable, although it failed to account for the distance between the individuals. The researchers propose the well-mixed model as a potential tool for creating simple, rule-based protocols to mitigate the transmission of aerosol-borne viruses.

This study explores the $\gamma$-transitions originating from the $\beta$-decay of even-even $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te isotopes within the $\beta$-vibration band of the $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te nuclei. The research also investigates the $\beta$-decay transitions of the odd-odd $^{137}$I and $^{135}$I isotopes within the $\gamma$-vibration band of the $^{137}$Ge and $^{135}$Ge nuclei, focusing on the coupled $\pi$ and $\nu$ particles. The findings provide insight into the $\beta$-decay 1np-1hp transitions of the $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te nuclei, shedding light on the np-ho TMO and hp-np TMO structures.

Recently, a new set of technical tools is needed to automatically identify breaches in existing exchange programs. These Breaches in Exciting Normal (BEN) tools will likely utilize unique theorems that have been developed in the research of homotopy type theory. This article discusses one instance of such a tool - detection of violations in symmetric enriched categories. It presents a homotopy type theory definition for a violation in such a context and proves that a violation exists if and only if a certain part of the theory does not have a unit. Using unique properties of homotopy type theory, we can prove that this part always has a unique value regardless of the inputs. These benefits come with a cost - the detection process may take longer as it depends on a specific entity called a choice, which may not exist in all situations. However, research shows that in most common exchange programs, a choice does exist and can be used to improve the detection process. Another BEN tool is being developed for a different type of program by using a different set of unique theorems.

The masses of the lightest $F$-wave bottom mesons, denoted as $B^*_{(s)}$, have been calculated using the lightest $D$-wave mesons as reference in the $t$-matrix formalism. It is discovered that the masses of these $F$-wave bottom mesons adhere to Regge trajectories, both for positive and negative parities. The calculated $t$-matrix elements for these $F$-wave bottom mesons are also determined. Furthermore, the masses of the $D$-wave bottom mesons, specifically $B^*_s$, have been computed in various models, leading to a comparison with our $t$-matrix results.

We examine Szabados's conjecture, which posits that for any minimal periodic composition of period $d$, with $h$ being the smallest height, there exists a $1\leq k\leq h$ such that $k$ mod $d$ has a valid decomposition with height $k$. Our results demonstrate that this conjecture holds for compositions with relatively simple period patterns, but may not hold for more complex cases. In particular, we prove that for a composition with a prime period, there will always exist a $k$ mod $d$ having a valid decomposition within the range $[1, h]$. On the other hand, we identify a composition with a composite period, whose heights do not satisfy Szabados's conjecture.

Dynamic mode decomposition has been widely utilized to extract significant characteristics from large datasets that evolve over time. However, for nonlinear systems, the solution obtained through DMD often lacks global validity. To overcome this limitation, a novel kernel-based DMD method was developed, which enables the retention of temporal and spatial coherence. The kernel enables the alignment of DMD modes according to their similarity, resulting in more robust performance when dealing with sparse or noisy data. The computational cost of this method can be controlled by adjusting the width of the kernel. The kernel-based DMD was successfully applied to multiple complex systems, producing more stable and interpretable results compared to traditional DMD.

The Fitness and Complexity algorithm evaluates strategies by assessing their performance and variability in response to different conditions. In the study, the algorithm was modified to assess the strength of chess openings, a highly structured domain with a finite number of variables. The analysis measured opening efficacy through a game tree search, a criterion for player skill was introduced based on public player evaluations, and the algorithm's findings matched these criteria, indicating that the model's assessments correlated with expert judgments of player ability. Additionally, the researchers used the model to analyze various topics in chess, such as the value of specific pieces and pawns, the effectiveness of different opening principles, and how player skills influence the application of openings and other strategic elements. The study's data supported several natural chess biases, demonstrating that the model's assessments aligned with expert intuition and empirical observations in the domain.

In a binary system consisting of a compact object, such as a neutron star or white dwarf, the process of accretion-driven orbital spiral-in occurs. As the object spirals closer to its companion, it undergoes a range of transformations. Ultimately, it may eventually merge with the other star in the system. Researchers have identified multiple distinct phases in the accretion-induced collapse and have used various models to study its complex behavior. Specifically, a new model was developed to track the evolution of the object from a compact star to a merged star. When applied to a binary system with equal initial mass, the model shows that a stable merged star can form, characterized by a core composed of iron and silicates, surrounded by a disk of gas and angular momentum. This model provides valuable insights into the processes underlying the development of merged stars and the formation of compact binary systems.

We examine a method to obtain first integrals for higher-degree Euler-Lagrange equations, starting with examples in two and three dimensions. The approach is applied to the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator and its modified variants. Additionally, we derive a method to calculate the first integrals of Euler-Lagrange systems in 'n' dimensional space with arbitrary order.

Three-dimensional shape retrieval is a challenging problem, particularly when it comes to retrieving 3D shapes from sketch-like inputs. Current retrieval methods are often based on learning features that are close to standard 2D sketch features but the problem lies in these standard features being designed for quick and coherent human drawing, not the abstract and intricate nature of 3D sketches. Our research introduces a novel framework for 3D shape retrieval from 3D sketches that learns sketch-like features directly from 3D shapes. These features, derived from the ViBE-RNN framework that mimics complex 3D shapes, outperform state-of-the-art approaches on several benchmarks and demonstrate better generalization in our experiments. Additionally, our framework allows us to generate sketches that are more relevant to the 3D shape in question, leading to a higher retrieval accuracy.

The planet HD80606b, a gas giant, was directly observed using Jupiter's size as a reference, in 2001. Its temperature rose from 1000K to 1900K in a 2000km thick atmosphere as it passed close to its star. Due to its low mass and close proximity to the host star, the planet's spin was slowed and caused its orbital and rotational axes to align. Researchers studied how the planet's atmosphere varied in response to its star's changing distance and illumination during its 111-Earth-day orbit. Using a three-dimensional climate model, they simulated the planet's temperature and winds, and discovered that its star's rapid changes in the early stages of its orbit triggered a and strong atmospheric flow that slowed down as the planet further increased in distance. As the planet continued on its orbit, a and the winds reversed, saving up kinetic energy to produce a and dramatic 27-part thermal inertia effect in the planet's orbit. As the planet continued on its orbit, a and the winds reversed, saving up kinetic energy to produce a dramatic 97-part thermal inertia effect in the planet's temperature. Researchers found that a and the winds reversed, saving up kinetic energy to produce a dramatic 107-part thermal inertia effect in the planet's temperature.

Researchers previously discovered that certain cosmological models contain singularities where the density and pressure become infinitely large. However, the density and pressure are highly variable in these models, making it unclear if they truly behave singular. To better understand this phenomenon, we investigated the density and pressure in these models using a mathematical approach. We found that even slight changes in the mass profile can significantly affect the density and pressure, making their behavior ambiguous. Despite this, we were able to prove that true singularities exist in these models for certain values of the Eddington fraction. Furthermore, we found that the way matter collapses changes over time, leading to a rough classification of models based on this phenomenon. We proposed a new framework to study this phenomenon and provided a list of models that exhibit this behavior.

The weak gravity conjecture suggests that in a higher derivative extension of a four-dimensional Einstein gravity theory, the mass of an extremal black hole should decrease in a canonical ensemble. We examine the basis of this inequality during the black hole thermodynamic phase transition. Our analysis focuses on a specific class of extremal black holes with a BPS boundary state. Our findings indicate that the inequality is violated in the canonical ensemble, however this effect can be avoided if the parameter governing the higher derivative interaction is less than a certain value. Additionally, we have demonstrated that the total entropy in the canonical ensemble exhibits a more complex behavior than previously considered.

We've integrated intrinsic motivation into reinforcement learning models by combining them with extrinsic rewards, leading to accelerated training and improved performance. A new metric, known as intrinsic gain, has been developed to measure an agent's capability to find its own goals within an environment. Experimental results have demonstrated that an agent can efficiently learn to accomplish both reward-maximizing tasks and innovative, creative challenges that originate from self-motivation. Furthermore, agents trained with our method exhibit robustness against noisy reward signals, a key feature in real-world applications. Our research showcases the potential for intrinsic motivation to increase an agent's ability to find effective solutions.

In Colored Poincaré gravity, simple particle models involving massive and massless particles have been formulated. A formal representation of these models is achieved by introducing coloured vectors and spinor variables into the extended Poincaré algebra. This approach allows us to describe the dualities existing between the different particle models. Furthermore, a proposal is made to rewrite the Coloured Poincaré gravity as a gauge theory of a coloured tensor field, thereby extending the standard Faddeev-Popov procedure to the Poincaré algebra. This formulation provides a prelude to constructing Coloured Einstein Gravity in the form of a gauge theory of a coloured tensor field.

We examine parameterized algorithms for directed acyclic graphs based on treewidth, and our findings reveal a significant contrast in algorithmic complexity between treewidth and pathwidth. Specifically, we show that treewidth allows for parameterized linear-time algorithms for multiple complex problems, whereas pathwidth is confined to quadratic-time algorithms. Moreover, our results demonstrate the utility of treewidth in solving parametrized graph theory issues, and our analysis yields a novel upper limit for the number of linear colorings of a graph of bounded treewidth.

In the realm of hybrid A\*-iters, finding the optimal path can be computationally intensive.
Our model, MemoNav, takes advantage of past navigation history by storing successful shortcuts in a heuristic map, allowing for more efficient navigation.
By converting the navigation problem into a series of simple lookups, MemoNav significantly accelerates navigation while maintaining nearly perfect accuracy.
For the most challenging scenarios, MemoNav's algorithm is adapted to exactly find the optimal path.
Our testing reveals that MemoNav achieves a substantial speedup of 2 to 4 times over the top hybrid A\* models, all with little to no additional computational cost.
Furthermore, MemoNav's adaptive algorithm perfectly balances efficiency with navigation accuracy.

Recent discussions around 5G New Radio (5G NR) focus on leveraging the millimeter-wave (mm-wave) frequency band and the millimeter-wave-like behavior of sub-6 GHz mid-band spectrum, despite the potential to use even lower frequency bands. Future cellular technologies, referred to as 6G, might cover the range from sub-6 GHz to sub-mm wave, with the mm-wave and sub-mm wave regions offering vast unlicensed spectrum resources. One newly considered mm-wave like behavior range, encompassing unlicensed spectrum from 27 GHz to 70 GHz, might be used alongside 5G NR mid-band in future. This paper, which takes a 3GPP-focused perspective, addresses key issues surrounding the coverage depth of 5G NR mid-band and the coverage depth of this proposed new unlicensed band. If the mid-band is based on frequency bands much broader than 500 MHz, it would limit the implementability of 5G NR mid-band in crowded areas. The new unlicensed band could rectify this issue as it can provide a coveragde depth of up to 100 meters without any adjacent channel interference concerns. This paper also highlights several key considerations for implementing the new unlicensed band correctly.

In systems of similar elements, where interactions and diffusive connections spread slowly, fast, or randomly, spatial patterns can emerge, even if initially homogeneous. However, understanding the origin of these patterns in such complex systems is challenging. Through computer simulations, we investigated how these systems respond to sudden changes and discovered that the patterns that develop are inherently unstable. When interactions or diffusive connections are strong, these patterns can break apart, giving rise to new, heterogeneously structured states. Our theoretical analysis shows that these system responses are universal, spanning across various types of diffusions, interactions, and initial conditions. Our findings shed new light on the underlying mechanism of spatial pattern formation in systems that are difficult to study mathematically.

The intricate behavior of intricate systems can become more manageable by leveraging symmetry. A renowned example from physics illustrates this point. Researchers have discovered that the study of quantum growth involves a more accessible symmetry property, analogous to the study of conformal symmetry in critical points. This breakthrough finds applications in the study of entanglement and operator growth in inhomogeneous systems as well. Building upon previous work, we broaden the scope of this symmetry property, demonstrating its presence in a more extensive family of intricate systems. Furthermore, we derive precise mathematical formulas for determining key factors associated with operator growth, as well as scaling of entanglement, in these systems. To achieve this, we integrate various mathematical concepts, including the study of central charges, higher spins, and spectral functions. This work has far-reaching implications and finds new applications in the study of quantum growth, as exemplified through the analysis of a system involving a flat geometric surface with quantum corrections.

The final word on the Hoyle state's final word has been spoken. A comprehensive theoretical framework is developed to comprehensively describe the Hoyle state's initial formation and its sequential decay. Utilizing a unique approach that combines the Applied Nuclear Physics's latest advancements, the theoretical framework successfully incorporates the 8.60 MeV state's excitation in $^{8}$Be, a crucial element previously overlooked. With the introduction of a novel non-sequential decay component, the calculated width for the Hoyle state's decay into $^{8}$Be and an alpha particle, 0.20 meV, is in excellent agreement with the experimental value, 0.22 meV. A previous calculation, 1.57 meV, is now considered an underestimate. This new theoretical framework provides robust support for the notion that the Hoyle state's primary character is indeed a compact 4-alpha ring state.

We've developed a new theory of fracture for brittle materials that takes into account their intrinsic length scales. This has allowed us to derive a unique expression for the stress-strain curve, which predicts the development of damage at a lower stress level than previously thought, followed by rapid crack propagation at a higher stress level. This theory is in agreement with recent experimental findings and provides a framework for understanding fracture in materials with intrinsic length scales.

This study investigates channel capacity under the constraint of causal state information. It demonstrates that channels with causal state information can store data volumes equivalent to those of reversible Markov channels, and more importantly, shows such channels can achieve lower error rates. Furthermore, a practical algorithm is proposed to efficiently determine the optimal state information structure for these channels.

In B20-type compounds like NiCl2(dilute HgCl), which exhibit spin-orbit coupling and local moment superconductivity, the interaction between spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity needs to be considered. The combination of these two effects induces a topological superconducting state, characterized by the presence of surface states. The study of transport phenomena in thin films of such materials, via measurements of tunneling spectra or momentum-resolved measurements, can confirm this topological superconducting state. The proposed mechanism of superconductivity in NiCl2 is analyzed, showing that it becomes a topological superconductor below the critical temperature. The band structure of the material becomes topologically non-trivial after the introduction of local moments and the interaction with spin-orbit coupling. The study also determines the topological surface rootdir and the dispersion of the surface states at the point.

In 2019, the Semantics in Task-oriented dialog Benchmarks for Semantics-driven Application of Common Sense Thinking initiative in co-organization with the 3rd  challenge launched SEM-TAB-FACTS with four sub-tasks, attracting nine participants who submitted work on three sub-tasks. This report examines evaluation results, highlighting participation and achievement statistics, then describes sub-task successes and areas requiring improvement.

This analysis argues that the inherent use of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics is not merely accidental, but rather stems from a fundamental necessity. In order to replicate the success of Wave-Particle Duality with real-valued mathematical approaches, it is essential to introduce the concept of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics as well.

Given a connected, undirected graph G and a real number t greater than zero, the t-distance metric of G is created by removing all edges whose distance is less than or equal to t. The number of distinct labels needed in a vertex labeling to identify any node in G is called the t-metric dimension. Research found that limiting the geodesic distance in certain graphs greatly affects their metric dimension. When t is less than the diameter of G, every node can be identified with a label, so the metric dimension for this condition is the total number of nodes. We investigated the metric dimension of graphs with limited geodesic distance, particularly focusing on trees. Our study found that for a tree T, if the greatest fraction of its geodesic distance that is less than or equal to 2t plus one is less than or equal to 2k-1, then the metric dimension of T given this condition will not exceed k, given certain conditions. Additionally, we found an algorithm that can precisely determine the metric dimension of a tree given a specific lower bound for the fraction of its geodesic distance and provided upper and lower bounds for the metric dimension of a tree given a specific lower bound for its geodesic distance.

The steady-state flow equation can be simplified by integrating the mass balance equation, assuming hydraulic conductivity follows an $a+bx$ relationship. After combining like terms and factoring, the integrated flow equation transforms into a nonlinear differential equation. Two integrals are required to solve this differential equation, leading to a complex expression involving the original parameters and integrands. However, this solution can be integrated again under specific conditions, resulting in a more manageable equation. Ultimately, the solution can be expressed as a function of one independent variable, but it requires numerical resolution due to its complexity.

The study utilized a CSTR-LOX-O3-UV reactor system to remove SO2 from flue gas under three different reactor sizes and residence times. It examined the effects of oxygen levels, ozone concentrations, and UV intensities on SO2 removal. Experimental results indicated that increasing oxygen levels enhanced SO2 destruction, while there was an optimal ozone concentration range for maximum efficiency. Additionally, larger reactors required longer residence times for optimal SO2 destruction. The study discovered that SO2 was primarily converted to SO4^2- through the homogeneous reaction pathway, with smaller reactors producing more sulfates due to higher space-time averages of oxygen and ozone concentrations.

Virtual platform segmentation is a widely accepted technique for evaluating hardware accelerators by dividing the DUT into multiple sub-regions and simulating one area at a time.  With the advent of virtualization in EDA tools, the concept of platform segmentation has been enhanced to include partitioning based on functional elements like CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs.  In this study, the effects of different virtual platform segmentation architectures on simulation speed were examined using a myrtle-based NPU model and two different architectures: a full-core NPU and a NPU-insole.  Results showed that an insole-based segmentation led to the fastest simulation speed among the options explored.

We introduce Indecision Trees as an alternative to Decision Trees, which we call Riesz Indecision Trees, by defining them through an optimization problem with a Lagrangian relaxation. This approach leads to a more flexible model compared to traditional Decision Trees, which can't be effectively computed efficiently due to the constraints associated with them. Our Riesz Indecision Trees are able to overcome two limitations of Decision Trees in that they can handle not only bounded losses but also varying losses as well as any possible hypothesis set, thereby providing improved accuracy. Moreover, Riesz Indecision Trees offer enhanced robustness to noise by minimizing errors based on bounded losses, which enhances their performance. This new model shares some characteristics with the, often overfitting, predictive state representation model, yet takes a more regulated approach. Implementations of Riesz Indecision Trees are provided, which demonstrate the benefits of our work in experimental settings.

The practical application of any index-based time series similarity search technique heavily relies on its ability to tolerate premature abandonment of parts of the search query. This capability allows the technique to stop shortening the distance approximations of subregions as soon as it becomes clear they will not yield any relevant results. In this paper, we revise and refine this concept by incorporating an enhanced version of tolerating premature abandonment. We also introduce a new version of the popular M\* tree index structure that incorporates this concept, resulting in significantly improved search efficiency. Our experimental findings validate the superiority of the proposed approach.

Recent research highlights the benefits of providing instant feedback to students learning to program. However, little is known about the impact of the specific type of feedback offered. To investigate this question, we developed an artificial neural network that mimicked the behavior of human instructors giving feedback to university students learning to program. The model was trained on data from 309 students with distinct identities, and its performance was compared to that of a model trained on data from a single student only. The results suggest that the type of feedback influences students' performance, with the optimal feedback type depending on the learning style.

In various situations, such as self-driving cars and medical diagnostics, the decisions made by artificial neural networks can be uncertain and difficult for people to understand. To address this, researchers have developed methods to create simpler mathematical models, which can provide insights into the decision-making process of these complex networks. However, the models developed so far have limitations, such as only being able to explain certain aspects of the network's behavior or requiring a vast amount of data to work accurately. In this study, we propose an innovative approach that creates highly accurate, simple mathematical models using only a small amount of data and allows these models to be generalized to new, unrelated problems. We also demonstrate that the accuracy of our method can be guaranteed theoretically, which is a first in this field. In practical testing, our method was able to explain the decisions of an advanced medical diagnostic network on lung infections, even when the network's outputs were manipulated with fake data that didn't reflect real patient symptoms.

Over-smoothing is a well-documented issue with Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), where the learned representations become progressively smaller with each convolutional layer. Research has provided evidence that the graph structure and network architecture are key factors contributing to over-smoothing. To address this challenge, several methods have been proposed, including residual connections and layer normalization. However, there is still no comprehensive understanding of the causes underlying over-smoothing. We investigate these factors through controlled experiments, drawing insights from the existing literature and proposing new explanations. Our study offers several contributions. First, we establish a general framework to study over-smoothing in GCNs, applying it to various graph architectures and networks. We also demonstrate that the number of parameters per layer significantly influences over-smoothing, which could help in developing over-smoothing mitigation algorithms. We conduct our study within the PyG framework, using the Citeseer dataset. Our work serves as a foundation for future research on over-smoothing, providing a theoretical understanding that can inform the design of new algorithms to tackle this issue.

We have simplified models for dark matter particle production in processes involving scalar, vector, and pseudoscalar mediators. These one-loop level models are based on spin-1/2 fermions and have a minimal number of variables. They can be used as a starting point for further investigations into dark matter phenomena. We have established relationships between the various production modes of dark matter particles and one-loop level cross sections. This allows us to create universal bounds on the interaction strength between the mediator and the dark matter particle, as well as between the mediator and standard model particles. These bounds are based on the mass of the mediator and the mass of the dark matter particle. We have also discovered that the universal bounds on the interaction strength are similar in strength to the leading four-fermion process in the standard model. We have found that the production of dark photons is possible, even when the mediator and the dark matter particle are not identical. We have found that the universal bounds on the interaction strength are similar in strength to the leading four-fermion process in the standard model. We have found that the production of dark photons is possible, even when the mediator and the dark matter particle are not identical.

We introduce new functions, $T_{a/b}$, to describe the transverse motion of $a$ within $b$, and derive equations that explain parton distribution functions (PDFs) such as the Qiu-Saito function describing the $x$-dependent transverse motion of quarks inside a proton. Further applications could involve studying the transverse motion of gluons and mesons.

This study demonstrates that specific types of spaces, including those combining products of spaces like the Closed Long Ray and the Long Line, with general metric spaces, exhibit the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property. Conversely, it proves the converse to be false in the case of products involving the Open Long Ray and the Long Line. Additionally, it shows that the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property is distinct from other related concepts like the Homeomorphism Property and the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property with compact support in the Long Line and Closed Long Ray.

The unique properties of graphene make it an ideal substrate for growing a variety of epitaxial materials. In this study, we explore the effects of varying growth conditions on the formation of epitaxial domains in PbSe through analysis of domain transformations across different temperature ranges. Our research reveals that at lower growth temperatures, stronger van der Waals interactions between graphene and PbSe lead to hexagonal domain formation, whereas at higher temperatures, oxygen surface termination facilitates the growth of cubic PbSe and results in epigraphene formation. Our findings demonstrate the importance of oxygen in creating a particular epitaxial configuration and show that oxygen surface termination can be crucial in producing specific material properties in epitaxial films.

This study provides an innovative estimator for determining the number of shared stochastic trends among multiple time series, capable of handling series with irregular patterns and limited data. The proposed estimator is based on a modified version of the canonical variates analysis model, which is originally used for identifying common stochastic trends in a group of vectors. The researchers initially establish the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimator and later demonstrate its consistency in the presence of heavy-tailed patterns. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations reveal that the estimator yields accurate results, even at small sample sizes, and its performance is comparable to the existing techniques in the literature. To illustrate the utility of the proposed estimator, the researchers apply it to analyze the number of shared stochastic trends in the S&P 500 stock market indices.

Galaxy cluster lensing observations are commonly used to establish the mass of these clusters. Recent discoveries by the KIDS and DES projects have uncovered evidence of small objects that significantly distort light around the main cluster. Research suggests that a large number of these small objects are likely young stars formed as a result of a binary encounter. If these small objects are abundant, they can greatly affect our understanding of the mass of the main cluster. In order to further investigate this phenomenon, we conducted a detailed analysis of a massive cluster called MACS J1206.8+52 (hereafter MACS1206) using data from the KIDS and Hubble spaces telescope. In the vicinity of MACS1206, we detected 28 small objects and a new galaxy that we have named MACS1206-2. These small objects cause 4 strong and well-defined ring patterns along with various less prominent rings and arcs. A computer model was used to create 100 different scenarios based on the mass and position of the small objects, these scenarios were then used to create fake images of the galaxy cluster and compare them to the real images to understand the mass of the main cluster. Our research suggests a mass that is significantly lower than previously thought, if the small objects are abundant, a mass that is 10-20% lower than the currently accepted value is suggested. This study examines a competitive market in content delivery, featuring multiple internet service providers and a content provider, from the perspective of a Bertrand game. To illustrate the effects of cooperation between ISPs, we contrast a scenario of sole ownership with one of joint ownership, among the ISPs. A key observation emerges: in the absence of cooperation, the content provider prefers exclusive contracts with individual ISPs, whereas, in the presence of cooperation, it prefers to share with the collective entity. Consequently, the content provider's payoff increases when ISPs collaborate. A second finding reveals that, in both scenarios, the content provider's payoff remains constant, but the cooperative setup encourages ISPs to invest more in delivery capacity, leading to enhanced efficiency. A third discovery shows that, in the cooperative case, the content provider can negotiate a fixed fee with the collective entity, resulting in higher payoffs compared to the non-cooperative scenario. To validate our analysis, we also develop a price game, demonstrating that cooperation among ISPs can lead to increased efficiency and higher payoffs for the content provider, while also facilitating cooperative bargaining.

The notion of weak naturality, analogous to the concept of naturality in category theory, is discussed in the context of functors. It is demonstrated that for any given functor, weak naturality is equivalent to universal derivability from naturality. Additionally, it is proven that for a given triangle of functors and natural transformations, the transformation from a weakly natural transformation to a natural transformation is universal and derives from the original, and this result has significant implications for adjunctions and coadjoints. As a consequence, it is found that the unit of an adjunction is weakly natural and that for an adjunction with weakly natural counit, the funtor is equivalent to a right adjoint. Finally, it is proven that weakly natural transformations that are local to a category can be extended to naturally in the category of sections.

We assess the performance of exponential and polynomial $\beta$-attractor models in fitting cosmological datasets. The exponential model exhibits similar fit capabilities as the polynomial model when using the exponential model's maximum likelihood parameters. Additionally, we discover that the exponential model's fit capabilities are also comparable to those of the classic Hill's model. Furthermore, we find that the cosmic evolution described by the exponential model is in line with the evolution described by Gaussian models. The study suggests that the exponential model is a simpler alternative to polynomial $\beta$-attractor models for attracting scenarios, while it is a more complex alternative to Hill's model.

We take a Fuchsian quasi-Fuchsian three-dimensional manifold taking up less space as it expands and calculate how its curvature changes when it's stretched. The method uses measured bending laminations, a concept derived from Thurston, to analyze the curvature's behavior, especially how it moves under changes in its shape. The findings show that the curvature has a one-to-one relationship with measured bending laminations, which is unique when the manifold is not Fuchsian. Additionally, for extremely thin manifolds, the curvature can be represented by a single vector that doesn't change, which is a unique feature. The proof involves proving that the curvature stays within a certain boundary, which is a unique property.

This study derives expressons for the short-horizon cross-sectional return distributions of individual securities and portfolios, based on empirical evidence of asset price dynamics. Building on the stability of specific distribution characteristics across assets, we model a portfolio's cross-sectional return distribution with a translated version of an asset return distribution, adjusting for static portfolio weights and variable equity values. Consequently, all distribution characteristics, including moments and quantiles, are directly proportional to corresponding asset distribution characteristics. Therefore, the cross-sectional return distribution's first four moments are perfectly correlated with those of asset returns. Furthermore, historical cross-sectional return data perfectly replicate the quadruple-moment process of asset returns, allowing us to invert this relationship to estimate asset returns from cross-sectional data, reversing the standard approach. In addition, our framework provides novel insights into the dynamics of asset price extremes and offers implications for managing portfolio risk and investing.

PCG signal detection accuracy significantly hinges on the accuracy of its time-aligned representation. However, detecting cardiac abnormalities using the standard time-domain approach in noisy environments is challenging due to distortion and signal misalignment. A proposed method, ECG-SD, offers an alternative representation that can mitigate noise through a signal transformation and utilize the heart rate to improve accurate time-aligned detection. A heart rate-based time-frequency map also enables cardiac feature extraction and provides supplemental information for final detection results. Evaluations conducted on 15,000 patient records revealed that ECG-SD outperformed the traditional approach, achieving 94% and 98.5% accuracy in detecting long QT and Brugada syndromes, respectively. A model and API are available for research and clinical use at https://github.com/cmu-delphi/ecg-sd.

A thorough examination of the linear rational EUT model's predictions for electric dipole transitions in $\zeta$-rich open-shell $^{3S_8}$ singlet states is presented. The study focuses on the EUT nuclear wave function's minor, core, and significant components. The evaluation of the transition amplitudes and probabilities is carried out with the aid of the UCF II code. To illustrate the EUT nuclear wave function's decay process, the oscillating nature of the minor and core components is examined, and the relevance of the Tail in describing this phenomenon is investigated. The analysis is based on three $\zeta$-rich nuclear states corresponding to the $5p_{3/2}$, $5p_{1/2}$, and $3p_{3/2}$ excitation of the $^1S_0$ dibaryon in isospin 0.

Let $G$ be a finite group and consider a torus $T$ equipped with a $G$-action. We can divide the Borel Weyl chamber of $\mathrm{Lie}(T)$ into $G$-invariant parts after choosing a chamber $C$. Each action of $G$ on $T$ gives us different twists in each of these sections. We can use the rational equivariant cohomology to construct a family of twists one twist at a time. This construction helps us calculate the twists for any $G$-action on $T$ using the first generator of the equivariant cohomology. Moreover, any $G$-action on $T$ can be expressed as a combination of standard actions, allowing us to determine the twists for any $G$-action on $T$ using the first generator of the equivariant cohomology.

This paper reports on our initial outcomes from a Third-person Feedback (TFP) intervention, which aimed to boost community and collaboration within our department. Prior research indicated that TFP could foster a more supportive academic environment. To evaluate the method's efficacy in our context, we conducted two experiments. Firstly, we sent TFP emails to all department members, followed by in-person gatherings to discuss the feedback. Secondly, we compared the pre- and post-intervention survey responses of willing participants. Findings show that TFP led to an improvement in the overall department atmosphere and may have contributed to increased collaboration. Notably, satisfaction with the department was highest among those who participated in both the email and in-person activities.

This paper examines the fractional series operator's boundedness within the $H^{p}(	ext{Z})$ space and its $L^{p}(	ext{Z})$ space, where $1 < p, q < \infty$, and the fractional exponent $\beta$ satisfies $0 < \beta < 1$. A key finding shows that the operator is not bounded for all possible exponents when $p$ is less than or equal to $q$, and a specific condition for boundedness is met when $q$ exceeds $p$. In particular, it is established that the operator is bounded from $H^{p}(	ext{Z})$ into $H^{q}(	ext{Z})$ provided that $\beta p$ exceeds 1. An important counterexample demonstrates that the operator fails boundedness when $p$ times $q$ is less than or equal to 1. An essential step in our analysis involves translating the fractional series into a convolution with a function and $M_{\gamma}$, where $\gamma = 1 - \beta$, leading to a more manageable investigation of the operator's properties. A crucial inequality in our context is the one introduced by Fefferman and Stein, allowing us to derive equivalent norms for $T_{ eta}f$ and $f$ multiplied by the convolution with $M_{\gamma}$, and thereby establish sufficient conditions for $T_{ eta}$'s boundedness. This study investigates the outcomes of the only second-price auction among multiple sellers, where the rules are not binding, and discovers a lack of profit maximization among untrustworthy bidders. To rectify this, our research introduces an auxiliary auction between each seller and an impartial agent, which enforces the payment rule. The cost of participation in this auxiliary transaction is negligible. The study shows that introducing this mechanism boosts the seller's revenue and provides statistical guarantee on the amount of enhancement. Furthermore, the experiment conducted on human participants yielded results consistent with those of the theoretical model.

We've explored how cosmic expansion affects local isotropy in the early universe, extending Roberts' and Turok's's work on flat regions to more general cases. We begin with a group action that defines isotropy, then derive a stability condition which enables us to conclude that on each flat region, a stable group action can be found. This involves a detailed examination of anisotropic regions, resulting in a theory that on each point, a stable group action can be found as well. Our work also addresses questions about the universe's geometry, such as whether it can be composed of multiple flat regions and what happens to these regions over time.

This study examines Gr\"obner fans of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on combinatorial aspects for types A and B. It expresses Gr\"obner fan coordinates as a result of a Gr\"obner basis computation for the local defining ideals of these varieties, which are parametrized by Hessenberg functions. Additionally, properties of Gr\"obner fan lattices, including polytopes and cones, are explored.

Using generative adversarial networks, researchers have created various forms of artificial culture, including music, writing, images, and video. Recent studies have produced generated brushstrokes with the potential to be used in computer-assisted art. This work takes it further by implementing a new method that uses existing stroke models to produce a more diverse range of brushstrokes. The resulting brushstrokes are then applied to generate full paintings in the style of two famous artists, Lucien Freulich and David Hockney. Expert evaluators assessed the generated paintings and found them to be comparable to the professionals' work in terms of overall quality.

We re-examine the possibility that the primary source of flavor anomalies observed in $K$, $B$, and $c$ meson systems is due to a non-universal $Z'$ boson with a focus on the constraints imposed by the $K^0-\overline{K^0}$ oscillations. Within the framework of minimal left-right symmetry, we outline the necessary conditions for the $Z'$ mediating $K^0-\overline{K^0}$ oscillations to be in conflict with the current experimental data. The potential resolution of the $r_D$ anomaly within this context is also explored, along with the implications for lepton-flavor universality and the constraints on new physics contributions to $K^0-\overline{K^0}$ oscillations, with new physics contributions sized by $(8\pm2)\times 10^{-4}$.

Conversational Question Answering, which retrieves relevant information from extended passages in response to questions, necessitates models with both language understanding and conversational abilities. However, current models fall short due to a lack of properly annotated data. To address this gap, we have developed the QASPER dataset, a comprehensive collection of 18000 conversations with detailed labels, sourced from the Quora platform. This benchmark represents an essential standard for evaluating the performance of models in conversational question answering and has already spurred improvement in this area, leading to a notable boost in scores of leading models. Moreover, through analysis of our dataset, we have identified and highlighted two significant challenges inherent to the Quora platform.

In a study involving 30 simulations of core-collapse supernova explosions, researchers found that explosions occurred in 12 out of 30 cases and fast instabilities in the remaining 18 cases occurred within one month after the supernova explosion. The study revealed key differences between the explosions and instabilities, specifically that the growth of instabilities was influenced by the same processes that determine the success of supernova explosions. Moreover, fast instabilities occurred more frequently when supernovae had cooler and more extended progenitor structures. The study presents various prospects for future research, including potential therapeutic approaches to delay the onset of instabilities following a successful supernova explosion, as well as a potential mechanism by which binary interactions may affect the occurrence of fast instabilities.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, a neurodevelopmental disorder, can be detected through functional magnetic resonance imaging by identifying pattern-based differences in brain activity. Current deep learning models rely on the entire brain data for classification, but this method is expensive and difficult to obtain. Our research reveals that certain regions of interest are more significant than others in identifying ADHD. A new model, called m-DenseNet, is presented by modifying the DenseNet architecture. It combines dense connections with a convolutional neural network, and its results demonstrate improved accuracy, with an impressive 70.46% using just the top 30 most important regions of interest. The m-DenseNet model is then tested on the minimal regions of interest, and its performance is compared with the state-of-the-art models. Additionally, our research examines the importance of brain regions for ADHD classification using a feature importance method, which confirms that some regions are more crucial than others. Consequently, transferring the knowledge from the m-DenseNet model to other deep learning models can be done without training on the entire brain, thus enhancing their performance.

We provide evidence of the uniqueness of an interior fixed point for a combination of mirror-operators in high-dimensional spaces. These operators have applications in solving mathematical models that are based on variational principles and exhibit symmetry. For example, this applies to vector-valued phase transition problems when they are invariant under mirror transformations.

Acronyms are commonly used in everyday writing and speaking, with many systems benefiting from them by shortening lengthy phrases. Despite their utility, they often remain unclear or ambiguous, leading to confusion if not contextually identified. To address this issue, various methods involve the use of surrounding text to infer possible expansions. However, such approaches may fall short due to limited context or domain-specific terminology. To improve this, we propose an acronym identification and disambiguation system that leverages a systematic approach. First, it develops a data-driven inventory of anticipated acronyms through statistical analysis. Next, it employs acronyms that are explicitly written in a corpus to inform the identification process in unseen text. To resolve ambiguity, the system compares suspected expansions to a comprehensive knowledge base. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through notable gains in performance on two publicly accessible datasets, surpassing current state-of-the-art techniques. To enhance transparency and trustworthiness, the underlying acronym inventory and knowledge base are openly accessible.

To tackle the heat transfer problem in quantum Hall systems, we developed a theoretical model that incorporates both edge and bulk components of these systems. Heat rectification was discovered to be feasible through an explicit temperature barrier in the bulk of these systems. A phenomenological model was also established to represent the edge modes and utilized to develop a simplified design for a quantum Hall heat rectifier. Our research demonstrates that both ferromagnetic and non-ferromagnetic quantum Hall systems can be employed for efficient heat rectification. Furthermore, heat rectification was found to be more effective in the intermediate quantum Hall regime compared to the high regime. A heat rectifier was conceived by combining the edge modes of two different quantum Hall systems, and our findings suggest that systems with a strong Landau parameter (low magnetic field) are more suitable for heat rectification compared to those with a weak Landau parameter (high magnetic field). This research sets the stage for the exploration of heat rectification in quantum Hall systems, offering promising possibilities for thermally controlled rectifier devices.

In a data storage system utilizing DNA, storage capacity is divided into separate areas, each holding various pieces of data, much like a file system with multiple folders. A central management system oversees DNA data storage by generating sequences used to retrieve information from stored data, ensuring storage capacity meets demand. A key component of this system involves short, unique sequences known as primer pairs, used in a molecular process to extract stored data. We have discovered that traditional methods of generating primer pairs lead to storage inefficiencies, causing some sequences to go unused. To resolve this issue, we suggest modifying primer design to take account of existing data already stored in the system, thus conserving sequence capacity. Furthermore, we have adapted our method to handle large datasets already stored in the system without prior knowledge of their sequence information. Our findings show an approximate 30% reduction in required storage sequences. We believe this new approach will significantly impact future DNA data storage systems.

Topological phases in three-dimensional systems can be characterized by points where the wave function momentarily vanishes in momentum space. However, these nodal points can be unstable under perturbations that cause them to merge and form rings. These nodal rings in momentum space pose an interesting challenge for experimental detection, making the study of the system's surface and bulk electronic structures crucial. To investigate this, we developed a new method to analyze the surface and bulk structures of the Mo$_3$Ge compound. Our method combines density functional theory calculations with the use of topological and bulk classification schemes. Our findings show that Mo$_3$Ge features a nodal ring in momentum space, and its surface exhibits a series of quasi-nodal lines. Additionally, we discovered that the material near this nodal ring exhibits a high density of states, suggesting that the ring may be stable and potentially appear at experimentally accessible conditions.

Researchers examined wave propagation through a medium containing neutrally buoyant soft robots, and found that wave speeds could be influenced by factors such as the type of movement, amplitude, frequency, and robot geometry. To better understand these dynamics, a theoretical analysis was developed, which identified the key factors affecting wave speeds and provided a mathematical representation of wave speeds as a function of certain parameters. This framework facilitated the design of optimized robot movements, like high-frequency movements, that could enhance wave propagation. In addition, a possible application of wave propagation in robotic navigation was explored.

This research develops a straightforward method for estimating the entropy of a discrete source that incorporates a confidence interval. Unlike previous entropy estimation algorithms, this new approach demands that the source entropy remain consistently nonzero. Given that many real-world sources have varying entropy levels, this method serves as a better choice for them. Building on top of a basic entropy estimation algorithm, we modify it to incorporate uncertainty, resulting in a procedure that accounts for a source's discrete partitioning. We further enhance this method to expand its applicability to sources with non-discrete symbols. To facilitate efficient implementation, we also provide an alternative version of the method that uses less computational resources. In addition, our study expands upon existing entropy estimation techniques, requiring only a single observation of each symbol. This new approach surpasses previous entropy estimation methods in terms of precision and accuracy. We support our research by including numerical data that validates the performance of our method.

As machine learning continues to evolve, there's a growing need for robust and sustainable imaging resources to support the development of highly accurate artificial intelligence systems. Key factors for creating an effective imaging biobank include using open, well-documented platforms, conducting thorough research on clinical datasets, adhering to established quality standards, and ensuring long-term sustainability through collaborative partnerships. Two notable examples of successful imaging biobanks are the Biomedicine, Imaging, Pathology and Medicine (BIP-MD) and the Medical Image System for Research and Treatment (MIRT). These resources have made significant contributions to advancing research in both machine learning and the medical and biological sciences.

Current deep learning models for diagnosing and treating diseases rely heavily on hospital data, but lack of access to labels and complex dataset preparation make AI-powered solutions impractical in resource-constrained settings. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored the effectiveness of data augmentation on medical image diagnosis, but its efficacy with limited labelling data and medical images is yet to be thoroughly investigated. This study delves into the end-to-end performance of data augmentation in medical diagnosis, comparing its effectiveness with and without clinical features. Our findings reveal that clinical context significantly affects the performance of data augmentation. When clinical features are available, data augmentation can enhance diagnosis accuracy; however, in scenarios where label information is limited or absent, data augmentation alone struggles to achieve impressive results. Notably, the presence of clinical features in scenarios with limited supervision enhances diagnosis accuracy, but lacks supervisory input, data augmentation fails to excel. This research provides valuable insights into the potential of data augmentation in medical diagnosis, uncovers its limitations, and opens up areas for further improvement, including the development of application-specific models and augmentation strategies.

Polymatroidal ideals, defined as nested sets of smooth polynomial equations, have ties to algebraic-Newton polytopes and are also hypothesized to be equivalent to binomial ideals derived from hypergeometric series. In this paper, specific polymatroidal ideals tied to duality and Minkowski's theorem are analyzed, with a classification of such ideals based on their combinatorial properties. Furthermore, an examination of a subcategory of polymatroidal ideals, characterized by combinatorial stability, reveals relationships to determinantal ideals and codimension two toric complete intersections.

We introduce a quantum version of the K-means clustering algorithm, incorporating both fixed and variable K values. The idea leverages quantum techniques such as quantum circuits, qubits, and the benefits of quantum computation like superposition and entanglement. The proposed algorithm shows an asymptotic complexity advantage over its classical counterparts.
