Recent advancements in RingCT technology aim to maintain the anonymity of cryptocurrencies. However, the standard RingCT scheme faces limitations in its large size, making it unsuitable for high-speed and high-throughput applications in the cloud. To address this issue, Delegated RingCT (DRC) has been proposed as a solution. DRC offers more efficient transaction processing by reducing communication costs and improving scalability. Specifically, DRC reduces the size of each transaction by compressing key elements and utilizing a previously established public key instead of including it in the transaction again. Experimental results demonstrate that DRC achieves significant improvements in transaction processing speed and scalability, outperforming the traditional RingCT scheme.

A new reduction theorem has been developed that demonstrates how approximate solvers for linear systems can be transformed into each other using a circuit complexity reduction, where the underlying linear system is defined by a symmetric positive definite matrix and bounded sparse matrix. The resulting theorem provides a method to obtain reduced forms of approximate solvers by applying specific splitting techniques to the matrix. The theorem also enables a proof of the existence of approximate solvers with optimal convergence rates for positive definite linear systems, as well as new infinite sequences of such solvers with optimal convergence rates. The theorem is also applicable to bounded sparse linear systems, enabling the derivation of optimal lower bounds on the complexity of approximate solvers for such systems. The theorem's results have been experimentally validated by implementing the reduced forms of solvers in a computational study.

An investigation into the individual production of the $W$ boson paired with a $W$ or $Z$ boson is carried out by utilizing the complete data set from proton-proton collisions, which was collected by the ATLAS experiment at the LHC. The data, equivalent to 139 inverse femtobarns of flux, corresponds to a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. The $W$ and $Z$ boson production is identified in the $W$ boson decay into electrons or muons and the $Z$ boson decay into the same two particles. The measured productions of $W$ with $W$ or $Z$ bosons are $51.1 \pm 3.3$ and $44.2 \pm 3.2$ femtobarns, respectively, at a 95% confidence, with systematic uncertainties included. The measurements align with the theoretical predictions from the Standard Model but with higher levels of production than previously recorded at a lower 7 TeV energy.

This paper significantly improves the state-of-the-art in Hebrew NLP by incorporating a comprehensive UD treebank. Our research demonstrates the value of enhanced annotation for Hebrew, particularly in the context of Modern Hebrew, by utilizing a sophisticated approach that leverages token-based annotations. To facilitate this endeavor, we develop a cutting-edge NLP framework, UDAN, enabling efficient annotation of complex languages like Hebrew. UDAN accelerates tokenization and morphological analysis while integrating a sophisticated agreement checker and a cutting-edge neural name entity linker. Our work on the Hebrew NLP dataset yields remarkable advancements in achieving state-of-the-art results in multiple tasks, encompassing dependency parsing, named entity recognition, and part-of-speech tagging, thereby establishing new benchmarks for NLP in low-resource settings. Additionally, our research enhances the understanding of Hebrew NLP by clarifying previous results and identifying areas for future improvement. Our work is openly accessible via links to our GitHub repository and publicly released datasets.

For every p in the range from 1 to infinity, a normed space is being looked at - specifically, the space of real zero-dimensional vectors with the ell_p norm. It's known that when p isn't 2, the unit ball of this space can't be reduced dimensionally by even a small amount using linear operators, which explains why there's no universal reduction formula that applies to this space. On the other hand, if p is 2 or greater than 2, we need to know how well a randomly chosen linear operator reduces the unit ball of a fixed dimensional space - specifically, the space whose basis has the same number of dimensions as a subset of ell_p called the qell_p sphere. It's also stated that a formula for this reduction will be similar to the one for the standard ell_p space.

To adapt a statistical model regularly without losing previously acquired knowledge, we propose a new method of continual learning. Unlike existing approaches that lose information from earlier adaptations, our method preserves knowledge of past adaptations by incorporating those parameters into future adaptations. Our statistical model uses a mixture of Gaussian distributions to model the historical-dependent plasticity behavior of solid mechanics, specifically in brittle damage, resulting in a complex adaptation process. Our experiments show that continually adapting this model leads to a complete loss of its historical dependencies. However, our novel method of continual learning adapts the model in small steps, preserving the dependencies and incorporating each step's new information without losing previously acquired knowledge. These adaptations are then combined into a single model that retains knowledge of all past adaptations. Our research combines the existing replay method, which repeats earlier adaptations, and introduces a novel random walk process that allows the model to incorporate past adaptations adaptively. Our experiments show the success of our model in maintaining its historical dependencies and improving its accuracy over time.

Researchers examined the performance of LDPC code belief propagation decoding when faced with a noisy transmission environment that includes packet loss. The study provided a comprehensive framework for determining the optimal maximum erasure probability under which regular and irregular LDPC codes will successfully regenerate the transmitted data. The analysis, however, revealed that negative degree-degree correlations significantly decrease the maximum tolerable erasure probability in irregular LDPC codes. As a result, the study offered a simplified approach to designing LDPC codes with enhanced maximum performance capabilities.

This paper introduces SL-MPSF, a safety control approach that uses model predictive safety properties with linear system constraints and bounded disturbances. SL-MPSF enhances the standard MPC optimisation by incorporating a safety validation step at each calculation interval. If the predicted trajectory violates any safety limitation, the algorithm seeks an adjusted trajectory that adheres to both system and safety constraints. In contrast to prior safety-first methods, SL-MPSF explores all feasible solutions when a safety violation is detected, rather than merely taking the first safe outcome. This is made possible through the use of a graph representation, which allows for a more efficient search. For systems without disturbances, SL-MPSF ensures completion, and in systems with disturbances, it guarantees safety but might not reach completion. However,, in a special case where the disturbance is bounded and can be perfectly predicted, SL-MPSF is shown to be both complete and safe. The performance of SL-MPSF is evaluated through simulation on a robotic arm and a driving scenario.

In a typical quantum key distribution (QKD) system based on the vacuum+weak decoy state, an eavesdropper can remain undetected by only attacking the weak decoy state, as she won't be detected in this scenario. However, detecting the attack on the weak decoy state is impossible since it only causes random errors there. We've developed a new idea for enhancing the existing vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system, which involves introducing a specific channel noise to random phase modulation (RPM) state, increasing its tolerance to specific types of attack, namely the attack that only affects the weak decoy state, by making it harder for the eavesdropper to leave behind only random errors in this state. As a result of this change, the tolerance to specific types of attack has been improved, reducing the critical error rate and thus enhancing the security of the system. We've demonstrated this through theoretical analysis and by experimenting with existing data, reducing the threat of undetected attacks on the weak decoy state, which has significant practical implications.

Recent studies on few-shot learning, particularly in-language modeling, point out the connection between language modeling and few-shot tasks. However, it's unclear if there's a direct correlation between language modeling performance (measured by perplexity) and few-shot task performance. To investigate this further, we examined the relationship using a large-scale dataset of 290k articles and discovered that there's no guarantee of a correlation between language modeling perplexity and few-shot task accuracy. To explain this, we looked at the differences in how language models process context and generate outputs, highlighting the role of inference biases and bounded context spans. Moreover, we found that there's no single explanation for the few-shot task accuracy, suggesting it's the result of various factors such as context representation, few-shot learning mechanisms, and downstream task characteristics. We dubbed this the "simple-because-it's-complicated" hypothesis and proposed it as an explanation for the few-shot success of language models.

Even minimal amounts of anisotropic heat flow can substantially amplify cold gas formation within galaxy clusters. A key factor is whether it adheres to standard spatiotemporal patterns or deviates from them through magnetohydrodynamics. To investigate this, we developed a theoretical model for anisotropic thermal conduction in a magnetohydrodynamic fluid under all three basic transport conditions, and then numerically solved it within a one-dimensional cluster model. When either viscosity or rayleigh-taylor instability prevail, anisotropic heat flow's unique properties lead to increased cold gas production due to reduced thermal front thickness. Conversely, when buoyancy forces are significant, our model indicates that cold gas formation is impaired as it prevents the cold and hot phases from properly mixing. Additionally, we observed at high Mach numbers, anisotropic heat flow's influence on cold cluster growth is somewhat mitigated by its inherent spatial and temporal correlations. Our findings are expected to be relevant to similar problems involving anomalous heat transfer in both astrophysical and laboratory settings.

Observations of $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and charm systems reveal distinct patterns, with the former exhibiting significant $C\!P$ violation and the latter showing nearly negligible effects. This situation poses a significant challenge for the electromagnetic origin hypothesis, which struggles to account for these differences. If $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and charm systems originate from the same source, this source would need to have a substantial magnetic moment. Additionally, there needs to be an unusual connection between the $C\!P$-nonconserving and $C\!P$-conserving interactions within the electromagnetic sector. On the other hand, if beauty baryons and charm systems have distinct origins for $C\!P$ violation, this would imply the existence of at least one new physical process beyond the standard model, its contribution being highly flavour-dependent. This flavour dependence would significantly affect the search for direct $C\!P$-violating phases originated by next-generation precision experiments in the charm and beauty sectors.

We've derived new high-energy string interactions that involve a vertical particle scattering process. These results confirm two notable hypotheses: the "Gliozzi-Scherer" conjecture regarding string independence at high loopy energies, and the "Klein transform equivalence" between horizontal and vertical particle scattering amplitudes. Our approach builds upon earlier string scattering amplitudes, and makes use of the vertex operators' charge operators to generate vertical particle scattering amplitudes. In contrast, horizontal particle scattering amplitudes were previously derived using the string worldsheet's coordinate transformations.

This research offers three optimization techniques to reduce edge computing facility's energy usage by extending the lifespan of equipment parts. These strategies involve jointly managing the Edge of Truth network and accurately forecasting resource demand, which involves predicting load and estimating hardware lifespan. We propose a 30-day optimization schedule, dividing the year into four periods with distinct optimization approaches based on resource demand patterns. To forecast resource demand, we use a 7-day advanced load predictor, which involves identifying patterns in historical load data and incorporating real-time traffic information to inform Edge of Truth network maintenance. Our proposed solutions are analyzed through simulations, which demonstrate a 14% reduction in energy consumption, prolonging equipment lifespan for 12 to 132 hours.

Current speech synthesis models produce highly coherent, structured speech by grouping speech segments into categories, yet the underlying organization of these categories remains unclear. Prior studies assumed a steady-state distribution, but this paper explores whether transient phase observations can yield more insightful insights into speech syntax. To address this question, the paper focuses on the syntactic structure discovered in the transient phase of a neural speech synthesis model, and finds that an intermediate regime, distinct from well-known speech syllable phonemes, exists and captures essential linguistic structure.

To optimize motion planning for multi-limbed robots, we introduce a novel multi-stage optimization technique. This approach initially identifies single-limbed trajectory connections that minimize time or energy. It then refines the search by considering the collective movement of pairs of limbs before switching to the full multi-limbed configuration for the most promising stage-one outcomes. This stage-by-stage process allows us to leverage the results of simpler sub-problems and avoid exploring vast motion planning spaces until the most efficient trajectories are identified. We demonstrate the efficiency of this method through simulation studies on a basic bimanual robot model.

Our study on distilling quantum states from subspaces serves as a foundational exploration into the trade-offs between fidelity and error tolerance in various quantum resource theories. The maximally resourceful states in these theories can be effectively obtained through a series of measurements, and we have derived efficient protocols for achieving this. The distillability of these states can be tracked via the fidelity bounds of the resulting states. These bounds not only quantify how error-resistant they are but also reveal their potential to be transformed into error-prone states. The efficiency of these protocols in reaching these fidelity bounds has been maximized, and we have derived efficient algorithms for achieving these bounds. The distillability of these states can be tracked via the fidelity bounds of the resulting states. These bounds not only quantify how error-resistant they are but also reveal their potential to be transformed into error-prone states. The efficiency of these protocols in reaching these bounds has been maximized, and we have demonstrated the efficacy of these algorithms through simple examples.

To investigate the dynamics of liquid within a rotating container, a cup of coffee was placed on a turntable that was driven at a constant speed.  The height of a droplet of coffee in the cup was measured while the turntable was set in motion at various speeds, ranging from 30 to 140 rpm, and these observations were recorded over a period of 2 minutes.  The rotation axis was then tilted at 10 degrees from the vertical, and the experiment was repeated.  In another set of experiments, the pivot point of the turntable was moved from its central position to a point 5cm off center in both clockwise and counterclockwise directions.  When the rotation axis was tilted, the coffee formed a spiral shape due to centrifugal force, but when the pivot point was shifted from its central position, liquid in the cup created waves that influenced its dynamics.  Notably, when the pivot point was at a 5cm radius from center and the speed of the turntable was 100rpm, liquid in the cup completed one revolution in approximately 40 seconds.  The shape of the liquid surface during these experiments indicated that liquid in the cup was in a state of static equilibrium.  The findings of these experiments can be applied in the study of liquid dynamics within rotating systems.

This paper investigates the convergence properties of Decentralized Rayleigh Quadratic Regularized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD), a distributed learning algorithm that bypasses central oversight by directly aggregating local gradients. In our analysis, we simulate an $L$-strongly-convex and $M$-strongly-convex-free loss function with access to DR-DSGD via simulated data. We demonstrate that DR-DSGD achieves a rate of $O(\sqrt{K} + \log_K (L/M))$, where $K$ represents the number of iterations. Additionally, we note that the algorithm's convergence rate is contingent upon the specific characteristics of the loss function. In particular, if the loss function is $M$-strongly-convex, we observe a rate of $O(\sqrt{K} / L)$, and if it is $L$-strongly-convex, we observe a rate of $\sqrt{K}$. Furthermore, DR-DSGD's performance is comparable to that of Distributed Average Aggregation (DAA) with optimal parameter selection, which also reaches a rate of $O(\sqrt{K} / L)$ in $M$-strongly-convex scenarios. Conversely, DR-DSGD experiences a slower convergence rate than DAA in $L$-strongly-convex scenarios. Furthermore, we derived a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{K} / L)$ for this

The concept of pre-equilibrium entropy production or quark and gluon production yields valuable insights into the initial stages of nucleus-nucleus collisions. Thermodynamic quantities derived from this phase can serve as a baseline for studying equilibrium establishment. This work examines entropy production during the pre-equilibrium phase of nucleus-nucleus collisions, employing an entropy model based on quark and gluon contributions. Calculations of entropy density are carried out as a function of temperature and energy density, and are applied to determine initial temperatures and in-medium energy densities following pre-equilibrium phases with distinct durations. This is done using experimental energy density and entropy density values from nucleus-nucleus collisions at a specific energy level. The resulting temperatures are then compared to corresponding equilibrium temperatures, and the influence of pre-equilibrium phase length is explored.

Investigating the mass flow within the early stages of protostar formation is crucial to understanding the protostar's growth through mass accretion. Using advanced simulations, this study delves into the protostar's inner regions under extremely high accretion rates greater than Einstein gravity's limit. It finds that extremely high accretion rates lead to the protostar's efficient early growth, accompanied by the ejection of massive amounts of material, significantly reducing the protostar's initial mass. However, this process can be altered by the equality of electron and gas temperatures, which primarily affects the outer layers and reduces the protostar's early growth. These simulations reveal that massive protostars with accretion rates greater than Einstein gravity's limit follow a distinct mass-radius path that differs from those in lower accretion rate systems, providing insight into the development of very massive stars.

Destabilizing factors, responsible for system failures, are typically overlooked in conventional safety assessment methods. This study reveals that these factors are explicitly considered in algebraic interpretation of event-driven state-space modeling, though in a negative light, which might lead to an excessive safety guarantee. This paper aims to provide a safer, algebraic-based safety assessment method by identifying a practical limitation in event-driven state-space models that prevents them from accurately representing a system's behavior. This limitation is attributed to the virtual transitions, occurring between event occurrences, which fail to account for the system's changes. A new hybrid model, combining continuous and discrete changes, is proposed to address this issue. Moreover, this study demonstrates that the boundedness of this new hybrid model ensures safe event occurrences, thus serving as a safety assessment tool. Finally, this study supplements the basic safety assessment model with a tool that actively prevents virtual escalations, thereby enhancing the model's capability to detect destabilizing effects early on.

This research project's primary goal was to create a comprehensive database for predicting how uncontrolled space debris responds to changes in its orbit resulting from solar radiation pressure effects. The project specifically focused on identifying resonances that result in significant changes to an object's eccentricity and inclination. A theoretical database was developed based on a mathematical model that accounts for the object's size, mass, and closure. This model was used to generate predictions for resonances in specific areas of interest, including the 1:1, 3/2, and 2 resonances. The accuracy of these predictions was validated through comparisons with existing studies and numerical integrations. The final outcome was a comprehensive database that includes predictions for resonances in various areas of interest up to the 5/2 order.

The velocity gauge is often utilized in finite-difference simulations of electromagnetic waves through periodic structures, but it has drawbacks in tight-binding models of quantum electronics. These models describe quantum states discretely using linear basis functions, yet the velocity gauge leads to inaccuracies in describing electromagnetic responses due to artifacts. To overcome this limitation, a new approach, the long-wavelength gauge, is developed for first-principles simulations. It modifies the electromagnetic vector potential to directly relate to the electric field within the quantum states, and this choice of gauge eliminates inaccuracies. When compared to the velocity gauge, the long-wavelength gauge shows significant improvement in calculating electronic properties and phonon modes in hyperbolic metamaterials.

We introduce a graph-theoretic framework for pose and shape estimation, focusing on improving robustness through efficient outlier elimination. Our approach represents both the target shape and the observed points on the camera's imager as weighted undirected graphs. By developing an algorithm that maximizes a score function, we can accurately determine the camera's position and the target shape, while also eliminating anomalous vertices. This algorithm is proven to converge to an optimal solution and outperforms state-of-the-art methods by dynamically removing vertices that contribute to suboptimal solutions. Experimental results confirm the framework's efficiency and robustness.

The parameter space of the Cauchy distribution is studied in the complex plane, allowing for a finite number of observations. A method to establish a confidence region for the distribution's parameters is developed, along with an examination of the region's geometric properties. Specifically, the confidence region is determined by a set of closed curves in the complex plane. The approach is analogous to traditional methods but incorporates the Cauchy distribution's characteristic likelihood ratio inequalities. The method is further generalized to account for cases where data points are paired.

Borrowing information between commensurate subgroups in clinical trials can be highly informative when subgroups share nearly identical treatment effects. However, this borrowing can be unhelpful or even harmful when subgroups have distinct treatment effects. To address this challenge, a new method is proposed which selectively enables information sharing among commensurate subgroups with similar treatment effects. The approach integrates a state space model with a change point detection algorithm to analyze trends in treatment effects over subgroups. The method offers a unified framework for estimating treatment effects and their uncertainties. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms traditional approaches in sample size estimation, even when subgroups have varying treatment effects. Conversely, the method slightly increases required sample sizes when subgroups have identical treatment effects. Notably, the method performs comparably to other informative prior techniques. The method's effectiveness is further validated through a real-world example and simulation studies in another accompanying article.

Current motion control systems rely on velocity and differential equation models that focus on the left and right hand sides. However, these models do not account for position dependent dynamics that can significantly impact performance in tracking. To address this limitation, a new representation called the sum-of-products (SOP) model has been developed. The SOP model uses logical operators and can represent dynamics dependent on the current state's position. By applying a novel identification method, the SOP model can be estimated from experimental data. A study demonstrated that the SOP model outperformed traditional velocity based methods in tracking. The SOP model was also utilized to enhance residual generation for fault detection and diagnosis. To evaluate the effectiveness of the new method, several simulation based studies were conducted. The proposed method was applied to a real world application - the control of an magnetostrictive sensor - and showed improved performance over traditional velocity based methods.

Our research builds upon the concept that point cloud registration networks can encode relevant data about object shapes and poses, which could be leveraged for classification tasks. In this study, we investigate how to harness this information by utilizing learned representations. Initially, we conduct an in-depth analysis of network capabilities, pointing out potential pitfalls in previous work. Next, we introduce three key approaches to tap into this knowledge: (1) training registration networks for multiple objects and leveraging their features, (2) employing contrastive learning to capture object characteristics, and (3) using classification labels to enhance point cloud registration. Our experiments demonstrate that these techniques not only improve classification but also address network training challenges, reduce data requirements, and yield more accurate and generalizable results. Moreover, through ablation studies and comprehensive evaluations, we showcase the broad applicability of our findings across various domains, networks, and datasets.

For every non-negative integer n, the R_n-all nilpotency degree of a group G, denoted by gamma_{R_n}(G), is the smallest possible nilpotency degree of any R_n-all nilpotent subgroup of G. In 2013, McCaughan and Rhemtulla introduced the concept of R-all nilpotent subgroups of groups, and they defined a class of groups with this property. In this research, we examine the R-forall nilpotency degrees of abelian groups, and we discuss a part of a broader question proposed by McCaughan and Rhemtulla in 2019.

A next-generation $e^+e-$ or $\mu^+\mu-$ collider is planned in the far future, and it's crucial to precisely measure key physical parameters during a test run using the latest technology. One of the essential parameters to be measured is the top quark mass. Our research shows that a top quark factory or a muon collider demonstrator can achieve a measurement accuracy of better than 0.26 GeV, which is equivalent to approximately 0.65 picobarns for the $\sigma_t$ in a test run lasting 5 inverse picobarns. This goal can be realized by combining measurements of the top quark using $t\bar{t}$ production experiments. If a Higgs factory path is chosen, a proposed upgrade to the Belle-II or a future super Belle detector could serve as a test run. Additionally, a muon collider can measure the top quark with an estimated precision of 0.65 GeV or 0.35 GeV depending on whether the detector is similar to the one planned for the 3 TeV muon collider or the 1.5 TeV one, respectively. This research focuses on a fast-shrink $p\bar{p}$ collider operating at an energy of 3 TeV. It discusses the potential for top quark mass measurement using $t\bar{t}$ production near the top quark pole, utilizing the precision that can be achieved with the precision Higgs

In ultrafast experiments involving photoinduced processes, researchers face significant obstacles in analyzing experimental data corrupted by substantial noise. A new invasive reconstruction technique is introduced, capable of recovering phase-sensitive information from such noisy data, at a reduced computational cost compared to non-invasive methods. By leveraging maximum likelihood principles and incorporating total variation minimization, this technique enhances low-frequency accuracy and resists artifacts influenced by high-frequency phases. A previously proposed stochastic optimization approach is adapted for complex data processing and validated through successful reconstructions of real data, at a computational cost roughly ten times faster than non-invasive techniques.

Using lattice QCD with a 2+1 impression of gauge symmetry, different distributions of light and strange quarks within various hadrons have been investigated. This study compares the light cone distribution amplitudes of several mesons, specifically the $\rho$, $\rho^*$, $K^*$, and $D^*_s$, and discovers notable differences in the spin and momentum distribution of the light and strange quarks within these mesons. Besides examining the light cone distribution amplitudes, the study also determines the path-like correlation functions of light and strange quarks within $\rho$, $\rho^*$, and $D^*_s$ mesons. The results suggest an increased correlation between the light and strange quarks within $\rho$ and $D^*_s$ mesons compared to $\rho^*$ and $K^*$ mesons.

This paper delves into the properties of growth rates in Gelfand-Shilov spaces, specifically $G_S(\gamma)$ and $G_S(\gamma')$, given a strictly convex function $\gamma$ and a strictly convex function $\gamma'$ with subanalytic growth. We explore the relationship between the growth of functions and the growth of their Fourier transforms within these spaces. We also establish growth rate estimates for functions in $G_S(\gamma)$ and $G_S(\gamma')$ based on their behavior at infinity. We reveal that this growth rate is determined by the growth rates of two convex functions, $M_1$ and $M_2$, which are derived from the growth rates of $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ respectively. Notably, the growth rates of $M_1$ and $M_2$ play a crucial role in the growth rate estimates for the functions in $G_S(\gamma)$ and $G_S(\gamma')$. We also establish relationships between the growth rates of $M_1$ and $M_2$ and the growth rates of the functions in $G_S(\gamma)$ and $G_S(\gamma')$ in terms of smoothness. We establish the relationship and the behavior of the growth rates of the functions in $G_S(\gamma)$ and $G_S(\gamma')$ when the growth rates of $M_1$ and $M_2$ tend to zero. We extend the results in \cite

Our research introduces CySGAN, an innovative solution for cybersegregation, an instance segmentation challenge. We developed CySGAN by integrating a cyber mask, derived from its corresponding semantic segmentation, with an SSGAN model. This integration enables the development of a cyber mask, which in turn facilitates the creation of a cyber image, essential for cybersegregation. We successfully applied CySGAN to the MSEG-2019 dataset, achieving exceptional results. Notably, our method surpassed SSGAN, a leading approach, in terms of performance. We also examined the applicability of CySGAN to the MSEG-2021 dataset, demonstrating its success on various difficulty levels. CySGAN is an efficient, computationally efficient approach that performs well even on limited training data.

In safety-critical human robot collaboration, anticipating actions is vital to forecast upcoming events and prevent potential conflicts. Current action anticipation methods, based on deep learning, primarily focus on predicting human body parts and use simple connection schemes to form potentials from shared representations. However, this straightforward approach falls short in capturing complex action-to-body-part ratios. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative action anticipation model that incorporates kernelized transformations, allowing for more accurate predictions. By utilizing kernel functions, we can translate potential mappings into more adaptable potential mappings. We employ Radial Basis Function kernels to capture the spatial relationships between body parts and anticipate actions with safety considerations. Our model, featuring kernelized transformations, significantly improves accuracy and reduces error rates compared to the basic method. Additionally, the kernelized approach offers greater generalization in anticipation tasks. We also introduce a new kernel type, Exponential Kernel, to enhance action transformation and achieve better results. Experimental evaluations on MINI-Action3D provide substantial evidence of the action anticipation model's superiority.

In a study involving K2 project data, we examined the broadening of hydrogen lines within stellar flares. It was discovered that this broadening is closely linked to the optical and far-ultraviolet continuum properties, developed during the flares. This phenomenon can be explained by considering the line broadening resulting from the propagation of magnetohydrodynamic waves in hot, high-altitude regions of stars experiencing flares. These waves cause hydroparticle interaction, leading to increased line broadening, and this idea is supported by observations of how line broadening changes over time during flares. Moreover, it was found that lines from ions with lower charges are more broadly affected, and this trend can be understood through simple analytical models, highlighting the influence of mass loss during flares, likely caused by strong stellar winds. These models also suggest that lines from ions with higher charges are more sensitive to the presence of winds, and this supports the findings from previous studies on the characteristics of stellar flares.

Building on earlier work by Daniel Alexander and Thomas Konrad, we investigate how non-linear deformations affect the rigidity of abelian G2-instantons. Our analysis reveals that abelian instantons have a rigid structure when considering deformations that are locally additive. Consequently, all abelian G2-instantons can be configured as fully stable critical points of a corresponding Mordell-Weil degree form.

This study examines the $C$-normality of two types of operators: the composition operator $C^\phi$ and the weighted composition operator $W^\psi$. It investigates how the hyponormality or hypernormality of these operators is affected by specific conditions on the symbols $\phi$ and $\psi$. Specifically, it is demonstrated that $C^\phi$ is $C$-normal when $\phi$ is a linear contraction or a Jouini type map, and $W^\psi$ is $C$-normal when $\psi$ meets particular weighted criteria. Additionally, it is established that both $C^\phi$ and $W^\psi$ are hypernormal if they meet certain conditions. A key finding shows that if one of the operators $C^\phi$ or $W^\psi$ is $C$-normal, then the other must also be $C$-normal.

We establish a formula for the $p$-core of largest $p'$-partitions mod $p$, using the number of $p'$-partitions with largest $p$-core mod $p$. This formula factors into two components: the first involves the $p$-adically varying generating function for partitions with largest $p$-core, and the second relies on the specific $p$-core values mod $p$. By examining the first component, we can determine the mod $p$ $p$-core values for a given partition, and understand how they behave under the action of the group $S_p$. Additionally, our work allows us to make conjectures about the second component, and thus about the structure of largest $p'$-partitions for any prime $p$.

Recent research from outside the Winogradshire region has proposed Certified Point Cloud Networks (CPCNs) that can verify the inaccuracy of inputs in non-Euclidean spaces through twisting transformations. However, the CPCN framework lacks a formalized connection to established notions of accuracy in Euclidean space and has limited applicability due to its reliance on geometry-specific features. This study presents the Trusted Positional Calibration Network (TPC), a framework that can be certified against a wide range of twisting transformations and is compatible with Euclidean space. The TPC framework is an adaptation of CPCNs, yet replaces their reliance on geometry-specific features with positional properties. As a result, the TPC framework can be certified against arbitrary coordinate rotations and is currently the only network framework capable of being certified against the full range of twisting transformations with a reasonable computation cost. The TPC framework provides a reliable accuracy guarantee for point cloud models, enhancing their trustworthiness. Moreover, the study showcases the TPC framework's practical utility by highlighting its value in securing key point cloud-based applications.

In Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar, creating a spectrogram from multiple transmitted chirps is done using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). This can be implemented in a radar network by dividing the transmission into packets, where each packet includes multiple chirps, by utilizing FFT. For each packet, a spectrum is determined and spectral power is calculated, then spectra from subsequent packets are stacked to form a 2D spectrogram. To determine interference, the difference in phase and spectral power between each packet and the previous one is found. Since radar communication is reliant on maintaining synchronization, packet synchronization is inherent. However, packets may become desynchronized due to random events such as fast moving objects or packet transmission disruptions. The cause of desynchronization is then identified through the calculation of the difference in phase and spectral power. An algorithm is developed to determine the number of chirps per packet that maximizes network throughput while minimizing desynchronization and interference. Through simulations, the optimal number of chirps per packet is determined as a function of the maximum allowable desynchronization and the probability of desynchronization.

Our research explores the phenomenon of entangled two-photon absorption in nonlinear materials by utilizing a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram. A theoretical model is developed to explain the visibility of the interferogram as a measure of coalesced photodetection events resulting from the common detection of both photons from a photon pair. Experiments involving cesium vapor and beta-barium borate eliminate variables and demonstrate that visibility can serve as an indicator of entangled two-photon absorption even in cases where detection rates are low. However, our study also reveals that a significant portion of the recorded events arises from spontaneous emission within the vapor, thereby limiting the maximum visibility to 60%.

We establish that $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology has a rigorous mathematical foundation, being derived from a singular version of $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology. This development is significant because it allows us to express any $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory as a module over the $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of a point, thereby providing an alternative method for constructing such theories. Our work also enables us to prove the existence of $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology theories that satisfy specific properties, such as being generated under colimits by certain basic constructions, and we apply this existence result to prove a corresponding extension of a longstanding conjecture in algebraic geometry proposed by Charles.

This research introduces a novel temporal knowledge graph completion method called
Time-Equivalent Knowledge Graph Completion (TEKGC). It addresses the limitations of
current approaches by incorporating a cycle-aware time-encoding scheme that
conserves cyclic temporal relationships. Unlike existing cycle-aware methods, our
scheme is adaptable to various time encodings. We propose an evaluation framework
for assessing the effectiveness of time encodings and conduct experiments with
three popular time encodings. The findings demonstrate that our cycle-aware
time-encoded model, combined with a simple ranking layer, achieves superior
performance on six public benchmarks. We also contribute a publicly accessible
code repository to the temporal knowledge graph completion field.

The sound produced by impacts on solid surfaces is commonly described using the HHM model, which however has limitations described in the following text. Through measurement-based analysis, it's found that when objects drop onto soft surfaces, the sound produced is significantly amplified, reaching levels loud enough to be heard. Contrary to expectations, the HHM model fails to accurately predict the high frequencies present in the sound, instead shifting towards lower frequencies. A new simple model is proposed, confirming that the high frequencies are indeed absent and the sound produced by objects dropping onto soft surfaces follows a different high-frequency model. It's observed that when objects drop onto soft surfaces, the sound produced is largely inulin, due to the object sticking to the surface, whereas when objects drop onto hard surfaces, the sound produced is largely shock, due to the object hitting the surface. It's also noticed that when objects are dropped onto a polar surface, the sound produced combines both shock and polarization, resulting in a more complex frequency spectrum.

Studies of Bell nonlocality play a crucial role in quantum information technology. We discovered that non-perfect correlations can exhibit Bell nonlocality, which has significant implications for the world of quantum information. Firstly, Bell nonlocality can be achieved through non-perfect correlations, challenging the conventional notion that perfect correlations are necessary. This finding could invalidate the Bell nonlocality criterion based on nonperfect correlations. Secondly, Bell nonlocality can arise from nonperfect distributions, threatening the conventional understanding of nonlocality as a phenomenon requiring perfect distributions. This discovery could render the nonlocality of perfect distributions criterion obsolete. In order to verify nonlocality in practical scenarios, we propose simulating Bell inequalities using nonperfect correlations.

Systems with flat bands, characterized by exceptional flatness in their molecular orbital diagrams, have the potential to be controlled through external randomness. By introducing a degree of randomness, the degeneracy associated with flat bands can be intentionally decreased. Utilizing numerical calculations on the double perovskite structure $Ba_2NaMCuO$_6," the effects of atomic position disorder on the electronic structure are investigated, revealing that the degeneracy of the flat bands is significantly influenced by the degree of disorder. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the band structure can be tailored to exhibit either flat bands or quasi-flat bands, thereby offering a means to control molecular-like electronic systems chemically or through statistical variations.

The electronic and structural characteristics of undoped and doped hydrogen boride monolayers are investigated through first-principles calculations, focusing on the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-phonon interactions. It is discovered that hydrogen's presence significantly alters the electron-phonon interactions by introducing structural disorder. Furthermore, it is found that the band dispersion induced by phonons has an energy dependence unique to each mode, with the longitudinal optical mode exhibiting the strongest interaction among the three phonon modes considered. Additionally, it is observed that the hydrogen bond's anisotropy gives rise to electron pocket formation on the Dirac points of the pseudomonolayer lattice, an phenomenon not present in the ideal lattice structure. Finally, it is estimated that doping with charged impurities could potentially exceed the energy scale of phonons, suggesting that phonon might play a crucial role in determining the monolayer's electrical properties.

The centralized partition function $f_{n, k}$ represents the count of partitions in the integer partition category, where each partition includes numbers from the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ modulo $k$ with even representations. We introduce a concept of flattened partitions to contribute to the study of $f_{n, k}$. Specifically, our work focuses on the occurrences of certain runs in these flattened partitions.

In our investigation, we demonstrate that for groups exhibiting virtual nilpotency of a finite nature, the character space's actions are bounded while those of toroidal dynamics are unbounded. To establish our findings, we derive a character bound by means of a nilpotent resolution. Conversely, for groups with toroidal dynamics, we present an action on the character space that is both continuous and faithful. Additionally, our study includes an examination of actions, both continuous and discrete, on the character space for surface group representations.

The introduction of autonomous automotive driving systems has introduced significant complexities into the evaluation of safety. Researchers have leveraged formal verification methods like model checking to enhance the reliability of this process, treating it as a formal verification problem and proposing various model checking-based approaches for checking the safety of driving systems. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of model checking applications in verifying the safety of driving systems, providing a detailed examination of relevant theories and formulas. Based on this analysis, the paper suggests a new method using nested temporal logic for verifying the safety of driving systems. The approach uses the MCRL2 model checker to verify the correctness of this method.

The Koopman operator theory provides an efficient approach to examining complex nonlinear systems by treating them as linear dynamics within a larger function space. This theory has mainly been applied to observation-based methods that utilize Koopman operator properties to analyze system behavior. However, the theory has primarily been implemented through matrix-valued operators that facilitate the exploration of system characteristics. Despite the potential for more sophisticated, operator-type representations, the framework has generally been limited to vector-based descriptions. Despite its utility, the Koopman operator theory has some significant drawbacks, such as the challenge of determining the observables needed to characterize system features. Despite these limitations, the theory offers a valuable way to understand and characterize nonlinear dynamical systems. This study aims to address these challenges by offering a data-driven approach to identifying necessary observables through an iterative process. This new approach aims to expand the observables used to describe the system, ensuring data consistency, and utilizes the temporal coherence of data to initialize the process. This study also includes results from several applications, including a simple chaotic system and a large-scale wind tunnel test, to demonstrate the effectiveness of this new method.

This study explores Leibniz's notion of infinity through the lens of earlier thinkers, specifically Cantor and Russell. Leibniz proposed a dichotomy between bounded and unbounded infinity, with the latter being inconceivable due to its excess beyond all bounds, as explained in his correspondence with the Abbot of Castel. Contrasting earlier interpretations, this study suggests Leibniz's concept of unbounded infinity represents an abstract class of sets infinite in magnitude. It is then examined how his concept of bounded infinity relates to potential infinity, as conceptualized by the ancient Greeks, as well as how it applies to geometric series. Building on this analysis, the paper discusses Cantor's influence on the modern understanding of infinity and how Leibniz's ideas are reevaluated in the context of naive comprehension.

Cosmic background measurements are compromised by foreground noise, which must be removed to study the universe accurately. The widely used removal methods, though efficient, may introduce artificial patterns that could mislead parameter estimation if not properly accounted for. The impact of these patterns on parameter estimation is currently unknown. We investigated how removing galactic foreground from CMB data using different methods affects accurate parameter measurement. The removal methods examined are COMPAS, which uses a source-separation technique, and COMMANDER, a module integrated in the Planck data analysis package. The analysis simulated 1000 parameter sets, each based on a template spectrum, and evaluated the distribution of residual power in pixel space for each method. The results showed that pixels with lower angular frequencies are more susceptible to removal artifacts, which are correlated with the pixels' intensity in the remaining parameter sets. The removal methods' ability to recover the template spectrum and estimated parameters were also assessed. The results showed that pixels with lower angular frequencies are more challenging to recover, and that parameters are more difficult to estimate from these pixels. These findings are consistent with a broader study that used a larger dataset.

The study focuses on sequences of vectors $\{v_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ that are transformed by a finite-dimensional operator $\Phi$, resulting in new sequences $\{\Phi(v)\}_{n=1}^\infty$. We determine the conditions under which the new sequences remain distinct and independently variable, and examine how these conditions relate to various operators, including difference, sum, shift, and stochastic operators.

For a particular user, certain items may not have enough information to provide a recommendation, as there may not be enough data to build a reliable model. Therefore, document modeling-based methods combine item and user models to utilize knowledge more broadly, but they can only draw from individual item data. To address this limitation, a new method called Cooperative Document Model (CDM) is being proposed, which uses both item and user knowledge to inform recommendations. CDM develops a single, unified model that integrates data from the pool of users and items, thereby expanding the training dataset and improving recommendation accuracy. Moreover, CDM offers additional benefits by allowing recommendations to be tailored to community standards and item descriptions. To demonstrate the strength of CDM, a variant of the model called CDM-Fuse is implemented and compared to existing methods on real-world datasets, showing a notable improvement in recommendation accuracy and overall performance.

We establish an exact connection between the conditionally free independence of non-Hermitian matrices and the Wigner semicircle distribution at a microscopic level. Our study delves into the characteristic function of a specific matrix element, leading to an intricate algebraic investigation involving the matrix's entry in a non-Hermitian generalization of the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This is further supported by an investigation of the matrix's eigenvalue distribution, which we demonstrate can be broken down into conditional freeness variables.

In real-time systems, timing uncertainty can lead to significant problems, 
even causing tasks to miss deadlines. As a result, it's crucial to develop a 
monitoring strategy that's aware of these timing uncertainties and is capable 
of adapting to unexpected changes. The traditional rate monotonic scheduling 
algorithm is limited by its assumption of known task periods, making it 
unsuitable for systems dealing with uncertainty. Our approach presents a 
method for monitoring and adapting to timing uncertainty in real-time systems, 
even when the uncertainty affects task durations randomly and independently. 
The strategy is based on a model that simulates the system's scheduling behavior, 
using a combination of statistical measures to adjust its monitoring and adaptation 
decisions. These measures include the average and standard deviation of task 
durations, which are updated in real-time using a simple and efficient algorithm. 
Our model is proven to be effective in achieving a high level of probability for 
all tasks to meet their deadlines, even in the presence of unlimited system capacity. 
Our strategy is then applied to a model of wireless communication systems, is proven 
to work in theory and is demonstrated to be functional in practice, achieving a 
given deadline probability of 98% for a real-world system.

An analysis of the $D_s^+ \to D^+ K^+ a_0(980)$ decay is carried out by examining the $D_s^+ \to D^+ K^+ K^0_S$ decay data collected by the LHCb detector, specifically 1.70 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity corresponding to 2011-2012 center-of-mass energy of 7 and 8 TeV. The study involves reconstructing $D_s^+ \to D^+ K^+ K^0_S$ decays using the $D^+K^+K^0_S$ vertex reconstruction technique, and calculating the $D_s^+ \to D^+ K^+ a_0(980)$ branching ratio based on this analysis. The 95% confidence interval for the $D_s^+ \to D^+ K^+ a_0(980)$ branching ratio is estimated as $ \left[ 0.154 \pm 0.071 \pm 0.030 \right] \times 10^{-3}$. The estimation of the $D_s^+ \to D^+ K^+ a_0(980)$ branching ratio is in accordance with the previously calculated rate, specifically $ \left[ 0.160 \pm 0.060 \pm 0.030 \right] \times 10^{-3}$. The GRAVITY project at the Very Large Telescope (VLT) is part of the Project 1010, which aims to develop a high-resolution, angular differential image position sensor. This innovative device seeks to make various astronomical observations more efficient by reducing data collection time. A key aspect of the sensor involves detecting position shifts within images taken at different wavelengths. To achieve this, the project utilizes a plain wave laser that creates a reference map, which is then compared to the acquired images. However, the project posed significant technical challenges, particularly in regards to stabilizing the camera used to capture images. A team of researchers conducted a study on the properties of the camera, which led to the development of specific stabilization techniques. These techniques, which contributed significantly to the efficiency of the GRAVITY operation, were derived directly from the properties of the acquisition camera. As a result, the project successfully completed all necessary tests in 2014 and launched an observational program. A recent software update in 2018 enabled the utilization of four of the VLT's 8.2-m telescopes, which marked another major achievement for the project.

We examine the approximability of the Capacitated k-Center problem, a well-known variant of the classical k-Center problem, with constrained capacity at each facility and limited demand at each client. In contrast to the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers, a related but harder approximation issue, we find that the former has a significantly more challenging "highway dimension" value of $d$. As an outcome, approximations within a factor of $2^{21} \log^3 n$ are not possible, demonstrating the sharpness of earlier algorithms with approximation factors $2^{O(\sqrt{\log \log n})}$ and $2^{O(\log \log n)}$. We also show that the difference in "highway dimension" between these two optimization challenges is indeed the source of this significant approximability disparity.

This study introduces a precise framework for the Brück conjecture in the scenario where an entire function has a hyper order less than 1/2. Our research complements the existing work by Chirita and Spring, who tackled the inverse problem of the Phragmen--Lindelöf principle. To arrive at our findings, we devised a novel approach that leverages the function's hyper order to derive bounds for its Taylor series coefficients. This paper's outcomes also hold implications for the Nevanlinna--Hartogs theorem.

Our research focuses on developing methods for solving polynomial systems under conditions of uncertainty, allowing for a limited number of errors. By relaxing the exactness requirement, we can reduce the number of evaluations needed during polynomial interpolation while maintaining a certain level of accuracy. This finding leads to two key outcomes. Firstly, we can improve the efficiency of polynomial linear system solving by incorporating error tolerance. Secondly, we can derive simplified formulas for basic polynomial problem-solving over finite fields, taking into account allowable errors. This results in a reduced number of computations compared to existing methods.

We suggest an experiment using a three-level $\Lambda$-type atom coupled to an optical cavity for the production of even and odd photons. By adjusting the relaxation time and the atom-cavity coupling strength, we can control the emergence of even and odd correlated photons. We observe that both the cavity and the atom follow a coherent state evolution. We further investigate the influence of incoherent processes on the photon emission and find that a specific parameter setting can isolate the odd correlated photons while suppressing the even correlated photons. This concept has potential applications in the generation of singletons and other non-classical states of light for utilization in quantum information technologies.

We have developed a single equation of state that incorporates the principles of corresponding states and non-corresponding states for alkali metals. This equation effectively models the divergent behavior of these elements' equations of state at high pressures, with a non-analytical transition that differentiates them. To achieve this, we considered two potential approaches: an equation featuring a pressure- and volume-dependent coefficient for electric interactions, and an equation with a non-corresponding states model featuring a change in boundary surface. However, both strategies were found to be impractical. Ultimately, a solution was found in an equation of state that includes a term representing the van der Waals interaction at lower pressures and a term representing a change in boundary surface with a non-corresponding states model at higher pressures. This equation of state aligns with the principles of corresponding states at lower pressures and exhibits non-corresponding states behavior at higher pressures. It has been mathematically proven that an equation of state that includes a term representing the van der Waals interaction at lower pressures and a term representing a non-corresponding states model at higher pressures will always display a change in boundary surface. Furthermore, calculations have shown that the values of $\kappa$ and $d\/dP(\rho/$/$)$ at critical points do not adhere to the principles of corresponding states. Additionally, experiments have confirmed the principles of corresponding states to be accurate below a certain threshold of pressure but diverge at higher pressures. This equation of state has

Local parity breaking in a medium can arise from chiral mechanisms, which often incorporate the Chern-Simons term into the action. To examine its effects, we've developed a CS-QED lagrangian with both gauge invariance and redshift transformations observed. The bound states of the lagrangian have been represented by kernel expressions, which are consistent with gauge invariance. The kernel expressions for vector mesons include both a longitudinal and transverse component, resulting from the breakdown of local parity symmetry. This is evident in the kernel's structure, which contains a mixed term representing the mixing of transverse and longitudinal vector bosons. In an external magnetic field, the mass spectrum of the vector boson exhibits a parameter (eB) that indicates a shift in mass, aligning with previous research. Additionally, we've calculated the kernel for scalar and pseudoscalar mesons, which are analagously affected by the magnetic field. The kernel's breakdown into local parity symmetry adds to our understanding of chiral spirit and possible applications in the study of local parity symmetry.

We introduce a randomized distributed algorithm to estimate the overall size of a network by its individual nodes, utilizing a breadth-first search approach over unknown and dynamic networks represented by an orientation of a probability graph. Specifically, our method works within variational networks, which are characterized by exponentially increasing average degree as the number of nodes grows. It has been developed to accommodate various common network structures, such as networks built from tree products and networks with tree-like connectivity exponents. In contrast to existing distributed estimation algorithms for network size, our proposal offers two significant advantages: it requires fewer messages in terms of the logarithm of the estimated node count and has a lower estimation error compared to non-parametric methods.

I'm looking at the numerical simulation of broad classes of f(R) gravity theories, which deviates from General Relativity based on a specific function. The Hamiltonian, the constraint that needs to be solved at the beginning of time, is typically solved using finite difference methods. The new method I'm studying, which modifies the metric to remove conformal factors, which usually causes simulation instability. The method solves the Hamiltonian constraint by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a suitable space, which is related to a elliptic equation. The method is similar to other methods but doesn't involve conformal factors. The method is more accurate than others, which usually simplify the Hamiltonian, and is stable, which isn't the case for simulations of these theories. The method is applied to a range of theories and the results are comparable to analytical solutions. The method is more efficient than other methods, which usually simplify the Hamiltonian, and is more stable. The method allows for the simulation of broad classes of theories without making assumptions about the geometry of the universe.

The primary components of the JUNO detector are 20-ton modules of Liquid Scintillator, surrounded by photomultiplier tubes that offer high energy and timing resolution. To ensure optimal performance, each module must have its PMTs calibrated to produce accurate measurements. The process of calibrating these PMTs involves recording the response of each tube to various light sources within the LS and applying corrections based on observed distortions. The most significant challenge lies in correcting for the inherent biases and limitations of each PMT, particularly those that suffer from pulse distortion due to the finite bandwidth of the detectors. To address this issue, researchers collected statistical samples of pulse shapes through both in-lab experiments and simulation-based data analysis. They then used these datasets to create pulse shape reconstruction models that account for the effects of pulse distortion, effectively using the pulse shape to determine the pulse arrival time with high accuracy. The results show that this method achieves time resolution of approximately 100 ps in laboratory conditions, and this technique will play a crucial role in maintaining the high time resolution of the JUNO detector once fully implemented.

The Informer model excels at capturing complex temporal connections in sequence prediction, yet it's limited to applications involving data with a single dimension. Extending its potential, we present a multidimensional time series prediction model (M-TS-P) built upon the Informer structure. To accommodate multiple dimensions, M-TS-P employs an encoder that divides each into sub-dimensions, then combines these to facilitate dependent relationship capture. Furthermore, an adaptive weight module aligns sub-dimensions for improved model performance. Experimentally, M-TS-P consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art models on diverse datasets. Notably, M-TS-P predicts sub-dimensions separately, allowing for individual performance analysis and potentially wider model applications.

The quality of optics can be marred by atmospheric effects, particularly 
atmospheric dispersion which varies according to wavelengths. This study 
investigates four atmospheric dispersion models: Hueveler's model, 
Hastings's model, Roulet's model and Roulet and Burch's model to determine 
which provides accurate readings. By comparing these models to actual data 
obtained from various sources, it appears that Roulet and Burch's model is not 
suitable for further study due to its inaccuracy. In contrast, Roulet's model 
is applicable but needs to be adjusted by considering temperature's 
quadratic effect on atmospheric dispersion. Generally, Hueveler's model is 
considered the best choice as it incorporates temperature's quadratic 
effect and provides positive results for atmospheric dispersion. This study 
also develops equations to enable quick and efficient calculation of 
astigmatism correction for 200mm and 300mm lenses affected by atmospheric 
dispersion.

Deep neural networks' prediction accuracy can be enhanced through ensemble methods, which incorporate multiple model votes. However, leading ensembles, such as Bagging and Pareto-Network, have limitations due to their tendency to favor majority votes and fail to utilize label information. To address these issues, we introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a voting system based on pairwise model comparisons that utilizes label information in its process. PILE first initiates a vote from 10% of models with accessible ground truth, then iteratively enhances prediction accuracy by incorporating more models, which are trained on artificially created datasets based on previous votes. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through significant improvements in image classification and semantic segmentation tasks.

The concept of bosonic dark matter existing as ultralight waves has gained traction in recent years. Current research has demonstrated that large-scale telescopes can detect its presence through its cross-polarized Stokes map, but only after significant post-processing has been applied. This work focuses on revealing the presence of quantum fluctuations within ultralight bosonic dark matter through its imaging. By modeling quantum fluctuations within an array of sensors, we have found that their correlation improves the detection of intensity fluctuations at lower signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, we have established that multiple sensors can be placed at different locations to enhance detection efficiency. Notably, we have found that an ideal arrangement of sensors lies along a circle where the distance between each sensor is equal. Ultimately, we have found that an array of sensors can be up to 35% more effective in detecting the stochastic intensity fluctuations compared to a single sensor.

The basis pursuit problem is a critical sparse reconstruction technique, which can be implemented through thresholding algorithms like coordinate descent. However, this method's stability and sparsity-regulating performance are heavily dependent on the matrix E, which can be influenced by its spectral characteristics. Research has shown that when the matrix E has a broad spectrum, sparse solutions may not accurately represent the original signal, even when using the same basis. In this study, specific conditions are established for choosing the optimization path and penalty parameters in basis pursuit, which guarantee that the thresholded solution and the original signal share the same sparse representation. Research has also demonstrated the importance of spectral conditions in regression problems, but this study's results are the first to address this issue in basis pursuit.

Advances in programmable switches have led to increased interest in switch-based network architecture, leading to a surge in related research. Although switches hold great potential, their evaluation is problematic due to a lack of freely accessible compiler backends, forcing researchers to rely on built-in and black-box compilers, which offer limited control. To address this issue, we introduce BC5, an open-source compiler backend for Brocade VDX 7000 switch. We also develop FlexNet, a flexible network mapping tool allowing for the creation of arbitrary switch-based network configurations. FlexNet's modularity enables researchers to change the switch evaluation paradigm, simplifying the evaluation process and making it more adaptable to various applications.

A novel finite element approach, combining conforming finite elements for the vector transport equation, offers an improved solution compared to traditional methods. This method mitigates solutions' non-physical components and avoids convergence towards incorrect fixed points. Unlike existing methods, which rely on fixed-point iterations, this approach introduces an optimal continuous transportation operator in tandem with a discrete transport scheme, yielding faster convergence and reduced computational costs.

To address machine learning's (ML) inherent shortcomings, researchers combine advanced mathematical techniques with ethical considerations. This research review provides a detailed examination of the mathematical approaches used to address three primary concerns: fairness, reliability, and transparency in ML. The review examines how the application of mathematical methods affects the training and deployment of ML models. Although ML's applications are diverse, this review focuses on using image transformations to illustrate the impact of mathematical mathematics on ML. The review also explores the interconnectedness of these concerns and highlights the ML models' 'blind spots,' which are challenges to be tackled in the field.

A comprehensive study was conducted using the LHCb detector data collected during Run 1 to search for the $B_c^+\rightarrow J/\psi p$ transition. The data sample equated to 0.9 pb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity was examined. Two $B_c^+$ excited states, $B_c^{*+}$ and $B_c^{'+}$, were discovered by reconstructing the $B_c^+\to J/\psi p$ transition. The $B_c^{*+}$ state was found at an invariant mass of 6407.2 $\pm$ 2.9 MeV/$c^2$ with a width of 21.0 $\pm$ 4.7 MeV, and the $B_c^{'+}$ state at 6522.2 $\pm$ 2.7 MeV/$c^2$ with a width of 11.7 $\pm$ 4.6 MeV. The observed properties of these states, specifically their masses and natural widths, were also determined. The research found that the $B_c^{*+}$ state had a mass of 6407.2 $\pm$ 2.9 MeV/$c^2$, the $B_c^{'+}$ state had a mass of 6522.2 $\pm$ 2.7 MeV/$c^2$, and the natural widths for both states were within estimated ranges.
