This study examines the ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations in high-dimensional spaces. Specifically, we find that the problem becomes ill-posed in dimension 4 and above for initial data with specific low-frequency patterns, and that this limitation is not affected by any constraints, such as being divergence-free. Moreover, we prove that the problem is not only ill-posed in the sense of divergence, but also in the sense of strong solutions, in these high-dimensional spaces.

The ability to create desired images using neural networks often relies on substantial prior knowledge of how to manipulate these networks.  However, this limitation can be overcome by using stable generators that can adjust to user-directed adjustments in the input bias without experiencing instability.  Unfortunately, transferring this stability to other generators requires a time-consuming and labor-intensive retraining process.  But what if we could achieve the same effect through a combination of data and techniques inspired by "style transfer," allowing users to control generated images without needing deep learning expertise?  Our approach, called Stable Artist, uses AI-generated art and a data-driven correction method to make a neural network stable and easy to control.  This method is fast, reliable, and understandable to non-experts, and has been implemented in a simple browser application that allows anyone to create their own unique, professionally-generated art.  Our video demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by showing various users with different abilities and backgrounds creating their own generated art.

Deep learning predictive models frequently rely on confidence estimates derived from the output predictions, however these measures are often inaccurate due to the disconnect between model uncertainty and prediction uncertainty. To address this discrepancy, we have developed a novel approach to quantify the limitations of predictive models by treating them as restricted stochastic processes. This framework, expressed through the lens of hierarchical Bayesian modeling, allows us to characterize the uncertainty surrounding predictions and accurately quantify prediction limits. Furthermore, we have derived a method for modulating a classifier's confidence bounds in real-time, enhancing the robustness of adversarial attacks and facilitating the discovery of effective attacks. Moreover, we have demonstrated that our real-time defense could protect against the powerful RFOO attack with only a 2.5% increase in the attack's success rate, whereas a 100% increase was experienced at the cost of this improvement.

Upcoming dark matter direct detection experiments will be able to detect even a millionth of a billionth of a gram of dark matter per liter of target material per year. Their limits will be significantly stricter than current ones, with implications for cross section values, making certain assumptions, currently popular, even more reasonable. We'll focus on final states with and without visible particles produced by dark matter interactions. The former is relevant to systems with two or more dark matter particles and can apply to certain baryogenic dark matter models. We'll examine fast-moving dark matter particles that occasionally interact with nucleons, resulting in undetectable final states, being a major factor in determining dark matter lifetimes. We discovered that post-therapy limits on dark matter-nucleon cross sections can be highly sensitive to dark matter lifetimes, even when they are much shorter than its natural lifetime. We explored various baryogenic dark matter models where LSP decays into Standard Model particles, enhancing limits on dark matter-nucleon cross sections by several orders of magnitude. We discovered that model parameters that keep dark matter mostly coupled to nucleons result in high LSP masses in the multi-TeV range. We examined visible final states produced by dark matter interactions and observed that FIMP (Frozen In Massive Particle) interactions with nucleons and other dark matter particles are often preferred over other visible processes. We discovered that model parameters that keep dark matter mostly coupled to nucleons result in high LSP masses in the multi-TeV range

Magnetic bright points, tiny magnetic flux concentrations, are key sites for their generation. Observations of these points in solar photosphere offer insight into solar magnetism's intricate dynamics. This study analyzes statistical characteristics of magnetic bright points identified in datasets from the SOT/Hinode and JSFP/SPINE2, focusing on their locations, sizes, and movements. It finds that these sites are mostly pole-shaped and have positive magnetic flux. Statistical distributions of these points' velocity vectors match the solar wind's, while their x and y components exhibit distinct distributions. This research is set to enhance our understanding of magnetic bright points' roles in the solar wind's dynamic generation.

We propose minimal videos, consisting of mere movements with altered optics, to better comprehend human visual perception and recognition abilities. Minimal videos serve as an ideal representation of intrinsic variability in human vision, distinguishing it from complex factor-driven perceptions. These videos exhibit inherent variability, regardless of the presence of various external factors such as lighting, occlusions, and motion ambiguities. Our research leverages the strength of minimal videos in facilitating robust perception and the development of more precise human activity recognition models via machine learning. To achieve this, we create a new minimal video dataset, MVCTN-Dataset, comprising 1,760 daily household activities and 1,440 artistic movements, accompanied by 50,800 flow fields. Our research reveals the efficacy of using flow fields in minimal video representation through an advanced machine learning model, comprising a convolutional neural network, designed to generate a 128-dimensional minimal video feature. Our model achieves a recognition accuracy of 70.6% on the full Olivetti dataset, surpassing the performance of a leading HOG-SVM system with an accuracy of 42.2%. Our minimal video features exhibit robustness against various external factors, yielding an accuracy of 50.6% when applied to the CMU self-paced walking dataset and 40.4% for the KTH dataset, in addition to providing a 40% reduction in model storage requirements.

The thermodynamic properties of a weakly coupled monopole system and the potential lattice gauge theory are examined as the monopole charge becomes infinitely large. In this limit, the bound monopole pairs consolidate into a single, long-range field. To calculate the thermodynamic properties, we used a 3D lattice and applied the Monte Carlo method to investigate the quasi-exact region between the gapped high-energy and free low-energy phases. Our findings show that an external magnetic field transforms the monopole ground state into a bound pair, which experiences dimerization. Moreover, we discovered that an external magnetic field can break the Z2 symmetry of the monopole dimer phase, resulting in a highly nonlinear field behavior and a Bogomol'nyi bound state. Our study also found that an applied magnetic field can drive a monopole phase transition from the dimer phase to an ferromagnetic monopole phase. Our results can contribute to the understanding of color superconductivity in quantum chromodynamics.

This research seeks to address the question of how weather forecasting performance is impacted by normalized data, a question previously answered in the context of deep learning for video car recognition and neural network training but not weather forecasting. To test this, several neural network models were created using real weather data, some of which were normalized and others not. The findings showed that normalizing data did not enhance the evaluation of weather forecasting models beyond 7 days. Furthermore, when comparing the predictions of 16 global weather forecasting centers, we found that using normalized data did not improve the evaluation of pre-trained models, even when the pre-training data did not match the distribution of the test location. Consequently, we suggest abandoning data normalization when evaluating weather forecasting models.

We've investigated the connection between the mass of a dark matter candidate and CP violation in three-Higgs-doublet models that incorporate naturally generated dark matter. The intersection of these models with the necessary conditions for dark matter stability is examined, with a focus on how CP breaking impacts the mass range of dark matter candidates. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the CP sensitivity that can be achieved through future LHC runs, particularly in searches for rare processes involving Higgs and Z bosons decaying into leptons.

The PPT conjecture proposes a connection between positivity and partial transposition in quantum systems. Although the PPT criterion is effective for detecting separability in finite-dimensional spaces, it is less reliable in infinite-dimensional spaces. To improve separability detection in infinite-dimensional systems, a new criterion based on the relative entropy of entanglement has been introduced. This entropy of entanglement criterion is able to detect all forms of entanglement and has been found to be capable of determining separability in bipartite Hilbert spaces of infinite dimensionality. Furthermore, research indicates that the PPT conjecture holds true in bipartite infinite-dimensional systems that are completely positive and trace-preserving.

The unique transport mechanisms used by neurons to move materials along their lengthy, branchy structures are facilitated by the delicate balance between microtubules, neurofilaments, and associated proteins. A key factor in understanding transport is to identify how microtubule properties, such as diameter and axial period, influence the flow of anterograde and retrograde traffic. To address this, we developed a theoretical model of transport, validated by comparing simulated data to previous experimental measurements, and used it to examine the effects of microtubule properties and branch geometry on material transport. Our results indicate that, under typical neuron conditions, the slow transport rate is largely determined by the diameter and structure of microtubules, especially at branches, and that alterations in transport are mainly caused by changes in these factors, rather than changes in the branch geometry. This suggests that, in neurons with pathologically altered microtubules, decreased material transport is likely due to altered microtubule structure, rather than other factors.

In the field of banking, analyzing transactions relies heavily on the customer's transaction history, often represented as a directed graph. Current studies on detecting fraudulent transactions typically use machine learning methods with the assumption of access to a customer's complete transaction history. However, providing access to all transaction history is impractical, especially if it's excessively large. Additionally, giving readers partial information risks hiding crucial data. To address these issues, we introduce an innovative method for generating valid banking graphs, allowing us to train a machine learning model to identify fraudulent activity without needing the entire transaction history. Our research uses generative modeling, creating a posterior distribution of banking graphs by minimizing an loss function that matches the generated graph to real transaction data. The method includes a novel heuristic for directing the generator and multiple methods for determining valid graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by training a machine learning model to identify fraudulent activity on a real-world dataset, outperforming existing methods.

In X-ray binary systems involving a black hole and a white dwarf, a stable high-latitude accretion disc usually forms when the white dwarf's magnetic field breaks through its surface due to mass loss. This disc then feeds energy into the surrounding space through wind momentum, a crucial process previously only modeled in specific scenarios. A new study introduces a unified theoretical framework for wind momentum that works regardless of the white dwarf's magnetic field or its mass loss mechanisms. Using observational data and supported by numerical simulations, this framework provides a coherent explanation for various X-ray binary system observations. Specifically, it accounts for the significant variation in Luminosity of Low-mass Ratio Systems within the mass range of 0.2 to 1 solar masses and the particular pattern of Hubble Space Telescope observed ultraviolet emission.

We examine the feasibility of distinguishing between the CP-odd and CP-even components in the three-body semileptonic decays of the tau lepton, $\tau^{-} \to Knox^{-} \nu_{\tau}$, through the application of a measurement method called difference ordering. This method has previously been utilized in events with high multiplicity and complex topology, such as events containing $B$-decay fragments. The application of the method in $\tau$-decay allows for a CP-sensitivity analysis, and assuming a very small electron contamination, we find that the CP-odd component can be isolated with high purity; the remaining contamination can be reduced by utilizing additional information derived from the decay pattern.

To address classification tasks with high similarity between classes, researchers often employ binary logistic classification models. However, this poses a problem, as standard training methods typically struggle with noisy labels, leading to decreased performance. To overcome this challenge, a new method, based on the $K$-mer symmetric Tversky ratio model, provides a way to leverage label similarities. This approach involves training $K$ binary logistic models separately and then combining them with a novel training scheme, exploiting the structural properties of the Tversky model. It turns out that this composite model achieves its extreme points in the space of possible metrics. Results show that these extreme points can be approximated efficiently using a new algorithm and, in experiments, applying this method to data from medical imaging and image classification yielded better results compared to standard training methods, particularly under noisy label conditions.

In a process called reblurring, we apply a blurring effect in reverse to a given image, specifically to recover it from a deliberately introduced artificial blur. Our method incorporates an innovative reblurring module within a standard generative adversarial network framework, enabling it to learn the reverse blurring process and adapt it to eliminate real-world image blur. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our model in successfully removing blur from both artificially blurred images, as well as actual images blurred by real-world factors. Additionally, we found that reversing blurring has a significant impact on various computer vision tasks that utilize image datasets, leading to improved performance in specific cases. Consequently, we suggest incorporating a reblurring module within the generative adversarial network to enhance its effectiveness.

To model autonomous, self-contained learning, we utilize chemical reaction networks (CRNs), applying existing methods to derive gradient flow from network structure. Focusing on a CRN capable of gradient-based optimization, we investigate the thermodynamic costs associated with maintaining concentration gradients. It is determined that these costs significantly decrease as the CRN approaches an optimal solution. We also examine a CRN designed to simulate Stuart-Landau oscillators and observe that the network, when coupled with an adaptive system, exhibits adaptive criticality, facilitating the transition between stable and chaotic dynamics. Lastly, we outline a strategy for CRN-based optimization of complex tasks, leveraging adaptive phase transitions.

We establish that the density of a original set influences its completeness in an ultrapower extension. Specifically, our findings indicate that if a set is complete and has a density less than a specific cardinal number, an ultrapower extension of that set exists with the same completeness properties. Conversely, if a set has a density greater than that same cardinal number, an ultrapower extension of that set exists with the same completeness properties but with a different density. Additionally, our conclusions refine and resolve two separate problems proposed by Kefer and Väänänen.

In data-driven science, benchmarking plays a critical role in validating systems and measuring performance, but the widespread adoption of benchmark suites has led to inaccurate measurements due to a key limitation - insufficient model complexity reproduction. This gap hinders accurate system assessment and performance measurement, especially for systems relying on heavy models. To bridge this gap, we introduce HyperBench, an innovative hyperscale benchmarking platform aimed at accurately measuring system performance while faithfully replicating the complexity of computer models. By integrating hyperscale technology, HyperBench accelerates model execution, enhancing benchmarking efficiency and simplicity. Furthermore, HyperBench enables real-time, fine-grained hyperscale system analysis, allowing for the detection and resolution of hyperscale-related issues during benchmarking operations. HyperBench supports both transparent and opaque hyperscale modeling and can be applied across various computing systems, from single-node to multi-node systems.

We show that for a given graph of t colors, if it includes a rooted branch set of size d+1 with specific properties, it will have a proper t-coloring for any d value greater than or equal to the size of the largest clique in a t-x-coloring graph, where x is less than t/2. This leads to the conclusion that certain graphs, including near-branching and extremal t-colorings, are linearly t-colorable. We then prove that there exist graphs that are linearly but not smoothly t-colorable, as well as establish a lower bound on the number of t-colorings of a graph with a K_t minor.

This paper investigates a fundamental issue in online learning and adaptive algorithms, namely how to effectively leverage past information. It demonstrates that the convexity of a cost function not only influences the performance of these algorithms but also potentially prevents them from achieving optimal results. Consequently, the paper suggests a new class of adaptive algorithms known as 'Look-Ahead' algorithms that capitalize on past information to deliver superior outcomes. Interestingly, the paper finds that the standard Follow-the-Reweighted-Gradient (FRG) algorithm, when modified to account for past gradients, does not yield optimal results in various scenarios, whereas a modified version of the Multi-Level Gradient Descent (MLGD) algorithm does achieve optimal performance. The study provide compelling evidence that supporting algorithms exist for fundamental problems, and it raises questions about the existence of such support for more complex problems. Additionally, the paper provides empirical validation of its theoretical findings by comparing the performance of these algorithms on a range of non-stochastic risk minimization tasks.

A theoretical model is developed for enhancing the sensitivity of quantum metrology using trapped ions. This model builds upon binary collision experiments by producing a large number of simultaneous collisions. A binary collision is achieved through activating a trigger switch on a ion trap's electrodes to induce the motion of a trap oscillator. To increase collision frequency, the switch is activated multiple times. The final collision is made entangling, turning individual events into a source of quantum correlation among all participants. The sensitivity of this process could be improved by increasing the frequency of non-entangling collisions. Research indicates that even with a low collision frequency, the resulting quantum correlation can lead to significant improvements in precision. The switch method's simplicity allows for the implementation of advanced triggering techniques to optimize this process for best possible results.

Using variational methods and specific function estimates, we obtain sharp bounds for the first eigenvalue of the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator subject to a second boundary condition on a bounded domain with smooth boundary. The obtained bounds are expressed in terms of the anisotropic vector field's parameters and they generalize known bounds for the standard $p$-Laplace operator.

The application of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) has been primarily confined to graph data. This study reveals a novel connection between conventional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), fully connected Neural Networks, and GCNs on graph, point cloud, and image data. Based on this connection, we develop a method to adapt existing CNNs to GCNs. This way, researchers can leverage and extend existing knowledge about CNNs to inform GCN design. Furthermore, we present a method to transform GCNs into equivalent CNNs, allowing for cross-training and a deeper understanding of the underlying representations. Our work is accompanied by experimental evaluation on various datasets, demonstrating the efficacy of these methods.

Current self-training methods, which enhance parsing models through self-supervised learning, often rely on label propagation. Yet, they inherently assume labels can be easily shared and propagated, which isn't the case when dealing with noisy, incomplete or highly specialized data. To address this, we're introducing Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST), a new method that adapts self-supervised learning for deep contextualized representations. DCST addresses the two main limitations of traditional self-training by 1) avoiding label propagation, instead using a self-supervised loss function, and 2) incorporating contextualized representations, which improves its effectiveness. DCST outperforms current self-training approaches and pre-training strategies using contextualized embeddings on multiple parsing tasks, showcasing its capacity to further improve model performance beyond what self-supervised learning can achieve alone.

We made the first predictions for how likely it is for a $B$-meson to decay into a $D$-meson, 
a tau lepton, and other particles, compared to how likely it is for it to decay into a 
$D$-meson, an electron, and other particles, or into a $D$-meson, a muon, and other 
particles. Our predictions were based on how fast these different groups of leptons 
travel and the amount of the $B$-meson's energy that they carry away. We calculated 
the chances of these decays happening with the help of the "quark by quark interaction" 
process and found that the branching ratios for decays with tau leptons are a few percent 
lower than the branching ratios for decays with electron or muon leptons. We also found 
that the decay rates for certain high-energy collisions are similar whether they involve 
tau leptons or electron/muon leptons, but that the spectrum of the energy carried away 
by the leptons differs significantly in decays with tau leptons compared to decays with 
electron/muon leptons. Our predictions were based on two models: one in which the 
$D$-meson and lepton are at rest, and one in which the $D$-meson and lepton are moving

The research develops introducing non-invertible charges, or symmetries, in field theories. Deriving the fusion table of non-invertible symmetries is achieved through a key method. This method employs a universal property to define the fusion of non-invertible symmetries. As a result, the fusion of multiple symmetries can be calculated. Furthermore, proof is provided that fusion of any symmetry with itself is equivalent to the original symmetry. Additionally, proof is given that the fusion of two symmetries is also invertible if their product is invertible. As an example, the research applies these concepts to non-invertible symmetries in the Ising and Moore-Tachikawa models.

Given a finite field $k$ and a system of linear equations in $n$ variables, we examine its representability within first-order logic over finite fields. It is demonstrated that, under specific criteria, the existence of solutions to this equation system can be expressed in a way consistent with the logic, whereas in other cases this existence is not consistent and may not be expressible. These boundary conditions are accurately described by an inequality involving the number of variables and fields, but in some instances a simpler alternative inequality applies. Furthermore, it is shown that similar principles govern the consistency of statements concerning quadratic equations and systems of equations that include quadratic terms.

The details about the chemical doping of the heavy fermion compound $\Eu_2$IrO$_4$ by Bi have been investigated through a series of experiments conducted on $(\Eu_1-x\underline{Bi}_x$)$2$Ir$2$O$_7$ with $x$ equal to 0.05, 0.10, and 0.20. The $\Eu$ content in the samples varied from $x+0.05x/5=0.065$ to $x+0.20=0.20$, denoted as $\Eu_{1+x}$ with a negative sign, and was examined via second generation tunable infrared spectroscopy, which showed that the spectra became weaker as Bi was doped. The analysis also revealed that the spectra can be broken down into three parts: the absorption related to the $\Eu$ doping at 340 cm^-1, the effect of Bi doping at 480 cm^-1, and an unresolved underlying spectral issue. The last part has an amplitude that changes with the $\Eu$ content in an inconsistent manner. In order to gain a deeper understanding, the samples were also examined using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, which confirmed Bi doping and provided valence band spectra. The spectra showed that Bi contributes to the upper part of the valence band spectrum, and the overall spectral shape becomes more metallic in nature as Bi is doped. The analysis of resistivity measurements confirms these findings,

A significant quantity of research has been devoted to broadening the scope of the Borsuk-Lipschitz theorem. Initially demonstrated for spaces with a differentiable structure, this theorem has been expanded to cover a range of other spaces, ultimately including general metric spaces. Our analysis builds upon existing findings by offering novel extensions of the theorem to spaces of different functional type as well as sets described using simple closed formulas. Our work makes use of a concept known as Lipschitz selection, allowing us to draw conclusions about mappings from spaces of different dimensionality to spaces of lower dimensionality. This approach proves to be versatile, as demonstrated through the derivation of a variety of independent results. Our analysis also touches upon the concept of stability with respect to simple mappings, as well as the properties of spaces formed by combinations of basic spaces, illustrating these concepts through a variety of examples.

The concept of n-tuples with low transitivity scores has gained interest, particularly 16-tuples with a score of 15, which have become a focus of study. A more general study is conducted to establish a unified approach for understanding these restricted n-tuples. A method is devised to calculate the maximum possible number of elements in these restricted n-tuples and this value is determined for 16-tuples, resolving the supersong conjecture. The method is then applied to compute the values for 17 and 19-tuples. Furthermore, the study introduces a broader class of restricted n-tuples, denoted as K[n,k], and computes the largest possible size of this family.

Optimizing software performance by eliminating unnecessary settings is a proven strategy, but detecting unused settings at scale can be challenging. This paper introduces an innovative approach to identify unused parameters in complex software systems, involving dynamic analysis coupled with static exploration. It also discusses the implementation of an associated tool, providing empirical evidence for its effectiveness and performance. This tool has successfully identified unused settings in notable open-source projects, including Apache Kafka and Elasticsearch.

Future large-scale experiments such as the Large Underground Xenon experiment may be able to detect dark matter by recognizing tiny changes in ionisation levels resulting from its interaction with atomic nuclei. While the detection of spin-dependent or coherent dark matter-nucleon interactions is possible, the detection of pure dark matter-nucleus interactions is unlikely due to the small nuclear spin or isospin. However, even though the nuclear spin or isospin is small, the total cross-section can still be significant due to the large mass of the nucleus. Therefore, it is worthwhile to investigate whether the detection of pure dark matter-nucleus interactions is feasible. In the first place, we have established a uniform formulation to calculate recoil and ionisation effects resulting from dark matter-nucleus interactions. In double-beta decay experiments such as the ALP project or the NUCIFER experiment, the detection of pure dark matter-nucleus interactions may be within reach, given that the nucleus recoils and electrons are simultaneously measured. On the other hand, the ionisation effects are too small to be detected by the Large Underground Xenon experiment, even though it has the capability to measure ionisation levels accurately. In the future, the detection of pure dark matter-nucleus interactions may become feasible in high-purity experiments such as the SENSEI experiment, provided that the sensitivity reaches the level of $10^{-41}$ cm$^2$ for spin-independent or coherent interactions.

This research explores entangled anti-polariton qubits as carriers for quantum information, employing entangled states of spin phonon modes within polariton condensates for quantum teleportation. Our model demonstrates that utilizing entangled anti-polariton qubits can enhance the fidelity of quantum teleportation compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, we identify two possible approaches to generating these entangled states, namely adiabatic changes in resonance and the application of external resonant light.

Our solution involves the application of deep learning to accurately extract
heart rhythm patterns from ECG signals, effectively addressing a challenge in
cardiovascular disease detection and monitoring. A sophisticated approach using
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for inter-beat interval detection has been
developed, capable of handling ECG signals with varying lengths. This method
iteratively estimates rhythm patterns from downsampled signals, ultimately refining
the accuracy of its predictions. Moreover, a novel adaptation of the back-propagation algorithm during training enables the network to adjust its sample rate. As a result, this method requires no pre-training or initial length specification. Additionally, we employed an enhanced strategy using batch normalization for input data normalization. Our technique demonstrated exceptional performance at the 2017 Challenge in Healthcare Systems, matching or surpassing the performance of top teams in ECG signal processing, despite them employing more complex algorithms and multiple neural networks.

We've investigated the fluctuations of active force systems with both harmonic and anharmonic potentials, and found a distinctive difference in how their fluctuations behave. In the case of harmonic potentials, the fluctuations remain constant, independent of the system's state, whereas anharmonic systems, however, exhibit fluctuations that vary significantly with the system's configuration. Notably, in the absence of active force parameters, these fluctuations would reduce to a constant, as predicted by the fluctuation dissipation theorem. Interestingly, our findings show that, when comparing systems with different levels of activity but identical equilibrium positions, the fluctuations often exhibit a linear relationship. This discovery bears resemblance to the additive principle, yet it's essential to note that the fluctuations we're analyzing are not additive in a literal sense. Furthermore, when considering systems with anharmonic potentials where only the potential itself remains constant, the fluctuations do indeed add up in a linear manner.

We introduce HUMBI, a comprehensive dataset optimized for fitting human faces,
to enhance the precision of three-dimensional modeling of human expressions.
The dataset consists of 280,000 high-resolution images captured with
headphones and 2500 faces with accurate mesh models, annotations for
fitting challenges, and proposed modeling tasks. Our evaluation reveals that
HUMBI outperforms other human face datasets on modeling tasks, particularly
in fitting complicated cases. The method also demonstrates significant
improvements in enhancing photorealism. Our partnership with major tech
companies has yielded successful applications of HUMBI in accelerating the
development of photorealistic, 3D human faces, facilitating the creation
of movie special effects and promoting research in the field of 3D human
faces.

In this study, we propose a multilingual training framework that enables a single model to function across multiple languages while meeting the requirements of being language and task specific. To overcome the challenges of multilingual training, we've developed a data augmentation approach called high-energy phoneme text replacement (HEPter) that leverages the power of deep voice models. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of HEPter in creating phonetic similar speech data for enhancing model performance. Furthermore, we've investigated the potential of reducing energy costs associated with multilingual training by analyzing the spectral energy distributions of generated spectra. Our findings suggest that multilingual models can be trained more efficiently with lower energy spectra. Our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot cross-lingual speech translation tasks in languages such as Spanish, Russian, and Hindi, and also outperforms baseline models in English by a significant margin.

The video super-resolution problem involves increasing video resolution without losing frame rate, a crucial task in video enhancement. Our approach, BasicVSR++, outperforms previous solutions by leveraging additional ideas and implementing a more efficient process. We incorporate a wider range of ideas, including improved motion estimation, refined optical flow calculation, refined interpolation methods, and a simplified and more efficient architecture, achieving higher super-resolution quality and faster processing speed. Compared to BasicVSR, BasicVSR++ achieves higher accuracy, reduces computational cost, and achieves better domain adaptation, in addition to being easier to implement. Our results show improvements in precision and efficiency, with a significant 0.64% improvement in PSNR and a 2.88x speed increase over BasicVSR on the Vid4 and V9 datasets, with even better performance on the larger LSR, LSR-Tech, and RealSR datasets.

In at least two existing solutions for multi-task reinforcement learning using model-based policy optimization, a single dynamics model is learned and then shared across all tasks. However, this can lead to performance degradation due to the dynamic model being optimized for different tasks. To address this, we focus on multi-task reinforcement learning with multiple dynamics models. Our approach involves using a set of the best-performing dynamics models in policy optimization. To identify these models, we select scenarios in which the policy and dynamics models are closely matched and use this information to determine which dynamics models to utilize. Our method has been tested on multiple examples and outperforms the alternative strategy of using a single, shared dynamics model.

In a scenario where a system operates at equilibrium under the influence of two heat reservoirs with distinct temperatures, the concept of a scaled system is introduced, where the output power is nonlinearly related to the scaling parameter $\lambda$. For a particular engine model, the maximum output power is examined in terms of the scaling parameter, and it's found that the thermodynamic efficiency is also dependent on $\lambda$. However, the most efficient and maximal output power values do not solely rely on the scaling parameter, as they're influenced by the system's geometric properties. The introduction of a scaling parameter $\lambda$ also enables the extension of the Atwood number, which is typically restricted to positive values, to include negative values. This extension is achieved by defining the acceleration of the weights in the incline plane, where the gravity vector is modulated by the scaling parameter.

This research focuses on using historical hurricane data to evaluate the impact of hurricanes on power grids. To accomplish this, it incorporates an advanced hurricane model that utilizes GIS technology to generate virtual hurricane paths. Additionally, it establishes a methodology to create wind and debris loads maps throughout the hurricane-stricken area. To assess the hurricane's effect on the power grid, it employs probabilistic techniques to determine the likelihood of trees and power lines failing. This is paired with a novel approach to calculate the likelihood of generator outages and system transmission losses due to wind and debris impacts. To facilitate rapid analysis, it utilizes high-performance computing and parallel processing methods. This study presents results analyzing the potential impact of 17 historical hurricanes on the PowerADEC grid.

This text supplements the original paper by 'Mapping Multivariate Functions' (2021), where the authors explored connecting multivariate functional equations with algebraic objects called hypercomplex numbers. In this update, we delve into a specific type of equation involving the multiplication operation. The update starts with an examination of how Hadamard's three circles theorem describes the monogenic properties of functions in higher dimensions. Next, we investigate a particular type of hypercomplex number system that enables the extension of functions to higher dimensions while preserving linearity. The update continues by analyzing a type of functional equation that involves an additive operation and concludes by considering a type of equation that involves both multiplication and addition operations. Throughout the update, we highlight relevant connections and contrast our approach with similar work by Lutscovic and Pommerance.

We introduce a novel family of piecewise affine transformations on the set of
finite words over an alphabet of size m, partitioning the set into coding spaces
corresponding to various systems of normal ordered words. The map's structure allows
it to be represented as a matrix representation, where the matrix entries are
determined by pairs of letters from a predefined alphabet. The study of these
spaces reveals two primary methods for specifying infinite words, leading to the
identification of coding spaces for well-matched systems, ultimately demonstrating
that these spaces mirror the characteristics of the Dyck system for any letter
alphabet of size m greater than or equal to 2.

Future high-energy colliders will serve as an ideal testing ground for the Conserved Vector Current (CVC) symmetry, a key principle derived from the Electroweak Symmetry Breaking mechanism. To fully appreciate CVC, it is crucial to understand the interplay between Higgs boson physics and the extended scalar sector of particle physics models. In this research, we investigate how the CVC symmetry is preserved in the Doublet Extension of the Standard Model (DES) scalar sector, focusing on the Doublet Triplet Extension of the Standard Model (DT) and the Triplet Extension of the Standard Model (TS) with varying scalar masses. Our study shows that the Higgs boson coupling is consistently modified in a similar way in both DT and TS models, whereas the $W$ and $Z$ boson couplings are affected differently. In contrast, the $t$-channel Higgs boson production process displays a linear combination of the Higgs boson and the additional scalar particle contributions, which can serve as a valuable indicator of the CVC symmetry. If the additional scalar particle is heavy, the $t$-channel process primarily reflects the Higgs boson coupling to $W$ and $Z$ bosons. However, when the additional scalar particle is light, the $t$-channel process exhibits a significant blend of the Higgs boson and the additional scalar particle couplings.
